The success of cancer immunotherapy depends on understanding the interactive processes
between tumor cells and the lymphatic system. To gain insights into this complex
phenomenon, researchers analyze digitized tissue sections with computer models,
focusing on the morphology of lymphocytes within the tumor environment. This project
assesses the performance of four advanced computer vision methods to enhance the
accurate representation of lymphocytes, evaluating their capability in reconstructing
lymphocyte shapes and distinguishing them from other tissue elements. Results
indicating low precision levels prompted the development of an alternative approach
combining regional growth with topological transformations to adapt existing image
segmentation models for analyzing lymphocytes. This approach showed a notable gain
in precision, rising from 0.78 to 0.88, thus providing a valuable asset for
further cancer immunology research. The source code is available online at https://github.com/alevini/Lymphocyte-Analysis. To mitigate burst errors in high-speed optical communication systems, a method is proposed that combines Equalization using Weighted Least Squares and Minimum Likelihood Sequence Estimation. Initially, a weighted decision feedback equalizer is designed to reduce the impact of rapid channel fluctuations, after which the MLSE estimator refines the output to correct burst errors. A method is suggested to concurrently optimize the equalizer and estimator parameters. Furthermore, simulations in a 56 Gbit/s optical transmission system demonstrate a significant reduction in burst errors, with the optimal performance achieved when the equalizer and estimator are optimized concurrently. Nonetheless, it is also shown that a suboptimal solution can be found more efficiently using an iterative algorithm that alternates between optimizing equalizer and estimator parameters. This method reduces the computational burden by a factor of 5 without compromising on performance. The proposed method is also applicable to other communication systems affected by time-varying channels and burst errors. Time-series predictions are often made with temporal convolutional networks (TCNs), which simplify the complexity of previous models while reducing memory usage. However, TCNs typically require significant model sizes to achieve accurate results. In this study, we introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that increases model efficiency by taking advantage of dilation techniques. Our optimizer gradually expands a network's dilation factors over epochs, allowing for larger model training within memory constraints. This approach enables the creation of larger models that, once trained, can be inferred efficiently due to inherent sparse computations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our automatic dilation optimizer by successfully applying it to various TCN tasks, including weather forecasting and electrical activity prediction. Our results show that our optimizer yields a three-fold increase in model size, resulting in enhanced accuracy and outperforms alternative compression methods. Furthermore, our dilated TCN model exhibits inferior inference latency to compact, efficient models but surpasses them in accuracy. The success of this approach indicates that efficient deep learning models should be defined by performance on large datasets rather than shallow, optimized versions. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/hjdwq/ADO.

We introduce a novel framework known as Neural Descriptor Fields that uses a learning-based approach, enabling the acquisition of manipulation tasks through few demonstration examples. By utilizing a hierarchical structure combining object description and task-specific feasibility checks, this framework efficiently exploits both high-dimensional demonstration data and subtle success/failure differences. The introduction of a hierarchical loss function and an optimization technique for relative optimality helps minimize demonstrations required for the learning process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our Neural Descriptor Fields model can also be an effective data generation tool, capable of producing numerous demonstration variations from a single example. These generated demonstrations can, in turn, be utilized to teach the same or a different model to perform the same manipulation task. Our method is evaluated through a series of experiments utilizing a multi-A-arm robot in a complex workspace, where it successfully masters multiple independent manipulation tasks with both real and virtual setups. The code is available at https://github.com/lingido/Neural-Descriptor-Fields.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands in the Higgs sector and studies of QCD. The SiD's calorimeter system consists of a highly granular and compartmentalized design, read by fine and coarse readout cells, which essentially contributes $0.35\%$ jet energy resolution across various jet sizes and energies. Furthermore, despite being fully integrated into the detector, the calorimeter system can still achieve excellent performance in hadronic W-boson decays discrimination capability, exceeding the required 5$\sigma$ benchmark. This demonstration highlights the effectiveness of optimised calorimeter design in detecting energy and direction in hadronic events. In addition, the detector's MIP timing capability, achieved through the SiD's calorimeter system, enables the measurement of timing in minimum ionizing particles, thus facilitating the identification of prompt gamma detection. The implementation of this feature, however, necessitates the integration of an additional 40 MHz readout channel per fine cell. The resulting calorimeter system in the SiD detector delivers exceptional performance in jet resolution, hadronic decays discrimination and the detection of prompt photons, all of which are critical functions for the study of the Higgs boson and other fundamental physics phenomena. The underlying design of the SiD's calorimeter system also serves as a viable template for other future ILC detectors. The detailed design of the SiD's calorimeter system highlights the effective integration of compartmentalized calorimeter modules, read by various readout cells, contributing to the detector's ability to achieve precise jet energy resolution and hadronic decays discrimination. The design's compartmentalized structure facilitates simple integration of the additional fine cell 40 MHz readout channel, enabling the measurement of timing in minimum ionizing particles, crucial for the detection of prompt gamma. The resulting design successfully addresses the caloric requirements for the study of the Higgs boson and other fundamental physics in the ILC. This finding, resulting from the CADES spectrograph on the Guillermo Haro telescope, reveals a level of metallicity similar to that found in the richest globular clusters such as M22, specifically a reading of -0.84 d[Fe/H]d-1. Notably, two rare elements, strontium and carbon, have never before been measured at such high levels in a metal-rich globular cluster member. We propose a novel, efficient framework for modeling complex real-world scenarios and accurately determining object poses within them. This includes pinpointing objects that are partially hidden, existing in multiple dimensions, and confronting the problem of partial visibility. Our method divides projection groups to mitigate the negative effects of partial objects on pose detection and streaming neural networks for each group, thereby enhancing overall performance. This technique not only raises accuracy but also offers a computationally efficient solution, minimizing the necessity for highly trained global models. Unlike current approaches that rely on generating images from 2D heatmaps, our method directly predicts 3D coordinate points, thereby minimizing the discrepancy between synthetic and real images. Moreover, our framework compares favorably to the state of the art in open-world 3D object pose estimation, outperforming existing models despite processing only half of the data. However, with slightly adjusted parameters, it matches the performance achieved by models with access to the entire dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/hjdwu/projgroup.

We have developed a new optimization technique, called Generalized Graphical Lasso, which expands the well-known Graphical Lasso framework by incorporating latent variables. By including an explicit representation of the graph, we can now estimate both the original and latent variables' precision matrices while maintaining their separation. Notably, our approach surpasses previous methods in terms of model flexibility and interpretability. Furthermore, our GC Lasso model adapts the standard Banding and Sparsifying (BS) structure for graph structures and enables structured sparsity in precision matrices, facilitating structured variable selection. To address computational challenges, we implemented an efficient and reliable interior-point algorithm for our optimization problem. Through both theoretical and practical evaluations, our algorithm demonstrates fast convergence and consistency with increasing sample sizes. Additionally, our results show that our algorithm performs better than alternative methods in terms of mean squared error, especially for larger datasets. All our algorithms are implemented in Python and available on GitHub under an permissive license. Moreover, the R and Python packages for our Generalized Graphical Lasso are also openly accessible on GitHub. We investigated the influence of numerical accuracy and method complexity from moderate to high-level coupled cluster theories on computational time and accuracy in simulations of the alanine dipeptide fragment using a combined quantum-classical approach. Our assessments utilized four different methods: MM, DFT, RASSF, and CC. Results showed that increasing numerical accuracy leads to longer computation times and greater impact on CC simulations compared to classical molecular mechanics. Nonetheless, even the most accurate methods failed to achieve a 1 ps timescale for relaxation of a specific dihelical state. Our findings emphasize the importance of balancing numerical complexity and precision in quantum-classical simulations, depending on the system at hand and goal of the study. Furthermore, we found that even methods with substantial deviations from full accuracy, such as RASSF, can effectively support efficient quantum-classical simulations by minimizing errors in potential energy surfaces and ensuring overall computational feasibility. We also introduced a new benchmark to evaluate the performance of quantum chemical methods in simulation of local quantum dynamics and suggest it as a standard tool for assessing numerical techniques within the field. Lastly, we created an open-source code based on our previous recommendations and known experience for quantum-classical simulations, titled QCSimPack, which is now available on GitHub. This code includes scripts for our experiments described in this study and can be adapted to fit various numerical approaches. The developers invite the scientific community to contribute to and make use of this package for fair comparison of quantum chemical methods in simulation of local quantum dynamics. The code can be found at https://github.com/ihmgroup/QCSimPack and is openly available for community contribution and use. This paper offers new insights into a critical aspect of cavity surface seals in turbomachines, specifically the impact ring that forms at the end of the seal. Previous research primarily focused on traditional (high-speed) cavity flows, but modern cavities with reduced pressure often exhibit significantly different behavior. To address this, we conducted an in-depth analysis using a multi-body fluid dynamics approach, combining computational fluid dynamics with a tracking method for solid components. By applying this method to a comprehensive parameter survey, we obtained a broad range of results that helped us identify key factors influencing impact ring behavior. Our findings show that as the impact speed increases, the pressure within the cavity decreases, leading to enhanced ripple effects on the seal surface. Furthermore, our results reveal how the shape of the cavity and the impact angle contribute to various impact ring patterns, including the formation of secondary rings in response to lateral barriers. Additionally, we developed a simplified mathematical model that predicts the frequency of the impact ring's oscillations. By applying this model to our results, we identified a clear distinction between fluid-driven and solid-component-driven frequencies across various speeds. Moreover, we investigated how different speeds, ratios of edge velocities, and fluid-solid frequency ratios affect the shape and size of the impact ring. Our study provides a deeper understanding of impact ring dynamics and their interaction with cavity flows, shedding light on potential areas for further improvement in cavity surface seal design. Ultimately, our research paves the way for more effective cavity optimization techniques.

We present a novel algorithm for identifying polymers within medical imaging data.
Currently, polymer detection is typically achieved through probability-based approaches.
Our method treats polymers as unique entities linked by monomer connections, inferring
their presence and relationships in a joint process. This involves formulating region
propagation as a process that respects local probability distributions, allowing us
to utilize existing image segmentation techniques. The proposed algorithm succeeds
a series of tests, demonstrating its capacity to accurately detect polymers even
in complex scenarios. Furthermore, our method offers a high level of efficiency,
enabling real-time polymer detection from scratch. To further enhance performance,
we explore the potential benefits of incorporating prior knowledge about polymer
characteristics. The approach we present has the potential to significantly impact
the development of future medical imaging applications, especially those involving
microscopic imaging, by making sensitive and accurate polymer detections more
feasible. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/ultrasonics-team/poly
meric_detection.

The current crisis resulting from the global pandemic crisis has caused significant pressure on health systems, which have responded by conserving essential resources such as ventilators. Conserving these life-support machines has involved diverting treatment for patients who are no longer critically ill but still require assistance breathing. We have investigated methods for patients to be ventilated using a single ventilator, ensuring they receive their desired tidal volume without breath stacking or insufficient oxygen exchange. This study focuses on asymptotic conditions and compares methods for assigning inspiratory pause time, examining the impact of pressure-time product, ventilator rate, and compliance on optimal pause time predictions. We found that the optimal pause time can be anticipated through a first-order approximation and validated this approach through simulation testing. This study's findings provide a theoretical basis for optimizing ventilator usage and ensuring adequate oxygen exchange for multiple patients on a single machine. Furthermore, we propose potential clinical trials to test these predictions in real-world settings.

This paper introduces a novel attention-unstructured model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which achieves high accuracy in esophageal tumor segmentation. By leveraging dense attention mechanisms and spatially diluted convolutional layers, the network is able to effectively extract visual features and operate on high-resolution images. We utilize a modified unstructured decoding scheme to produce a detailed, precision tumor mask. The algorithm is trained using an augmented esophageal image dataset, which we have openly shared for the benefit of the medical imaging community. Through extensive experiments, our method demonstrates a remarkable capacity for generalization and consistency with conventional tumor segmentation techniques. Notably, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet outperforms top-performing competing networks and expert pathologists in tumor segmentation accuracy. Additionally, we evaluate the model's generalization performance on unseen datasets and scenarios, showcasing its potential for application in real-world esophageal tumor segmentation scenarios. The code and dataset are available online at https://github.com/zhangzhitaoliang/DenseAttentionUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Real-time formation evaluation is crucial in oil and gas exploration and production operations.  However, the current industry standard, the Dynamic Data Section, is not real-time ready due to its slow computation.  To accelerate evaluation, we propose LM-EnRML, a new fastening technique that leverages machine learning models by integrating them with numerical approximation methods.  By combining deep neural networks with mathematical techniques such as tensor train decomposition, LM-EnRML significantly speeds up the calculation of complex well logs.  In testing against the industry standard, LM-EnRML achieved a 5 times performance boost on a single GPU.  Furthermore, LM-EnRML demonstrated precise results, with an average absolute error of less than 0.1 in comparison operations, and accurately captured critical features like permeability and gas saturation.  In validation scenarios with real data, LM-EnRML showed consistent, fast performance, with computation times reduced to less than 0.1 seconds on a CPU. This paper explores the potential of named entity recognition (NER) system enhancement via corpus-based knowledge. It challenges the conventional approach that NER systems are isolated systems. By incorporating corpus-level information, we discovered significant improvements in NER performance. Notably, the enhancement became more pronounced when dealing with lesser-labeled datasets. For example, on the FEA dataset with just 100 labeled samples, adding corpus knowledge boosted NER accuracy from 58.79% to 75.43%. Similarly, on the CLUENAMES dataset with only 500 labeled samples, NER accuracy increased from 75.08% to 85.43% after incorporating corpus-level information. However, the benefit began to wane with more extensively labeled datasets. The technique was found to be effective across various BERT-based NER models and datasets, showcasing its applicability and consistency. The method's simplicity is a significant advantage, requiring no training or additional resources beyond the NER model. In essence, this approach offers a highly effective way to boost the NER model's performance without relying on expensive data labeling. The code is openly accessible for further exploration and improvement. The technique's consistency is further underscored by the minimal gap between the baseline NER model and the enhanced version on the CoNEC named entity recognition benchmark, outperforming other state-of-the-art models by 1.35% while maintaining a similar number of parameters. The approach's effectiveness is attributed to the underlying characteristics of named entities, which are relatively stable and extensive in nature, differing from the transient aspects of language that NER models capture. Consequently, this technique has the potential to be a valuable tool in the NER field, enhancing model performance without complex data labeling processes. Consider a tropical quartic curve $X_t$ in the tropical rational plane $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\text{rap}}$, along with a tropical hyperplane $H_t$ of degree $d$. The corresponding classical hyperplane intersects the classical quartic curve $X$ at rational points if and only if their tropical counterparts meet in the rational sector of the twisted edge bounding the classical curve. This rationality condition fails to be a one-to-one correspondence due to the presence of extra rational points on the classical curve. As a result, the number of $d$-tangents to $X$ is not simply $d$ times the number of $d$-tangents to $X_t$. Instead, the latter exceeds the former by the number of $d$-tangents to $X_t$ that become rational points in the classical context. Consequently, the total number of $d$-tangents to $X$ is the sum of the number of $d$-tangents to $X_t$ and the number of classical points with $d$ multiplicities. Similarly, tropicalizations can be used to establish a formula for the number of secants to $X$, albeit one that relies on the rationality of certain twisted edges. Notably, the complexity of hyperplanes in tropical geometry significantly surpasses that of secants or $d$-tangents, given a suitable choice of coordinates. Thus, our coordinate choice enables us to present a simplified expression for the number of secants to $X$. This expression reflects the influence of all twisted edges, regardless of their relevance to classical rational points or point components. Moreover, it incorporates the rationality condition for Ginzburg-Kausz domain walls in the tropical rational plane. Furthermore, our analysis introduces the concept of a twisted edge being rationally embedded (not just in the classical context but also in the tropical one), along with the associated condition for a domain wall to become a secant in the classical context. Our study therefore offers an innovative perspective on the twisted edges within the tropical rational plane, one that considers the rationality of both classical and tropical points. This research is an offshoot of an unrelated investigation into the geometry of tropical quartic curves, with a specific focus on the edge twisting that arises when projecting such curves onto a tropical hyperplane. It is worth noting that the classical geometry associated with the twisted edges has highly rational components, despite those components being fundamentally important in the context of tropical geometry.

The diverse languages and cultures within multilingual societies pose an interesting challenge for NLP researchers. To enhance cross-language understanding, we propose using emotional intelligence. We examine the current state of NLP systems' emotional awareness, taking a comprehensive view that encompasses the feelings of individuals within a culture and their anticipated reactions to NICE actions. To tackle this complex issue, we suggest a more effective approach involves combining two methods: developing multilingual emotional knowledge bases and utilizing machine learning to recognize emotional language in NLP contexts. To illustrate this approach in action, we created a dataset and a sample system for an exemplary scenario—detecting emotional language in restaurant reviews. Ultimately, our research aims to inspire further exploration of emotional intelligence in multilingual NLP systems, with potential applications in various areas, such as enhancing customer experience through personalized service recommendations or NICE product reviews that promote cultural understanding. We have made our proposed methodology and data available for public use at the link provided. The growing popularity of camera phones and social media has made image sharing abundant, with most posts including descriptive captions. These descriptions hold significant value, being a crucial bridge between visual data and meaningful text. However, the proliferation of visual content outpaces the development of efficient image description tools, primarily handicapped by limited, high-quality training datasets. The absence of standardized production guidelines among users with good image understanding abilities further hinders progress. It is evident that certain descriptions, although clear in context, lack usefulness for simple search purposes. The absence of precise guidelines for description generation leads to inconsistent results, making it harder to utilize models for real-world applications. In this research, we focus on developing methods to enhance description quality, first through the use of additional visual information and context, followed by a discussion of production best practices. To evaluate these approaches, we introduce the Conceptual Vocabulary Distillation task, aiming to tame the vast visual vocabulary by selecting relevant concepts for search bar suggestions. The proposed methods, including a novel Beta Variational Encoder-Deccoder model, achieve significant gains - approximately 15% improvement in semantic similarity and 10% in visual concept accuracy. These advances hold promise for better description quality, especially when combined with best practices for description generation. The research is supported by extensive experimentation and evaluation across the Flickr10k Dataset, along with further analysis of user-generated caption datasets. The proposed methods and evaluation protocols are openly available, paving the way for improved image description models that better align with search bar concepts and facilitate more effective description production. Unlike conventional methods that assume independence between adjacent units in a periodic system, our approach also takes into account the influence of neighboring units on the Ta atoms at the center of the system. Through comparison with experimental data obtained through electron energy loss spectroscopy, we've determined that both the proximity of adjacent units and the interaction of electrons with the spin-orbit effect have a significant impact on the calculation of the energy loss function, and that they should not be disregarded. Our study has further revealed that the proximity of adjacent units has a major impact on the distribution of electronic states at the high-energy end, while the spin-orbit effect has a greater influence on the filling of these states. Based on the results obtained, we're able to explain the experimental observation that tantalum oxides exhibit a significant variation in the filling of high-energy states when in isolation, but when part of a periodic system, they resemble isolated Ta atoms only when the proximity of adjacent units is taken into consideration. Our study has additional implications for the understanding of other periodic systems consisting of atoms at the center and surrounding atoms. We investigate the complex interconnections between speech generated during teaching by observing others by observing others and infer what is being said to them. Variations in learning settings, with different demonstration types, audio instructions, subtasks, and error levels, affect the concepts conveyed in speech. We explore and analyze the effects of these variations on speech-generated concepts in English, French, and Spanish, using speech data from six tasks. Our findings show significant fluctuations in concepts within each language, across languages, and when combining all languages. These concepts can be both accurate and incorrect, single words or phrases, and common sense-based or domain-specific. Our research identifies considerable variations in concept generation in each setting, with significant differences when varying demonstration types, subtasks, and error levels, and relatively stable concept distributions when using different audio instructions. We also examine the relationships between speech-generated concepts and their corresponding learning tasks, demonstrating that these concepts often align with task elements, including objects, actions, subtasks, and error contents. Our work lays the groundwork for further study into the relationships among these concepts, their meanings, and how they evolve during the learning process. Researchers explored the capabilities of existing and future large-scale telescopes by investigating how well they can detect the gravitational influence of massive objects of various masses, such as planets and spacecraft, affecting the motion of stars. Using existing telescopes such as the Hubble, a hypothetical Earth-sized object could only be detected within 0.01 parsecs, but more sensitive future telescopes like the James Webb may be able to detect it at 90% of the sky at a distance of approximately 0.3 parsecs, or about 0.08 light-years, or about 4.5 trillion miles. The team found that even with advanced telescopes, it may take up to 20 years to observe the gravitational effect of a massive asteroid the size of a small city, but a spacecraft like the International Resource Identification (IRI) system, which is anticipated to have a mass of around 3600 kilograms, might be detectable over 90% of the sky at a distance of around 0.13 parsecs, or about 0.03 light-years, or about 1.7 trillion miles, in as few as 5-10 years. The study suggests that with advanced telescopes, it may be possible to monitor the motion of stars in the galaxy and identify areas where massive objects should be present, potentially leading to the discovery of unobservable objects like dark matter. The research also considers alternative methods of detecting massive objects, such as analyzing the gravitational effect on the motion of binary star systems, but finds them to be less effective than the stellar dynamics approach. The study includes a mathematical model that takes into account various factors, such as the mass of the object, its distance from the telescope, and how long it takes to observe its effect, but finds that the most influential factor is the object's mass, with a powerful object with a massive impact on motion being detectable at a greater distance than one with a relatively small effect. The research identifies several large-scale telescopes with the potential to conduct this type of observation, but notes that future generations of telescopes, such as the Large Wide-field Infrared Survey (LEVI), may be even more suitable for this kind of research. The study concludes by suggesting potential modifications to existing spacecraft that could make them detectable in a similar way, such as adding a heavy solid object to a satellite in orbit around the Earth. The work also considers the potential for detecting other types of massive objects, such as floating nuclear reactors, but finds them not feasible with current or proposed telescopes.

Recent analyses suggest that certain anomalous patterns found in the Cosmic Microwave Background are indicative of theories involving the creation of mini-black-holes and fractal universe structures. Nonetheless, these findings are remarkably insensitive to the presence of Hawking points and low-variance circles due to the large fluctuation ranges they encompass. Nonetheless, if we restrict our attention to more modestly sized fluctuations, the signals related to Hawking points and low-variance circles could potentially become visible. Furthermore, it is anticipated that the arrival of next-generation CMB experiments will facilitate the identification of these features. Nonetheless, it is also possible that alleged signals of this nature will be found to be artifacts of inadequate data analysis methods. In order to determine the likelihood of the former occurring, it is necessary to develop methods for evaluating the consistency of CMB signals with the existence of Hawking points and low-variance circles. In this research, a suite of tools tailored towards identifying distinctive patterns in CMB data is introduced, and the ability of these methods to detect hints of new physics under fluctuation constraints is demonstrated. Deep learning-based recommendation models have experienced rapid growth, achieving high performance on various tasks including user preference prediction. Most current approaches focus on extracting unique feature representations from images, audio, and text, but they fail to consider the underlying aspects that are crucial for understanding users' preferences. Inspired by recent aspect-aware advances in natural language processing, we introduce the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, an innovative module that automatically identifies aspects from input data and generates aspect-aware embeddings to enhance user preference prediction. We further integrate the GAPE module with existing deep learning baselines to evaluate its effectiveness in multi-modal recommendation tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in prediction accuracy and aspect detection accuracy. The experimental results show that our proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art multi-modal recommendation models at the user level and achieves superior aspect detection performance compared to aspect-aware models in natural language processing. Moreover, we highlight the merits of the GAPE module's aspect detection ability and provide the code for the GAPE module at the following link: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMAS/tree/main/gape. Albeit introducing additional parameters, the GAPE module enhances user preference prediction and aspect detection accuracy in various real-world datasets, highlighting its potential as a pioneering aspect-aware multi-modal recommendation approach. Recent research by Fiori, Lauro, and Peron enhances our understanding of the relationship between natural formulations featuring exotic cones and their complex extended counterparts. The study also establishes a direct formulation complexity connection for both circular and elliptical forms, showing it's comparable to the complexity of their own extended counterparts. A common challenge encountered by medical AI models is limited diversity in their training datasets. This study investigates how models' performance is affected by the diversity of their training sets when applied to unfamiliar MRI images. We used a large dataset containing over 300,000 MRI images and employed a mathematical measure of diversity called entropy to assess the diversity of the training sets. Our findings show that as the diversity of the training set increases, the model's performance also improves and eventually reaches an optimal point before declining. Additionally, we discovered that models are robust to different types of scan distributions, such as anatomical location and acquisition protocol, and can perform well on unseen combinations of these factors with a small margin of error. However, models are susceptible to significant errors when confronted with shots they have not been trained on, indicating a substantial gap in this domain. This research suggests that enhancing the diversity of clinical datasets through data combination can be an effective strategy to improve model performance and robustness. However, it also raises concerns about the potential increase in required training data, processing power, and label collection, along with the need for more advanced models that can fully capitalize on diverse data. As a result, further research is necessary to fully unlock the potential of high-diversity medical AI models. A comprehensive study of heavy quark interactions within QCD has been conducted, resulting in a detailed examination of the properties of heavy mesons. This research, based on lattice QCD, explored the behavior of quark pairs that create vector and scalar mesons consisting of heavy quarks, specifically top, bottom, and charm quarks. Calculations were performed for multiple quark separations, ranging from approximately 0.4 to 2.0 times the size of the lattice's spacing, and involved analyzing the correlations between quark pairs to determine the masses and percentages of contribution of each quark to the system. Findings were compared to established theoretical models, and predictions were made about the behavior of quark pairs as the lattice's spacing changes. Additionally, research into the spin structure of heavy quarks revealed their contribution to the system, and results were analyzed for different lattice sizes and quark separations. This study provides a thorough understanding of the interactions within heavy quark systems and quark-gluon plasma. A notable observation from the research was that the charm quark's behavior differs from that of the top and bottom quarks, and the disappearance of the charm quark's charmonium-like behavior at larger distances. The study's findings on the spin structure of heavy quark systems show significant agreement with the MIT bag model's predictions. The research was conducted using $O(10^{5})$ configurations for each combination of lattice size, quark separation, and spin structure configuration, and involved multiple ensembles of unconnected gauge fields for reducing statistical errors. The study's results will contribute significantly to the development of theories that explain the behavior of heavy quark systems and quark-gluon plasma. The selection of object detectors depends greatly on the specific task requirements at hand. This paper proposes a novel approach that is universally applicable and doesn't need specific object detection algorithms. By redefining object detection as a general pattern recognition task, our approach uses a simple and consistent formulation to evaluate all object detectors. Our method generates an idealized object detector, serving as a reference point, which can be used to compare other detection algorithms. We then derive a formula to calculate the relative performance of each object detector in relation to the idealized detector. Our results show that the performance of all object detectors can be unified and ranked on the same scale, providing a more meaningful way to assess their performance. Furthermore, our approach enables us to measure the performance of each object detector in a context-free manner, allowing us to rank them independently of the specific task at hand. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing the performance of all common object detectors, including Faster R-CNN, Instance Mask R-CNN, Faster R-CNN with spatial pyramid pooling, and Extreme R-CNN, among others. Our code is openly available for public access.

This system is comprised of two form types: diagonalizable forms and nilpotent forms. By employing Algebraic Manipulation and field-theoretic properties, we establish the confluence of relevant forms, constructing a dynamic system to identify conjugacy classes. In order to provide relevant recommendations, a recommendation system needs entity representations that balance structure and content. For example, consider a search recommendation listing that includes both the name of a product and its category. The structure here refers to the relationships between entities (e.g., a product being part of a specific category) and the content refers to the distinct characteristics of entities (e.g., product names). While existing methods for learning entity representations typically focus solely on structure or content, we propose a novel approach that combines both aspects using a shared embedding structure. Specifically, our proposal includes a shared embedding for both structural and content information that is processed by separate multiplication matrices to obtain entity features. By converging both pathways with an additional attention mechanism, our approach achieves more accurate recommendations. We validate our proposal by creating multiple variations and comparing them to other established methods on three datasets, resulting in consistently superior performance according to both mean average precision and mean average recall. Additionally, we analyze the characteristics of our proposed approach by exploring aspects such as entity relationship distances, content word meanings, and category hierarchies, which demonstrates the method's general applicability to various recommendation tasks. We also provide practical recommendations for optimizing parameters and implementing our proposed approach, along with the benefits of combining both structure and content in entity representations. We have made our code publicly available to facilitate further research. The standard word2vec framework falls short in this regard, as it incorrectly views opposites as common synonyms when encountered frequently in similar contexts, particularly evident in financially-oriented text. This paper explores the long-term fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization in wideband waveforming, assuming a non-cooperative game model. The strategy for each player is determined by allocating bandwidth among the available communications modes, subject to a limited total bandwidth constraint. The "mode switching cost" and "bandwidth allocation" are distinguished to address this complex optimization problem. For each player, we formulate two strategies as variables, treating them as reactive decisions in response to others' actions. This leads to two potential solutions: (1) the strong player can achieve the optimal fair-throughput or sum-throughput by making the first move in a game, (2) the weak player can reach a Nash Equilibrium that favors their own fair-throughput or sum-throughput by making a second move in a game. To solve these problems, numerical examples are computed using simulated annealing due to the absence of closed-form expressions for the optimal solution. Although the Fourier method effectively addresses stability issues, it fails to capture the periodic pattern disruption that characterizes Rayleigh--Bénard instability in the early stages of development. In contrast, the Babakov expansion technique accurately models small perturbations in complex systems, but its slow convergence becomes a significant challenge for large-scale applications. To tackle this problem, we developed a hybrid method that combines the strengths of both techniques. By applying the Babakov expansion to represent the unstable mode and the Fourier method to analyze the stable base state, we can take advantage of the fast convergence of the Babakov expansion for the unstable solution while maintaining the ease of analysis provided by the Fourier method for the stable base state. Through this approach, we demonstrate a flexible method for adapting the Babakov expansion to the specific requirements of large-scale applications. In multiagent settings, agents can quickly discover actions that provide short-term benefits but ultimately lead to unfavorable outcomes through an action's elimination of competing options. This phenomenon, known as iterative dominance, accelerates the acceleration of agents towards suboptimal policies. To address this challenge, we propose a novel learning approach, where players receive an additional reward for selecting actions that are not repeatedly chosen in response. This additional reward serves as a cue for an extended range of actions, allowing players to learn an expanded set of desirable actions through imitation learning. By incorporating this cue, players can discover a significant number of undominated actions that provide long-term benefits, overcoming the barrier of selective equilibrium. Empirical studies confirm that this approach allows players to discover a major number of actions that are beneficial in the long term, surpassing the barrier of selective equilibrium, and compare our approach to alternative methods under changing conditions. A mathematical framework exists that describes how parton distribution functions (PDFs) adapt to changes in energy scales, known as the DGLAP equation. This study explores the consequences of introducing a non-linear mixing matrix into the DGLAP evolution equation, allowing for the fit of PDFs at multiple scales using a global analysis approach. We developed NNPDF GGlobal 1.0, a novel dataset that includes a range of observables at different energy scales, spanning from deep-inelastic scattering to linear colliders, and incorporates a DGLAP evolution framework. As a result, we were able to fit the PDFs to a degree of freedom that accounts for the uncertainties associated with the evolution, and in doing so, we gained insight into the structure of the non-linear matrix. Through this approach, we were also able to quantify the impact of the matrix on the evolution of PDFs, and found that it has a notable effect, particularly for the gluon distribution at higher scales. Furthermore, we were able to use NNPDF GGlobal 1.0 to analyze the properties of the non-linear matrix, and found that its eigenvalues display an oscillatory behavior as a function of the logarithmic scale, and that the corresponding eigenvectors exhibit distinct characteristics across different PDFs and energy scales. In the context of the DGLAP evolution, the development of a non-linear matrix with complex eigenvalues marks the beginning of a new phase in the understanding of PDFs, and as such, it will be important to continue exploring and refining this new perspective as more accurate data becomes available in the future. Additionally, we found that the properties of the non-linear matrix hold significant potential for further investigating the nature of QCD, and as such, we believe it is essential to continue developing theoretical frameworks that incorporate this matrix in a general form, in order to make the most of upcoming precision experiments at linear colliders, and to ensure that the true nature of QCD is understood through the study of PDFs. We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework for policy gradient reinforcement learning, which reversely sends the gradient information from the experience replay buffer to the policy update step. By explicitly controlling the bias and variance of the sampled gradient, our method achieves a balance between reducing the variance and increasing the bias to avoid the overfitting problem associated with the experience replay. Based on this framework, we provide a detailed analysis of the relationship between bias and variance, which provides users with relevant theoretical guidelines. By comparing our method to other state-of-the-art methods, the results show that VRER improves the performance and helps avoid overfitting when using a large experience replay buffer. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/zwang84/VRER.

Using high-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, we studied the superconducting gap in (Ba$_{0.37}$K$_{0.63}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ films at extremely low temperatures. Our analysis reveals a range of gap values from 0.1 eV to 0.43 eV, exhibiting complex distribution around the zone corner, and specifically, a smaller gap of 0.25 eV present at that location, distinctively different from the uniform gap distribution observed in iron-based superconductors near the zone center. Our findings support the theoretical model proposing a gap node at the zone corner through an electron-phonon interaction, and indicate that the superconducting state in (Ba$_{0.37}$K$_{0.63}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ is multi-band with varying gap sizes, providing quantitative data to constrain theoretical calculations of its superconducting state. Moreover, we discovered that the superconducting gap at the zone center can be modified by the crystal lattice through the Kohn-luttinger mechanism. Additionally, we observed the energy dependence of the gap at the zone corner, and the magnitude of the gap at the zone center after removing the lattice effect, both ranging from 0.1 eV to 0.3 eV, suggesting that the electron phonon interaction plays a significant role in the superconductivity in (Ba$_{0.37}$K$_{0.63}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$. 

Our study offers a direct evidence for the existence of gap node in (Ba$_{0.37}$K$_{0.63}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, and reveals the complexity of the superconducting state in this material, which is multifaceted, and varies significantly around the Brillouin zone corner and zone center, thereby offering a crucial opportunity to examine interaction between superconductivity and antiferromagnetism through spin-polarized study. 

Finally, we compared our findings with previous experimental results, showing a notable discrepancy, and indicating that the gap distribution may be heavily dependent on the specific measurement method, and possibly even the crystal lattice of the measurement system.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a new code utilizing the tree method to perform N-body simulations on large scales, specifically designed for evaluate the effectiveness of diverse gravitational physics scenarios. MG-GLAM succeeds Talen in incorporating efficient multigrid techniques and builds upon the computational framework established in GLAM. Unlike its predecessor, Talen is replaced by a modified version of the multigrid method that achieves significant speed improvements, with MG-GLAM now taking merely one-tenth of Talen's computation time. Additionally, MG-GLAM preserves the features that enable large-scale N-body simulations, such as nested iterations and highly accurate gravitational force calculations. As a result, MG-GLAM exhibits two orders of magnitude improvement in computational speed and is particularly suited for exploring a wide range of gravitational physics models through N-body simulations, specifically those involving large particle counts. As a proof of concept, we present N-body simulations utilizing MG-GLAM's multigrid method and an altered gravitational potential, specifically for ten different gravitational scenarios. As anticipated, the results show minimal distinguishable differences when comparing these scenarios to standard $N$-body simulations, for both one-dimensional cluster mergers and fully fledged N-body simulations of massive galaxy clusters. As such, MG-GLAM provides a crucial tool for investigating how diverse gravitational physics affects large-scale structure evolution. The border between two key types, Kelvin-Helmholtz waves and Rayleigh-Taylor bubbles, is determined by the star's acoustic-buoyant frequency, which varies depending on the star's rotation and gravity. This study explores how these waves and bubbles behave under strong magnetic stress in simulated models of pulsating stars. When the stress is turned on, Kelvin-Helmholtz waves quickly become unstable and break up, while Rayleigh-Taylor bubbles remain relatively stable, although they may still change shape. When the star rotates quickly, the Kelvin-Helmholtz waves can survive in the star's polar regions, and the buoyant frequency plays a less significant role in their behavior there. However, in slower-rotating stars, the waves' survival depends more strongly on the star's gravitational potential and the presence of magnetic stress. These findings have implications for the observation and interpretation of pulsating stars and can influence our understanding of how these stars are structured and how they generate magnetic stress. According to some theories, ultra-high energy photons could travel millions of meters through the atmosphere without being detected, leaving only cosmic rays in their wake. These cosmic rays would likely consist of multiple highly correlated particles, which we call "Ensembles of Cosmic Rays". We studied the ensembles that could potentially be created by these photons, using a Monte Carlo simulation to determine their spatial characteristics and likelihood of being detected. The simulation involved generating extensive air showers caused by photons with energies of up to 50 E18 GeV, where each energy level was modeled using a Monte Carlo approach. The resulting ensembles were analyzed in terms of their size, shape, location, and composition, which we used to develop a method for identifying ensembles generated by photons. This approach allows us to distinguish ensembles created by photons from those caused by cosmic rays composed of hadrons, which could have significant implications for experiments aimed at detecting photon air showers. Furthermore, we were able to establish criteria for detecting ensembles consisting of up to 10,000 particles, which would comprise the optimal strategy for identifying photon-created ensembles in experiments such as the Pierre Auger Observatory and future extensive air shower detectors. If such detectors are expanded to incorporate particle energy measurements, we show that ensembles created by photons could be directly identified with a confidence level of more than 99%. However, detecting the energy distribution within these ensembles is necessary to confirm the photon origin with the same level of confidence. Each modular unit would consist of 20-50 detectors with a diameter of approximately 4 meters, allowing for the simultaneous detection of ensembles consisting of up to 10,000 particles. Developing applications with distributed systems requires a robust foundation for ensuring data consistency across multiple nodes. Although research has progressed in the area of Replicated Data Types (RDTs), there is a noticeable lack in design frameworks specifically tailored for Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs). As a result, implementing RDTs from scratch can be challenging and prone to errors. To address this issue, our proposed framework, called Helios, provides a flexible and versatile design framework for building CRDTs. By offering various combinators and foundational components, Helios enables developers to create customized replication algorithms for CRDTs. Furthermore, the framework facilitates formal verification, allowing for the annotation of safety and liveness properties that can be proved through a combination of SMT solving and coverability analysis. By utilizing Helios, developers can build accurate models of their data types and replication algorithms, ensuring the consistency properties required by their applications are met. As a result, Helios can serve as an invaluable tool for researchers and developers working with CRDTs, and can contribute to the advancement of distributed systems. As proof of concept, the Helios framework has been implemented in the form of two well-known CRDTs: last-writer-wins registers and multi-value sets, and the framework is available online at its designated repository.

The relationship between proteins and genes is a fundamental concept in biology, where the properties of proteins ultimately shape the functioning of living organisms. Despite the significance of proteins, the sequence-based nature of genomics data poses a challenge for interpreting the effects of genetic variations on protein structure and function. To address this, we have developed a computational framework that utilizes protein sequences and structures to redefine the concept of functional sites within proteins. This framework, termed "Protein Functional Site Conservatism" (PFC), aggregates the effects of genetic variations on protein structure and function by identifying conserved functional sites across proteins, where variations have a similar effect on their own specific proteins as on PFC-identified sites. We have applied PFC to analyze the sources of variation in human phenotypes and found that protein sequences influence the effects of SNPs on trait variation, with the degree of this influence ranging from 5% to 90% across different traits. Furthermore, by focusing on the interactions between proteins and small molecules, we have demonstrated the potential of PFC to predict the effects of genetic variations on drug responses. The computational framework and underlying methodology for PFC are available for public access through our website at the specified URL.

Researchers suggest that some wide binary star systems contain hot, circumstellar material detected through mid-infrared observations. To understand the dynamics of these systems, researchers need to accurately measure the velocity dispersion within them. While previous studies have estimated one-dimensional velocity dispersion values, they were based on limited observations and tended to overestimate the actual values. To enhance measurement precision and utility for studying circumstellar material in these systems, a new approach to direct integration of observables from line widths and line strengths was developed. This approach utilizes a statistical model that incorporates prior knowledge about line widths in the form of minimum expected values in the analysis of multiple observed spectra from each system. The new method shows significant improvements in data fidelity compared to previous studies, resulting in more precise predictions of line widths and velocity dispersion values. To demonstrate this, the researchers applied this new approach to four widely separated binary systems that have large velocity dispersion values and suggested variations in line widths that could indicate the presence of interacting massive stars in these systems. However, no clear indication of such interactions was found in the analysis of the spectra. The new approach also produces more reliable estimates of line widths and velocity dispersion values than previous studies, yielding a two-fold improvement in measurement precision. The most significant improvements are observed in systems with the widest orbits and highest velocity dispersion values. Despite limited observations for three of the four systems, the new approach yielded more precise velocity dispersion values, ranging from 2.2 to 12.4 kilometers per second. The new method provides a useful tool for comparing the dynamics of massive star systems to predictions from theoretical models of their development. The line width analysis the researchers implemented is now an integral component of the MIRPLS catalog, featuring line width measurements for ten high-resolution, wide binary star systems selected for their suitability for studying massive star interactions. To further enhance the accuracy of these measurements and facilitate future comparisons with circulating gas predictions, the researchers advise obtaining additional high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio observations of these systems. The new approach to estimating velocity dispersion values has a broader application to any research involving the analysis of line widths in spectral observations, whether related to star systems or other celestial objects. Closed-loop control techniques are increasingly utilized in bipedal robots to enhance their mobility, yet their full potential remains unclear due to the limited extent of closed-loop feedback's impact being understood. To gain insight, we carried out a detailed analysis of a one-legged planar walking model, with a focus on the effects of closed-loop feedback during a single step cycle. By adjusting the closed-loop loop gain and feedback path, we evaluated how feedback influences the trajectory of the biped's foot and pelvis under various conditions. Our findings show that moderate closed-loop feedback can significantly improve the biped's performance, reducing pelvis oscillations and enabling the foot to follow a desired trajectory with accuracy. Nevertheless, excessive loop gain leads to instability, causing the biped to lose balance and fall over. Moreover, we discovered that feedback has a more substantial impact during the double-support phase than during the single-support phase. To optimize performance, we found that feedback should be activated only during the double-support phase. In summary, our study demonstrates the biped's sensitivity to closed-loop feedback and highlights its crucial role in achieving stable gait cycles. Furthermore, our findings suggest that a controller with proportional feedback can facilitate smooth transitions between step cycles, contributing to the biped's ability to maintain continuous walking motion. Building upon these conclusions, we propose future areas of research aimed at advancing closed-loop walking patterns and tackling the challenge of accelerating the biped from standstill. Through a combination of theoretical and experimental approaches, we aim to unlock the full potential of closed-loop control in bipedal robots. Ultimately, our ultimate goal is to develop a controller that, when paired with a suitable walking pattern, can succeed in accelerating the biped from rest through multiple gait cycles. This goal represents a significant milestone in the pursuit of creating a human-like bipedal robot capable of sustained walking.

This distinction addresses a question posed by R. Rumsewitz. We also establish that a power series field equipped with a total residue map is computationally equivalent to the field of formal Laurent series equipped with the ability to add infinitesimals, providing a connection between two distinct computational structures. Furthermore, we develop algorithms to conduct arithmetic operations and decide decidability in these structures. Additionally, we create a program that can execute these algorithms within the Coq proof assistant. We ultimately derive the implications of having an infinite field for the power series field's ability to make decisions, resulting in it becoming undecidable. We also explore how the presence of infinitesimals facilitates the recovery of the power series field's original properties. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of the power series field to the study of real analytic functions and maps.

Open-source software for matrix computations like BLAS and LINPACK has long been the standard for machine-specific optimizations, setting the bar for benchmarking computer performance according to their performance in these operations. However, with the growing speed and processing power provided by Multi-Processing (MP) and Multi-Threaded (MT) systems, it's now possible to achieve substantially higher speeds for sensitive applications like linear algebra using parallel computations, often outpacing several orders of magnitude the improvements seen in recent computer processors. 

In this study, a BLAS implementation was developed, utilizing both MP and MT techniques, with assessments conducted to determine its performance in comparison to various computer systems, including recent GPUs, FPGAs, and Advanced Vector Extensions, as well as a survey of other available parallel BLAS implementations. 

Our findings indicate that despite initial concerns about poor performance due to the overhead of process and thread management, very large team sizes can lead to significant speedups, with results showing speeds approaching 99% of the optimal performance across a wide range of applications and computers. 

In particular, our tests found that even relatively simple MT implementations could achieve near-optimal performance on modern computers with multiple cores, surpassing the performance of complex GPU and FPGA implementations that incur substantial memory access limitations. 

Therefore, it's recommended to utilize very large team sizes in parallel BLAS implementations and that further research is necessary to fully understand the performance of these computations in certain applications and computer systems. 

This research is significant because it has implications for other numerical software libraries that often rely on BLAS functions and could potentially leverage these speedups, giving them the ability to approach optimal performance themselves. 

In addition, this study provides valuable performance data that can serve as a standard of reference for evaluating the effectiveness of computer systems in solving actual problems and could also be used to assess the performance of other parallel BLAS implementations.

This research investigates the Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique's (GNAST's) potential to enhance the energy efficiency of SWIPT-enabled networks. By incorporating an energy-harvesting base station, we analyze a NAST-enabled network consisting of multiple file transmissions. For each transmission, we decide between using GNAST and conventional antenna-switching techniques (CAST) based on the received signal power. Simulations show that GNAST outperforms CAST in terms of energy efficiency, with GNAST offering a significant EE improvement of up to $10^4$. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that GNAST's EE benefit arises from its ability to redirect energy-harvested power to existing transmit antennas during some transmissions. Additionally, our work demonstrates that GNAST's EE advantage can be achieved without compromising data rate performance. Human-made intuition is developed to identify the GNAST-CAST boundary, and our results demonstrate that GNAST's highest EE gain occurs when the received signal power is moderate. As a result, GNAST is an effective method for enhancing the energy efficiency of SWIPT-enabled networks.

Deep neural network-based object detection models, particularly those incorporating Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN), have achieved high accuracy in this task. However, we found that, despite being optimized, the base networks in these models still struggle to identify small objects. This issue seems to be exacerbated in modern backbone networks, which are highly efficient but seem to exacerbate this challenge even further. To address this problem, we first examine various configurations for combining FPN with modern base networks and discover that simply concatenating the downsampled feature maps to the pyramid levels, as done in Bi-FPN, significantly improves the accuracy when using these efficient backbone networks. This prompted us to delve deeper into understanding this phenomenon and ultimately propose an intuitive framework to model FPN. Based on this model, we derive an optimization framework that minimizes the error induced by directly combining the base network features. Inspired by this model, we explore several straightforward strategies to enhance the performance of objects of varying scales within FPN-based detection frameworks. Our findings serve as a guiding principle for constructing cost-effective, efficient backbone networks and prompt us to experiment with various fusion techniques in neural networks. Our experiments validate our findings and showcase notable improvements in accuracy across multiple datasets, demonstrating the robustness of our proposed approach. In this paper, we address the high pilot demand of XL-MIMO systems by adapting Non-Orthogonal Variable-Ranking (NOVR) protocols for Fast Random Access (RA). We introduce NOVR-XL RA, a new scheme that incorporates an additional ranking step in RA signal processing to distinguish between XL-MIMO base station signals. By combining an energy detector and two successive orthogonal detections, NOVR-XL RA can accurately identify RA codes, including those from multiple XL-MIMO connections. We analyze and optimize various NOVR-XL RA protocol parameters to minimize RA attempt time, and evaluate the efficacy of our proposal through numerical simulations and real-world implementations. Results show that NOVR-XL RA significantly enhances RA performance in XL-MIMO systems. In particular, it increases the successful RA detection rate and reduces the base station's signal detection failure rate in RA scenarios. Moreover, NOVR-XL RA can effectively mitigate the negative impact of insufficient initial pilot resources on RA performance. In addition, we investigate various scenarios involving multiple XL-MIMO users and highlight the NOVR-XL RA approach's general applicability to various RA scenarios. To further minimize complex calculations during initial RA attempts, we also introduce a novel, efficient propagation model-based antenna ranking scheme. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate NOVR-XL RA's capability to tackle the pilot scarcity challenge in XL-MIMO systems with limited initial pilot resources. To this end, we also present a large-scale XL-MIMO system architecture that integrates NOVR-XL RA and highlights the technique's potential for widespread adoption in future wireless communications systems. We also anticipate that NOVR-XL RA's innovative RA signal processing techniques and efficient propagation model-based antenna ranking scheme will serve as a valuable reference for further research into XL-MIMO RA technologies. We have made the software tools used in our numerical simulations publicly available. We have also conducted several real-world implementations that validate our approach's efficacy in actual XL-MIMO scenarios. We suggest that substantial structures in the early stages of development could serve as the foundation for small bodies, and a new generation of planets might form from the remaining material. To better understand this two-step planetary formation process, we need to identify how multiple small structures can merge to form larger ones. By combining the grand design pattern of protoplanetary disks with a collision detector, we simulated the formation of a large object from multiple substructures. We found that in many cases, a single massive planet forms, but there's also a chance for multiple small planets or one large planet with accompanying smaller ones. These results resemble those of traditional direct formation simulations. However, when we looked at the intermediate steps, we found that many large objects do exist, and it's likely that some of these could continue growing into massive planets. These findings fit with the existing research on planetary growth, and they suggest that a two-step formation process could explain the diversity of planetary sizes. Finally, we propose that future observations of protoplanetary disks are capable of detecting the small bodies that could pave the way for planetary formation.

Our study reveals that the combined effects of these correlated states,
particularly those at the Mott-Hubbard gap, contribute significantly to the
complexity of the spectral structure. The presence of intragroup interactions
leads to spectral coherence within sets of energetic levels, resulting in well-
defined features at the upper and lower of the Hubbard gap. The application
of DFT alone fails to accurately reproduce the spectral structure, particularly
at the upper Hubbard gap where extra weight appears on the low-frequency peak,
an observation that can be understood through the combination of DFT and DMFT. 
Notably, the spectral shape is transformed by the choice of initial conditions
for the DMFT equations, highlighting the potential for separating correlations
that influence the spectral gap from those that shape the associated sidebands.
The findings of our research provide a new perspective on the inherent spectral
complexity of SrMnO$_3$ and offer a more detailed understanding of the effects
of correlated orbitals on its spectral structure. Our study also identifies the
need to integrate DMFT with a greater number of initial conditions to achieve
a more accurate representation of the spectral structure of systems with multiple
correlated sets of states. Our analysis confirms the presence of sideband-like
features within the Hubbard gap and identifies the potential for customizing
the shape of the spectral structure through the integration of correlated orbitals
with distinct energies. Our study focuses on the spectral characteristics of
SrMnO$_3$, yet the underlying principles can be applied to a broader range of
heterogeneous compounds based on transition metal perovskites.

A single face image can generate a range of faces from the same individual based on different face poses, or entirely distinct faces from different individuals based on specific facial components. This complexity hinders efforts to reconstruct 3D faces. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new approach called the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), which breaks down the process of building a 3D face from pose-dependent and independent factors. The fundamental threat model we've developed targets pressure sensors in nuclear power plants, specifically focusing on the potential vulnerabilities in their digital form. Our research involves analyzing the pressures inside these sensitive areas and identifying potential weaknesses in the associated safety protocols. In particular, we've chosen to examine the pressures measured by differential pressure sensors in relation to the maximum allowed pressures set by the plant's control system. Our initial findings show that under normal operating conditions, pressures are relatively low and often comparable to system thresholds. However, our analysis also reveals that certain safety critical functions can be compromised by manipulating these pressure sensors, potentially putting the plant and its surroundings at risk. Furthermore, our results indicate that in some instances, the pressure levels measured by these sensors may be sufficiently high to allow physical access to the areas in question, potentially allowing malicious actors to gather valuable information by sight. Our methods for assessing this threat can be applied to other potential vulnerabilities in the nuclear power system. Still, more research is needed to fully grasp the extent of this pressure-based attack vector. This concept of the threat may also be applicable to other industrial pressure-based systems. Ultimately, our work highlights the critical importance of properly securing sensitive areas within these facilities and the fundamental need for rigorous security protocols to be followed stringently. This work is a part of our ongoing research to develop a holistic approach to addressing security vulnerabilities in complex industrial systems. This approach, which we call Risk-Oriented Security Validation, aims to monitor and assess the security of these systems through an ongoing process of threat analysis, risk evaluation, and security rule checking. This approach will serve as the foundation for our future research in this domain. Current active learning methodologies often assume ideal conditions, such as perfectly labeled selection data and unbiased model performance. However, real-world scenarios, such as those involving large-scale datasets like ImageNet, pose significant challenges to these methods. Typically, active learning protocols involve repeatedly iterating between labeling a subset of data, based on predictions from models trained on existing labeled data, until a desired number of labels is reached. However, this process is highly resource-intensive when applied to large datasets. For example, to achieve 1000 labels on ImageNet using standard methods would require labeling over 200,000 initial proposals. This work introduces a novel, efficient framework for selective sampling based on dataset characteristics, one that can achieve superior results with significantly fewer labeling iterations. This approach, called Adaptec, incorporates an innovative model that ranks data points according to their potential to influence model performance when labeled. This model is trained by sampling data, creating a hierarchy that allows for the identification of high-priority data points. These data points are then labeled, and the model is updated using an ensemble method. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields significantly better model performance on multiple large, benchmark datasets, including ImageNet, following the same resource allocation as existing methods. This is equivalent to achieving 1000 labels on ImageNet with performance equivalent to having labeled over 200,000 proposals, using essentially the same number of labeling iterations as smaller benchmark datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. This work is the first to overcome the limitations of traditional active learning algorithms in large-scale datasets like ImageNet. It has far-reaching implications for the broader field of machine learning, particularly in relation to the potential negative consequences of selective sampling on model diversity. The methods introduced here provide a significant step towards addressing concerns about the bias introduced by selective sampling in large-scale datasets. Researchers studied the properties of vortices in a $^3$He-A film under shear stress using the method of constant shear stress relaxation. By analyzing the motion of vortices as the temperature changes, the speeds of the vortices were determined and the energies required to create vacancies and sole vortex lines were calculated. The findings indicated that vacancies and sole vortex lines have similar activation energies, with the value being approximately 2.4 kK. Furthermore, the energy of sole vortex lines was discovered to be significantly lower than that of isolated quasiparticle states. The displacement of the vortex line core was found to occur gradually at higher temperatures, and was associated with an energy of about 0.7 kK. The results also revealed that increased shear stress leads to a decrease in the energy required for sole vortex lines, and allows for the creation of vacancies at lower temperatures. The findings of fast motion at higher temperatures and slow motion at lower temperatures were consistent with previous studies, and may have important implications for the understanding of vortex line motion in $^3$He-A under shear stress. The techniques used to analyze the time dependence of the vortex line density distribution also provided valuable information on the properties of vortex lines. Our studies were performed on a square lattice at the critical temperature, and we found that the normalized cumulants follow the same universal behavior as the magnetic field is raised, ultimately converging to a common point. Our findings also revealed that the magnetic field has a nonlinear effect on the shape of the order parameter, and we demonstrated that this nonlinearity can be removed by rescaling the magnetic field, resulting in a universal curve for systems with neighboring spin interactions. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach successfully induces a non-linear relationship between tasks in the data manifold, outperforming a basic generator and an LSTM-based model on the MNIST dataset. Furthermore, we observe that this method establishes a connection between optimal optimization methods and optimal initialization parameters, and that the generated optimal initialization parameters exhibit a non-linear relationship with tasks in the data manifold. Lastly, our work demonstrates the potential for Hamiltonian Neural Networks to model a wide range of gradient flows, and suggests several possible applications and research directions.
