A deep-neural-network framework called Low-Dose PET Image Reconstruction Using MRI Information (Ldpi) was developed to create high-quality low-dose PET images using MRI data. The Ldpi framework was trained on a small sample size of 10 PET-MRI pairs. Experimental results show that Ldpi-produced images have improved quality when compared to conventional reconstruction methods, specifically HDRRECON, SONECRECON, SONECRECON_W, SONECRECON_WH, and ANN-BPR, according to the TSPO quantitative value and MRI-MI. When tested on larger datasets, the Ldpi framework showed variable performance. Nonetheless, the easy-to-implement Ldpi framework has promise for creating accurate low-dose PET images using MRI images at a low dose. However, further research is needed to enhance the framework's ability to handle larger datasets and diverse clinical scenarios. 

The Ldpi framework consisted of a cycle-consistent adversarial network (CCAN) that included two primary components: a encoder-decoder network (EDN) and a universal decoder (UD). The EDN used MRI data to create high-quality PET images, while the UD used the low-dose PET images and MRI data to create high-quality PET images. A study of different network depths and the elimination of the UD component was also conducted. The Ldpi framework was trained in an end-to-end manner and with fixed encoder and decoder components to compare the results. When the UD component was eliminated, the framework was trained on two datasets. The Ldpi framework with variable-depth CCAN and UD component was tested on three depths, while the ud-component-eliminated Ldpi framework was tested on two depths. Nonetheless, further research is needed to establish guidelines for CCAN depth. 

Quantitative values for the TSPO and MRI-MI showed that the Ldpi framework with variable-depth CCAN and UD component outperformed conventional reconstruction methods. The ud-component-eliminated Ldpi framework produced similar results. The easy-to-implement Ldpi framework with variable-depth CCAN showed consistent performance when tested on larger datasets, while the ud-component-eliminated Ldpi framework showed variable performance. To examine this impact, we modify the existing NERC model to integrate contextualized embeddings into a coreference-based evaluation design. In a multi-pass energy recovery linac, the recirculation process involves multiple interactions between passenger beams and RF fields in different phases.
As a result, the interaction between beams and RF fields depends on the filling pattern used.
Therefore, the filling pattern used has significant implications for the threshold current and beam-RF interaction effects in these systems.
This paper examines how different filling patterns influence the beam-RF interaction and threshold current, assuming that the input passenger beam current is kept constant to maintain the same average current in the ring.
In addition, the optimal filling pattern is identified that results in the lowest threshold current and beam-RF interaction effects.
In order to investigate various filling patterns, a simple model that accounts for horizontal phase space area and symmetry is employed.
The model includes the effects of synergetic interaction between passenger beams and RF fields in different passes.
The study reveals that the optimal filling pattern occurs when all bunch trains in a fill share equal average current, and that this optimal pattern results in the lowest threshold current and beam-RF interaction effects.
The study also examines different filling patterns for different types of energy recovery linacs and highlights the importance of taking into account the specific characteristics of the linac when selecting a filling pattern. 
Finally, the study demonstrates that by choosing the optimal filling pattern, the threshold current and beam-RF interaction effects can be reduced by half or even more, depending on the type of energy recovery linac. 
Therefore, selecting the optimal filling pattern is critical to maximizing the efficiency and stability of multi-pass energy recovery linacs. 
Finally, the study suggests several possible design improvements for existing energy recovery linacs, such as changing the threshold current by carefully selecting the filling pattern, and potentially reducing beam loss by selecting a filling pattern that avoids certain beam loss patterns. 
In addition, the study indicates that choosing the optimal filling pattern can result in greater user capacity in future energy recovery linacs.

To enhance neutrino detection sensitivity at the KOTO experiment, a new technique involves measuring secondary neutrons generated by final state interactions of anti-neutrinos with mesons. This requires accurately measuring neutron interactions across a range of energies from almost zero to several hundred MeV. A specialized detector filled with scintillator was created to record neutron cross section data within its material for energies between 98 and 688 MeV or up to the neutron decay point at 1814 MeV for certain reactions. This detector also accounted for delayed neutron decay energy across the measured range. Multiple techniques were employed to control systematic errors including independent measurements of neutron flux and flux spectrum. The resulting total neutron cross section was found to be in the range of 32.69 to 642.58 barns with a 0.34 to 0.75 percent precision. The data also revealed a reaction angle dependence for several interactions which was used to validate theoretical models with a focus on measuring low energy cross section more precisely through improved detection techniques. This research was used to develop a practical method for detecting neutrino peak signals within the KOTO experiment data. This detection technique is set to significantly improve the experiment's sensitivity to certain rare decay processes such as the rare anti-neutrino decay of Kaon particles. This detection technique is also applicable to other experiments involving neutral current anti-neutrino detection such as the detection of two neutron decays at once in decays of Omega negative particles. This research was also used to validate delayed energy spectra for various two body anti-neutrino decay reactions which involve neutron decays and also to establish precise measurements of neutron flux and its spectrum which is essential for making accurate anti-neutrino decay measurements. This research was conducted in the form of a 805 hour measurement run that took place in 2018 at the KEK 12 GeV proton synchrotron in Japan using the LUMI and LEPS detectors. The research was also used to establish a practical method for reducing systematic errors in anti-neutrino decay measurements which involves independently measuring neutron flux and its spectrum. The research was further used to establish a practical method for detecting neutrino peak signals within the KOTO experiment data that involves detecting secondary neutrons generated by final state interactions of anti-neutrinos with mesons. This range emerges from our simulation of how sticking forces increase with temperature in different scenarios. In particular, we found that in very dry environments, binding energy's enhancement with temperature allows smaller particles to stick together, leading to a surge in planetesimal formation at temperatures below 10 K. Robot skills are often governed by rules that must be followed to maintain safety and effectiveness. Conventional imitation learning methods can efficiently teach robots to mimic human abilities but fail to account for critical constraints. To address this issue, we introduce Constrained Imitation Learning, a framework that incorporates strict guidelines for skill learning. Our approach develops a loss function to minimize deviation from both optimization objectives and these constraints. Although the optimal solution is inherently non-linear, we leverage the capability of high-dimensional optimization techniques to yield local minima. To avoid getting stuck in a niche, we employ an efficient algorithm for robust convergence. Our method achieves exceptional results when tested on the complex task of converging to a balance posture on a soft-actuated robotic arm, significantly outperforming other constraint-based imitation learning techniques. The success of our approach demonstrates the potential for constrained imitation learning to play a key role in developing safe and practical robot skills. Additionally, our framework encompasses multiple constraint formulations and is adaptable to various imputation algorithms, enabling its broad application to various robot learning environments. The code is openly available at https://github.com/lingco/hybrid-constrained-imitation-learning.

Our research offers an alternative explanation for the vortex lattice transition in NbSe$_3$ by incorporating the effects of both $d$-wave superconductivity and van Hove singularities. By integrating the heat capacity and local density of states, we find that the influence of the vortex core on both superconductivity and normal state electronic properties leads to a highly stable vortex lattice structure beyond the initial transition point, even if this transition is not fully solidified by a van Hove singularity. Interestingly, we observe that the core's influence on the heat capacity near the first-order transition is comparable to that of a $d$-wave behavior, resulting in a similar heat capacity behavior in both cases. Additionally, our study reveals that the peak in the local density of states at the van Hove singularity can further stabilize the vortex lattice even if this peak is located far from the transition point. Our results provide new insights into understanding the vortex lattice transitions in the presence of both $d$-wave superconductivity and van Hove singularities.

Given a finite connected graph G and an integer k, the k-truncated geodesic distance is defined as the set of all pairs of nodes in G with a distance of k or less. We denote this as G^k. A recent study suggested that if a graph G has a metric dimension of d, then G^k also has a metric dimension of d, provided that k is greater than or equal to the diameter of G and less than the minimum of the graph's radius and its metric dimension. In this study, we investigate the validity of this claim for all possible values of k. Specifically, we show that if a graph G has a metric dimension of d, then G^k also has a metric dimension of d, provided that k is greater than or equal to the diameter of G and less than the minimum of the graph's radius and its minimum degree, assuming it is greater than 1. Furthermore, we provide examples to demonstrate that the proposed conditions are necessary. We also explore the relationship between a graph's truncated geodesic distance and its distance multipoles, as well as examining the validity of the proposed conditions for specific types of graphs. Finally, we introduce the concept of beta-truncated distance and investigate its relationship to a graph's metric dimension. We conclude by presenting several open questions related to these topics.

To efficiently detect binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys, we propose a new statistical approach using point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques. Despite limitations in resolving the binary system's components, the PSF analysis is highly sensitive to changes in a binary's orientation and distance. By evaluating the coherence of in-orbit asteroids under various binary configurations, we can pinpoint those with unusual trajectories that may indicate a binary system. To apply this method on a larger scale, we developed a high-performance computational framework that can rapidly analyze large datasets of potential asteroid targets. Leveraging this system, we conducted a comprehensive search for binary asteroid candidates from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer and Pan-STARRS catalogs. Our study identified 33 new binary asteroid candidates and confirmed the temporary binary status of five existing candidates. Among these discoveries, we highlighted Pencil Neil (1999 KD5), a binary candidate that may explain the unusual shape of the asteroid KD5. Finally, we discussed potential future observations and missions that could further expand the list of binary asteroid candidates. Our research delivers the most comprehensive list of binary asteroid candidates to date and offers the most effective statistical approach for detecting these systems from wide field surveys. The implemented framework is also readily available for other research applications. The full dataset of 33 new binary candidates, including Pencil Neil, is included in the new binary asteroid candidate catalog: The First Comprehensive Binary Asteroid Candidate Catalog (FBACC1). The catalog can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icars.2022.103437. For further information about the catalog's contents, contact the authors at {jhkim, jhlee, yjsuh}@kau.ac.kr. The code for the point spread function analysis and binary candidate selection is available at https://github.com/JHKKim/BinaryAsteroidCandidate. We analyzed a large dataset of around 6000 galaxies at around 0.4 z $\le$ 2.6 without interferences from cosmic reionization, using BPT diagrams to classify their ionization processes and map the evolution of galaxy populations. During the early stages of galaxy evolution, we observed a significant shift in the location of galaxies in BPT space due to their growing reservoirs of gas subject to radiative feedback. This feedback results in a diverse mix of radiative and non-radiative processes within galaxies, especially in regions with high stellar masses. As a result, BPT diagrams reflect little variation with redshift, mainly because the abundance of gas is consistently high enough to prevent the appearance of narrow nitrogen lines, a signature of gas without recent starburst activity. Instead, we observe a shift in BPT classification primarily due to the variation of metal abundance with redshift, which affects the position of galaxies in BPT space. Furthermore, we observed an alignment between galaxies classified as starburst in BPT space and peaks of far-IR radiation, as well as a tendency for galaxies classified as low-ionization nuclear engines to have overabundant metal quantities. These findings provide a physical basis for using BPT diagrams to study the coevolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes during galaxy evolution. It is implied that feedback from radiative processes facilitates the growth of black holes, affecting the surrounding gas, including enhancing metal abundance, facilitating further galaxy evolution. Therefore, we propose a new phase-space model that incorporates the relationship between galaxies classified as low-ionization nuclear engines and peaks of far-IR radiation, offering a tool for predicting the coevolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes. This model may be applied to analyze galaxy populations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the relationship between galaxies and supermassive black holes and shedding light on the role of black hole growth in galaxy evolution. It is also suggested that future studies should investigate factors influencing galactic nuclear engines, including black hole growth, paying particular attention to how this process influences the surrounding gas, specifically metal abundance, in these engines. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a comprehensive study of galaxy-supermassive black hole binarity and the influence of black hole growth on galaxy evolution. It is also proposed that BPT diagrams be adopted as a benchmark for identifying galactic nuclear engines and studying their abundance in galaxy populations at all redshifts. Our study offers a new explanation for the formation of the Gondwana margin, specifically the extended continental fragment along the South Atlantic, Africa-Drc-Madagascar and Antarctica. We suggest that rapid rod-like extension of this region led to the creation of a marginal continental fragment shaped like a dumbbell. Early in the process, a thin stretched crust gave way to a cycle of crustal rupture and regeneration driven by infusing mantle rocks, which resulted in the growth of significant sediment-filled basins. Over time, further expansion caused the rod-like structure to split, with areas like West Antarctica and Drc breaking off as a continental fragment known as a microcontinent. This microcontinent formed through the rotation of an irregular shape that broke off, and experienced a distinct history compared to the surrounding areas. It took part in a unique cycle of deformation influenced by changes in the direction and speed of extension, which caused areas like the Ellsworth Mountains to develop substantial mountain ranges due to horizontal stretching leading to folding. These events occurred as the rod-like structure split, and this led to renewed activity in the microcontinent's internal basins, which resulted in the deposition of thick sequences of rock recorded in mountains like the Neny and Ellsworth Mountains. This research provides a new perspective on the geography and history of the Gondwana margin, and offers a range of predictive models for understanding the development of marginal continental fragments. It also highlights the value of integrating analytical techniques for isotopic dating, geochemical analysis, and geological mapping in deciphering the breakdown of a rod-like continental fragment. Furthermore, it emphasizes the importance of considering the macro-scale tectonic processes that shape continental fragments through extension, and the subsequent development of these areas at a micro-scale. It also sheds light on the complex break-up history of Gondwana, and provides a framework for comparing the development of different marginal continental fragments. A new unsupervised pre-training framework, named Contrastive Distillation with mixed Label learning, has been proposed by our team. This framework combines two key principles - Contrastive Distillation and Label learning - to develop a unified approach to unsupervised object segmentation. Unlike traditional unsupervised methods which rely on reconstruction or mutation errors, this framework leverages both the contrastive learning approach to object representation and the label learning approach to object segmentation. Specifically, it employs a multi-resolution segmentation strategy to object segmentation. In this framework, objects are first segmented into parts by implementing a simple and efficient contrastive learning approach, followed by sorting these parts by a label learning approach based on their likelihood to belong to an object. To enhance the robustness of our approach, we introduce both a contrastive distillation method to object representation and a label learning method to object segmentation. Ultimately, our method outperforms existing unsupervised object segmentation methods on the MS-COCO dataset, delivering a mean accuracy of 35.5 for instance segmentation. Moreover, our approach outperforms existing unsupervised object segmentation methods on various benchmark datasets, including PASCAL-3D and Annotated Dataset for CityDRivable (ADC), delivering improved mean accuracy of 26.9 for 3D instance segmentation and demonstrating robust performance on cityscapes. Understanding why other players' actions succeed or fail in collaborative games is crucial for improving performance. Our new approach, based on a theory-of-mind framework, incorporates an inference system to determine the consequences of other players' actions by considering the game rules. This framework is versatile and can be applied to various collaborative games. We tested our approach on the well-known Hanabi game, implementing it as a joint inference and planning problem to develop effective action plans. Our experiments showed that incorporating this framework led to a 25% increase in goal achievement compared to a rule-based system, and the optimal action plan was obtained through a combination of logical deduction and simulated trial actions. Our results also demonstrated that players using this framework outperformed those with a basic rule-based system in experiments conducted with 3 to 5 players. The source code is available online.

Our research focuses on understanding how shallow and deep knotted proteins fold into their complex structures. We studied a recently discovered class of shallow knotted proteins, as well as two deep knotted proteins, using sophisticated computer simulations that account for the actions of thousands of atoms. By analyzing these simulations, we identified key events that lead to the formation of the knotted structure and compared them to computer-generated models of these proteins. Interestingly, we found that shallow knotted proteins follow a different folding pathway than deep knotted proteins, with intermediate states that resemble the starting structure. In contrast, deep knotted proteins fold quickly, with only minor deviations, into a compact structure that quickly assumes the knotted form. These findings reveal the intricate folding mechanisms of knotted proteins and highlight the significance of comparing theoretical models to experimental data, as well as the value of distinguishing between shallow and deep knotted proteins. Furthermore, our results suggest that the folding pathways of shallow and deep knotted proteins may benefit from the presence of disordered regions, as seen in the two deep knotted proteins studied, and that the action of chaperone proteins can significantly impact the folding process. Recent studies in generating counterfactual data have focused on crafting scenarios that could have occurred, yet do not account for the underlying mechanisms driving real scenarios. In contrast, we introduce DISCO, a innovative counterfactual data generation framework that utilizes causal models to create scenarios that would have occurred with a different causal structure, thus bridging the gap between current counterfactuals and hypotheticals. By utilizing a causal graphical model and a counterfactual data set, DISCO generates counterfactual data that is not only distinct from the observed data but also consistent with an intended causal framework. We demonstrate the advantages of this approach by showing that machine learning models trained on DISCO-generated data exhibit enhanced robustness and better generalization when subjected to scenarios generated through the same causal process, as well as those produced through different causal variations. Additionally, we find that incorporating causal knowledge into counterfactual data generation leads to a reduction in artificial diversity when compared to non-causal methods. We further highlight the benefits of targeted generalization, where models learn to distinguish between scenarios that would have occurred under different causal structures and demonstrate the importance of causal models being consistent with observed data distributions. We anticipate that the counterfactual data generated through such mechanisms will provide valuable training data for machine learning models, leading to a boost in their robustness and ability to generalize well. We showcase the capabilities of DISCO through a range of experiments involving both synthetic and real-world data sets, as well as different machine learning models. The code for our framework and accompanying experiments is available at https://github.com/google-research/disco.

Our model reveals how temperature affects the distribution of adatoms and diatoms, and provides a theoretical basis for previous experiments that observed distinct outcomes at different growth temperatures. Our results demonstrate that, by selectively activating or inhibiting the formation of certain bonds at various temperatures, it is possible to choose whether two-dimensional materials grow in a layered or integrated form on top of graphene. This choice can be made over a wide range of temperatures - from low temperatures where mostellers prevail (activated in our model but not in the experiment) to high temperatures where dimerization is inhibited, and domain walls start to form. A significant finding from our study is that the duration of synthesis has a minimal impact on the distribution of adatoms and diatoms. To verify our model, we used it to calculate various electrical properties of devices made from transition metal dichalcogenides on graphene, and found that they match closely with the results of previous experiments and theoretical studies. Our model also reveals that one type of device, where a layer of a transition metal dichalcogenide is removed to create a hole, has an electrical property that can be modified by changing the distribution of adatoms and diatoms caused by changing the growth temperature. This suggests that the performance of this type of device can be improved by adjusting the growth temperature. However, our analysis indicates that the benefits of integrating a transition metal dichalcogenide directly with graphene may come with the draw back of reducing the device's performance by one type of charge carrier, in exchange for an improvement in the other type of charge carrier. Nevertheless, our study provides a theoretical foundation for further research, and suggests that the performance of such devices can be enhanced by modifying the growth conditions, or through the use of alternative two-dimensional materials that have unique electronic properties. This could potentially enable the development of optoelectronic devices with improved performance that combine a transition metal dichalcogenide with graphene. Notably, these codes share connections with repeated lines in projective space $PG(r-1, p-1)$. A significant finding states that for a prime power $q$ and $p > 2$, every $Z_3 Z_9$-linear code of rank $r \leq 4$ can be constructed from the set $R_{3,9}$, providing a crucial tool for building certain codes and configurations in $PG(4, 2)$. A few specific codes of high minimum distance are presented, and it is shown that these codes contain a specific subset of topologically distingushed vertices in $PG(r-1, p-1)$. Finally, some open questions related to code construction and topological distingushed vertices in projective space are posed.

This study examines how different viscosity functions affecting polymer injection in mixing systems can be modeled using a Bingham-Bernoulli equation. Various viscosity formulas are tested, including power law, Helmholtz, Arrhenius, and Michaelis-Menten models, in a numerical model that considers laminar flow and constant pressure gradient. Our findings indicate that the power law model most accurately represents the polymer injection profile, while the Helmholtz model best fits data under both low and high shear rate conditions. Furthermore, introducing a Bingham-Bernoulli model into a network of tubes reveals that the model can effectively capture key features of the polymer injection process, including injection rates, pressure drops, and retinal transition layers. This research has significant implications for understanding polymer injection in complex flow systems and informing the design of such systems. Additionally, this work lays the groundwork for investigating rheological properties in response to changes in temperature, using the Michaelis-Menten model, and could have broader applications in research on non-Newtonian flow. This research investigates how the presence of a persistent diffusion affects the most valuable payoff in a specific scenario, where the underlying asset's future values are assessed through a backward stochastic differential equation. By solving a generalized variation principle, we derive an optimal payoff that increases the asset's value, and its connection to a HJB equation is established. Although the equation does not have a persistent diffusion term, we can still establish the optimal payoff's connection to the solution of a related HJB equation with a constant coefficient, which is derived by transforming the original BSE. This approach enables us to obtain the optimal payoff in a simplified case where the underlying asset follows a geometric Brownian motion. Finally, numerical methods are introduced to quantify the optimal payoff in different scenarios. Numerical results demonstrate the impact of varying parameters on the optimal payoff. This study provides an initial exploration into the application of backward stochastic differential equations to valuation problems, and it raises significant research questions for further investigation. To explicate the leptoquark pair production process, where one leptoquark has negative helicity and the other has positive helicity, we derive a relevant effective theory. This effective theory allows us to compute cross-sections and asymmetries accurately, provided that the leptoquark mass exceeds the decay width of its decay product, which includes a charged lepton and a quark. For this scenario, we develop a visual tool to illustrate the asymmetry in cross-sections resulting from leptoquark production, which depends on the leptoquark pair's helicity structure. By utilizing this effective theory, we can also modify the asymptotic behavior of cross-sections and asymmetries in relation to the leptoquark mass, which we show can comply with various experimental bounds on leptoquark mass constraints. Furthermore, we can incorporate this production process into a global analysis of leptoquark parameters. As an example, we analyze the impact of this production process on the parameter space of scalar leptoquarks with zero helicity asymmetry, which we find can significantly reduce the mass threshold for their existence. As a result, we can decrease the mass threshold for scalar leptoquarks from 1.4 TeV to 1.1 TeV, which we argue should be considered as a reference point for future production experiments. Additionally, we propose that experimental findings be compared with theoretical predictions through detailed simulations of detector responses, which we demonstrate using a case study of the ATLAS experiment at the LHC. We highlight the importance of distinguishing true leptons from fake ones, which we show can significantly impact the validity of experimental bounds on leptoquark mass parameters. We also advocate for the inclusion of fake-lepton discrimination techniques, such as the use of matrix elements, in such production experiments. We anticipate that our effective theory, cross-section calculations, and simulation results will contribute meaningfully to further research into leptoquark production and associated phenomena. Understanding how genetic changes affect cell behavior and lead to cancer progression is complex due to the large number of genetic variables involved. High-throughput sequencing technologies generate extensive transcriptome time series data, providing opportunities to investigate the interaction between genetic variables and the dynamic expression levels of genes. Although existing methods can effectively identify essential genetic variables based on their past values and relevance to current and future expression levels, they suffer from limitations in handling large datasets in a parallel computing environment. Moreover, they often assume a steady-state condition and linear effects between variables, which might not hold true in actual biological processes. To address these challenges, we introduce a new algorithm that learns variable importance through reinforcement learning, allowing for the exploration of complex interactions between genetic variables and expression levels at a scalable cost. By incorporating a neural network observer to estimate expression level predictions and a value function network to evaluate the significance of variables, our method leverages parallel computing to optimize policy learning. By applying this algorithm to a lung cancer dataset, we reveal previously unknown relationships between genetic variables and expression levels and confirm our findings through experimental validation. Moreover, we observe that certain genetic variables, despite having no apparent impact on the expression levels of cancer-related genes in the early stages of the disease, become crucial at later stages, making them promising targets for early diagnosis and treatment. Overall, our reinforcement learning algorithm enables a deeper exploration of the intricate mechanisms governing the development of cancer from gene expression levels and paves the way for the discovery of novel therapeutic strategies. The phenomenon of lepton-flavor universality (LFU) has been repeatedly broken in experiments involving the decay of mesons, specifically $K$ and $B$ mesons, where combining certain decay rates reveals a difference of up to three standard deviations from expectation. In this paper, we propose a theoretical framework based on the involvement of a light, exotic particle - referred to as a 'flavon' - that influences the behavior of these mesons. Its properties are determined by contributing to the diamagnetic effect in a similar manner to the phenomenon observed in the circulation of superconducting currents. As a result, the flavon's interaction with the decay processes of these mesons is closely tied to its mass, which could range between 0.1 and 100 eV. The involvement of this light particle is tested through calculations of various observables in the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, involving radiative decays, $CP$ violation, and the violation of LFU in certain decay modes. If the flavon has a mass within the intermediate range of 1-50 eV, it could significantly impact the behavior of these mesons, otherwise its effect is minimal. Nevertheless, the proposed framework also predicts that the flavon's influence should be observable in other areas, such as in the decay of mesons into photons, where current experiments have already partially closed the gap to standard model predictions. Furthermore, the implications of this framework are considered in relation to ongoing and future experiments in the $K$ and $B$ meson systems. In addition, the potential for the flavon to influence the behavior of other particles, such as leptons and photons, is also explored. Ultimately, the unique features of this theoretical framework provide a potential explanation for the observed LFU violations in the decay of $K$ and $B$ mesons, which could be verified or rejected through further experimental data. We investigate the largest intersection of two metric balls within the Cayley graph of binary strings, utilizing the Hamming distance. By formulating an iterative approach, we derive a closed-form expression for the largest intersection size, valid for error rates p less than or equal to 0.5, and for word lengths n that are greater than or equal to 2. For p less than or equal to 0.5, the intersection size is given by (d+1)/2, where d is the smallest integer such that 2^d * p is less than or equal to 1. Notably, this expression also applies for word lengths greater than or equal to 1, making it a general solution. Additionally, we explore the concept of a Hamming ball's "diameter," defining it as the maximum Hamming distance from the origin to any point within the ball. We demonstrate that the diameter of a Hamming ball with a specific radius is equal to the smallest integer greater than or equal to the natural logarithm of (2^r - 1), where r is the error rate expressed as an integer. For binary strings of length at least 2, the diameter can be further simplified to log(2^r - 1), where r is the error rate expressed as an integer. As a substantial contribution, we provide a general expression for the largest intersection of two metric balls under the Hamming distance, expressing it as a sum of binary digits of a specific number. This number is the product of the two error rates and the number of bits. We demonstrate that this intersection size can be achieved through a particular symmetric distribution of binary strings within the ball, providing a closed-form expression for this sum as (x_k + 1)/2, where x_k is the kth binary digit from the right in the product of the two error rates expressed as integers. This expression holds for error rates p and q, each less than or equal to 0.5, and for word lengths greater than or equal to 1. Notably, this expression also applies for word lengths greater than or equal to 2. As a final contribution, we establish an upper bound for the largest intersection of two metric balls, formulating it as (min(p, q) + 1)/2 times the number of bits, where p and q are the error rates expressed as integers. This upper bound holds for binary strings of any length and for error rates p and q, each less or equal to 0.5.

When applied to the QASPER dataset, our proposed method outperformed existing state-of-the-art models in both graph-based and non-graph-based methods. Additionally, we observed that our method achieves a higher scoring average than baseline models when scored on a scale of 1 to 5 by human evaluators. We set out to examine the velocity distribution of a second-class particle in ASEP (Associative Substitution and Elimination Process) in relation to its initial position. We demonstrate that this distribution becomes uniform at a rate of $1/t$ by analyzing the expected value of the normalized number of sites visited by the second-class particle divided by time. We further establish that the velocity of the second-class particle, defined as the rate at which it occupies new sites, converges to the speed of ASEP with $\lambda\mu$-permutations at a rate of $1/\log t$ for sufficiently large initial distances. These results are derived from analyzing the system's dynamics in the context of $\lambda\mu$-permutations and the rotation invariance of the stationary distribution. We also develop a method to estimate the probability that the second-class particle maintains a certain velocity over time, enabling us to establish bounds on the velocity of ASEP. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings on the mixing time of ASEP. Ultimately, our work offers a preliminary exploration into the study of ASEP with second-class particles, a variant where certain particles undergo independent Brownian motion rather than following the standard ASEP rules. We anticipate that this new perspective may prove valuable in understanding the fundamental properties and behavior of ASEP. We conclude by highlighting potential directions for advancing our results and broadening the scope of this research. We support our theoretical findings with numerical data obtained from extensive simulations. We observe that the velocity distribution is biphasic, consisting of a fast phase with a strong peak and a more gradual tail. We demonstrate that the velocity distribution undergoes a shift from a fast phase to a slower phase at a critical time that divides time into two distinct parts. We further find that the expected velocity of the second-class particle converges to the speed of ASEP at a rate of $1/\log t$ for sufficiently large initial distances. This paper introduces a new approach to shadow computation, based on an analysis of how ray tracing algorithms suffer from cascading errors due to approximate intermediate results. We develop a shadow computation framework that utilizes a combination of high-performance hardware components, including vector processors and tensor core units, and demonstrate how our method offers greater accuracy and performance than both traditional ray tracing and earlier shadow computation techniques. We also examine the challenges of implementing this method on current graphics processing units, and present various workarounds to overcome these obstacles. A practical application of our framework is shown in the form of a realistic simulation of the behavior of fluids under gravity. Our approach can be applied to any simulation that relies heavily on ray tracing and uses a large number of particles, such as smoke, water, or stars. Our framework is highly compatible with various computing architectures that support vector operations and matrix multiplication, including Linux-based clouds and mobile devices. In our experiments, we found that our shadow computation algorithm could achieve a 10 times to 100 times improvement in performance, and a 10 to 100 times improvement in visual quality, depending on the specific hardware being used. This study presents an iterative BDDC preconditioner based on Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC)(eta, gamma, omega). The domain decomposition subproblems are solved iteratively using a point-Jacobi method with a meshsize-based tolerance (eta). The coarse problem is solved exactly, with an exception for a previously proposed variant that uses a limited motif iteration. The performance of the BDDC(eta, gamma, omega) algorithm is analyzed for a model problem, and the results are used to guide the selection of parameters for both a simple code and the finite element framework FEMOOS. Numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the BDDC(eta, gamma, omega) algorithm for both implicit and explicit solvers, and the results demonstrate that the algorithm achieves comparable performance to other efficient DD solvers while maintaining flexibility and ease of implementation. Furthermore, the code has been successfully applied to an explicit finite element simulation for a real-world industrial problem. The source code is available under request. The rise of video persuasion through social media necessitates the development of automated music generation techniques that can engage viewers and promote a persuasive message's effectiveness.
We introduce a novel approach called "persuasive music generation" in response to this challenge.
Our method incorporates a model that simulates the interaction between music and viewer emotions, allowing it to produce musical elements that align with the underlying message and elicit the desired emotional response from viewers.
We evaluate our approach through various experiments, using both human-led evaluations and automatic assessment techniques to assess music-generated videos.
The results show that humans prefer music-generated videos over static visual content and demonstrate an emotional connection with the music.
Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the generated music promotes a more positive attitude towards the perspective presented and increases the willingness to adopt that viewpoint.
The findings also highlight the benefits of our approach over traditional animation-based video presentation methods. 
For instance, music-generated videos lead to a greater willingness to adopt the presented perspective (63%) compared to animated videos (41%).
Our research paves the way for the development of music generation techniques that can evoke emotions in viewers and, in the context of persuasion, influence their attitudes and behaviors. 
The associated code and data are available for replication purposes at https://github.com/huskyflow/PMG. 
The supplementary materials include additional evaluation results and visual examples of generated music videos.

Neural network-based defenses have largely focused on avoiding specific attacks rather than being universally robust. Despite this limitation, some defenses can still provide value as specialized solutions for particular security challenges. However, it's essential to understand the underlying principles of these defenses to effectively utilize their benefits. This study investigates the prevalence of gradient masking, a fundamental technique employed in several defenses, across various network architectures. To facilitate comparison among these networks, the research quantifies gradient masking and reveals that many of these networks exhibit minimal masking. Furthermore, it's observed that networks with significant masking tend to lack other beneficial properties, such as efficient resource utilization and simplified training. As a result, the study recommends avoiding defense networks that rely heavily on gradient masking and instead advocates for the development of secure neural networks that prioritize universal robustness. These secure networks should be capable of performing well across various architectures, without relying on subtle differences found in previously studied cases. Finally, the research introduces a new evaluation standard for neural networks, defined as the ability to function accurately in the absence of synthetic attack data. With this standard in mind, the study presents the Simple Robust Neural Network, a model that achieves outstanding results in the absence of defense mechanisms, outperforming existing baselines across multiple benchmark datasets in both classification and regression tasks. Notably, the Simple Robust Neural Network exhibits exceptional performance in the absence of synthetic attack data, meeting the new evaluation standard for universal robustness. Moreover, the study confirms that complex architectures with significant gradient masking have minimal value and may be unnecessary for secure neural networks. In particular, the research finds that multi-task learning and efficient neural networks possess inherent robustness properties and can effectively compete with their defense-based counterparts. Ultimately, the study underscores the importance of moving beyond attack-specific defenses and focusing on developing universal robustness in neural networks. As a starting point, the research presents the Simple Robust Neural Network as a premier example of a secure, high-performance network. With this new benchmark in place, the study invites the community to join the effort in developing and evaluating robust neural networks that excel in the absence of synthetic attack data. As a initial step, the research has made the source code for the Simple Robust Neural Network available openly on GitHub. Consequently, this study aims to trigger a broader investigation into universal robustness in neural networks and pave the way for a new generation of secure and reliable machine learning models. This study proposes a multiscale enhanced super-resolution GAN model that leverages spatial and spectral information to improve the representation of complex turbulent patterns. Unlike traditional GAN models, this approach utilizes a range of turbulent flows with varying Reynolds numbers to create a mixed-scale training dataset. By incorporating spectral information from Fourier analysis, the model is capable of tackling the inherent challenge of persistent turbulent signals. Our numerical investigations employ Fourier-decomposed maps of turbulent flows at low and medium Reynolds numbers, in addition to high-Reynolds-number simulations, to evaluate the performance of the proposed model. Comparative studies with conventional GAN models reveal significant improvements in predicting accurate turbulent patterns across multiple scales. As a result, the multiscale enhanced super-resolution GAN model demonstrates outstanding efficacy in mimicking real turbulent flows and extending previous findings. Moreover, the model's capability to generalize across different flow types is demonstrated through applications to external turbulence and rotating turbulent flows. Overall, the proposed multiscale enhanced super-resolution GAN model excels in generating highly realistic turbulent patterns and is poised to contribute to breakthroughs in modeling turbulent signals. Alongside the code, the training dataset employed in this research is also made publicly available for use in future research. Traditional deep neural network classifiers are largely incompatible with efficient prediction evaluation, as they frequently produce uncalibrated predictions that fail to differentiate between high and low confidence levels. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, efficient framework for training deep neural network classifiers that prioritizes the creation of a confidence score associated with each classification prediction. This score ensures the consistency of predictions and confidence assessments, and can be utilized for data cleaning and the development of robust evaluation metrics. To achieve this goal, we modified the standard classifier loss function to incorporate a difference-criterion component, which adapts the soft-max function to provide confidence scores directly compatible with prediction classifications. To facilitate seamless integration with modern optimization algorithms, we also developed a technique to gradient-project constraints onto the feasible region defined by suitable margin-based criteria. By leveraging this framework, we achieved notable improvements in efficient classification tasks, achieving up to 32% reduction in error rates when working with large datasets. Moreover, this approach enabled the creation of reliable prediction confidence scores, which proved particularly useful in the development of efficient evaluation metrics. We also introduced a new framework for model selection, based on balancing prediction accuracy and confidence levels, and showcased its effectiveness through a range-restricted model selection experiment. Temporal process evaluation involves comparing multiple versions of a same process occurring over different time frames. Typically, this comparison is made with processes that produce similar outputs, such as web clicks leading to the same destination. In contrast, this study focuses on processes that produce distinct outcomes from a same set and assesses their evolution over time. A novel type of graph, called the Multi-Time Dependence Graph (MTDG), is introduced to capture these processes and their changes thoroughly. MTDG is an extension of existing approaches and offers a more comprehensive view of process relationships across time. An emerging technique of graph summarity can also help to summarize large graphs and their underlying processes for better understanding. Two new techniques of graph summarity are introduced along with their applications to analyzing process changes across time frames. These techniques involve process evaluation and comparison with static and dynamic processes. A novel type of time series graph, called the Dynamic Dependence Graph (DCG), is introduced for this purpose. DCG represents sequential process relationships and helps to identify process changes by detecting distinct sub-components in different time frames. A novel approach of temporal process evaluation is presented using all these innovations and is validated with real-world data. The proposed methods can also be adjusted to accommodate various types of processes and data. delocalization. Adding a specific type of interaction, we break the algebraic 
extension of the Schr\"{o}dinger operator and instead obtain absolute continuity

one causing destruction of absolute continuity and the other overcoming it in the

understood through a mathematical approach and validated through numerical simulations

However, our studies reveal that in ecosystems with this condition, certain features such as the location of equilibrium points, peak values in fluctuations, and the length of time before a population collapses cannot be determined by the model. Additionally, our results show that even if the condition of conditional stability is met, the model may still fail to predict the timing of a population's collapse. To better understand these findings, we examine the effects of changing parameters on the ecosystem's behavior with both analytical and numerical methods. Our results highlight the complex interactions between species movement, interaction rates, and the ecosystem's response to changes, emphasizing the importance of early warning signals in ecosystems where species are free to move across different areas. Nonetheless, our research also indicates that in stationary prey and a roaming predator model, a distinct early warning signal is absent, and the ecosystem's equilibrium is only visible in the long term, but is expressed as a stable equilibrium that is accessible only through a stable trajectory. Transfer learning has become a widely adopted strategy in NLP, allowing models to excel in multiple languages despite being initially trained on just one. We investigated the possibilities of multi-language sentiment analysis with BERT and essentially found the opposite of what was expected. Our goal was to determine how well a model, primarily trained on English, could be used to analyze sentiments in a different language. We tested this by using the BERT model to analyze sentiments in Spanish, with the model being trained on no Spanish, a little Spanish, and a lot of Spanish. Our findings showed that using the BERT model to analyze sentiments in Spanish was not as effective as previously believed. When using the model on just one language, the results were actually worse than those achieved with basic classifiers that operate on individual words. On the other hand, using the model on multiple languages yielded results that were only slightly better than those achieved with basic classifiers. Our research also involved testing the model with various other languages, including Portuguese and French, with the model performing worst on languages that are more similar to English and better on those that are more distinct. Ultimately, our study indicated that NLP models can be sensitive to languages that are both very similar to and very distinct from the languages they were initially trained on, with a model being able to effectively analyze sentiments in a language that is neither very similar to nor very distinct from the languages it was initially trained on. Our research is available online as the paper "Multi-Language Sentiment Analysis with BERT".

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. For the set $A$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, denoted as $H$-Hölder continuous with index $\alpha$ in the interval $[0,1]$, we examine the conditions under which the density $\frac{d}{dt}|_{t=0}M_{t}^{-1}[B^{H},A]\,dt$ has a continuous version. Here, $M_{t}[B^{H}]\,dt$ represents the fractional occupation measure of $B^{H}$ up to time $t$. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for this density to have a continuous version, taking into account the Hölder continuity of $A$ and the dimension of the set. Specifically, the density has a continuous version if and only if the Hölder index $\alpha$ exceeds the greater of $H-d/H$. This result demonstrates the sensitivity of the density with respect to changes in the set $A$, influenced by the dimension of the set that corresponds to a singular integral controlled by the fractional Brownian motion. Additionally, we establish the condition for the continuity of the density when the set $A$ has a fractal dimension that matches that of a self-similar set constructed through iterated function systems. Finally, we provide an analysis of the continuity of the density under a Taylor expansion of Gaussian random fields, and discuss its connection to the occupation measure measure whose density was previously investigated by Berman and Shafery. 

This work is motivated by an earlier result from Berman and Shafery, who examined the continuity of the density of the occupation measure of a fractional Brownian motion with respect to a set of points, and we extend this result to a continuous domain. The study of the density of the occupation measure with respect to a set of points has various applications in the context of fractional Brownian motion, and this work aims to shed light on the sensitivity of this density with respect to changes in the set of points. 

The conditions we derive for the continuity of the density are matched with those required for the almost sure existence of an approximation of the occupation measure with a step function, and we establish the connection between these two properties. Furthermore, we discuss the role of the Hölder continuity of the set in this context.

We compared the performance of action recognition models with varying training dataset sizes, specifically 1.6 million frames for a comprehensive sports dataset and 1 million frames for a dataset consisting of daily activities. Our findings revealed that even a small increase in frame numbers significantly improves action recognition accuracy, with a 0.5% reduction in error rates. However, beyond a certain point, additional frames have a minimal impact on model performance. This led us to investigate the concept of actions as "compact" data objects, and we proposed a new metric called average Frustum Volumine (AFV) to measure how compactly actions are represented within a given dataset. We utilized AFV to analyze our results and demonstrated its potential as a valuable tool for understanding the internal structure of actions in various datasets. Additionally, we explored other factors that influence action recognition accuracy, including frame selection and model architecture. We observed that both a simple baseline model and a more advanced model utilizing temporal pyramid pooling (TPP) achieved notable action recognition performance, with error rates below 20%. Our study provides valuable insights into action recognition and can serve as a foundation for further research in this domain. It also raises significant questions regarding the inherent nature of actions and the effectiveness of current recognition approaches. Anomalous pattern detection in large-scale datasets is often hindered by the sheer size of the data, leading to computational challenges when employing conventional methods. To address this, we present an incremental anomaly detection approach, based on the Conceptual Neural Network, which can handle streaming data and contribute to the formation of concept learning. By incorporating a time-aware penalty module, our model can identify anomalies by distinguishing concepts across different time points. The incremental nature of our model facilitates concept updates by retaining only the current weights, which can be discarded without impact when a data batch expires. As a result, our approach offers an efficient solution for concept learning in an incremental fashion. Experimental evaluations showcased our method's effectiveness in comparison to prominent anomaly detection algorithms handling static and streaming data. Furthermore, our method successfully applied concept learning to supramodal processing, demonstrating promising results in time-aware concept learning. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zhangdaisk/INC-CNN. Moreover, the project website is available at https://zhangdaisk.github.io/INC-CNN. The project has been accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems.

This paper compares the average age of information (AoI) in discrete and continuous time settings for a stationary AoI process. We analyze a discrete time system that can update its information instantly and a continuous time system that can only update its information at random time points. Focusing on the latter, we model a system where updates occur according to a non homogeneous Poisson process and characterize the steady state AoI distribution analytically. We then derive the AoI distribution for specific update policies, including fixed time intervals and random time points, and demonstrate that the discrete time AoI can be approximated by a continuous time AoI with appropriate update intensities. We also establish the relationship between updating information frequently and the AoI distribution through a Lagrange multiplier method. Numerical examples and simulations validate our analytical findings. We demonstrate that the discrete time AoI can be highly accurate when modeled as continuous time with high update intensities and that some intuitive strategies can lead to suboptimal AoI performance.

In addition, the article includes a discussion on the limitations of transfer learning and potential future directions. With the continuous growth of deep learning techniques and the increasing amount of medical imaging data, transfer learning is expected to play an even more pivotal role in the development of computer-aided medical analysis applications.

The glueball spectrum in quantum chromodynamics can be studied through correlation functions of certain operators, specifically by analyzing two-point functions of a specific field called the trace anomaly, which is closely linked to the stress-energy tensor. Although this approach has been computationally confirmed through lattice QCD simulations, the theory itself remains poorly understood. Our research proposes a perturbative approach to compute the trace anomaly two-point functions in QCD, focusing on the gluon contribution, and develops a method to extract the glueball spectrum from the calculated correlation functions. By employing a bootstrap method to analyze the spectral function, we were able to determine the masses of various glueballs, confirming their consistency with the lattice QCD scale and identifying specific mass ranges for different spin states. Notably, our results indicate that lattice QCD simulations may overestimate the mass differences between high-spin glueballs. Additionally, we observed that the bootstrap method allows for more precise determinations of mass splittings between glueballs with low spin values. As an example, we found that the mass of the spin-2 glueball is approximately 3.48 times the mass of the spin-0 glueball. Upgrading this approach to include non-perturbative effects holds significant potential. Our study provides a foundation for exploring the glueball spectrum in other quantum field theories, such as quantum chromodynamics with additional quark flavors or in the presence of a strong magnetic field. By doing so, we can gain a deeper understanding of how the glueball spectrum relates to the properties of QCD itself. Twitter has emerged as a source for real-time public opinion monitoring, where understanding users' sentiment is crucial. To effectively identify and interpret public sentiment on Twitter, it is essential to utilize machine learning algorithms that can efficiently handle large amounts of data. In this study, a deep neural network known as the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model was successfully applied to classify the sentiment of individual tweets and combined with spatial weighting, this model could also accurately determine the sentiment expressed in short text sequences. When testing the basic LSTM model, a precision of 0.82, recall of 0.81, and F1 score of 0.81 were achieved. To further assess the algorithm's performance, a dataset of negatively expressed short text sequences was created and the lattice structure of the Chinese language was integrated with the LSTM model. Results showed that when the model was trained on positive data, it could accurately classify text sequences with negative wording but expressed positivity, achieving a precision of 0.75, recall of 0.73, and F1 score of 0.74. To enhance accuracy in real-world applications, it is recommended to incorporate semantic analysis and combine the lattice structure of the Chinese language with the LSTM model. Additionally, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the LSTM model in analyzing public sentiment on Weibo by comparing it with the widely used Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm. When testing the basic LSTM model, it outperformed the SVM algorithm with a precision of 0.82, recall of 0.81, and F1 score of 0.81, indicating that the LSTM model is a reliable tool for monitoring public opinion on Weibo. To make the model more interpretable, it is suggested to integrate the lattice structure of the Chinese language and implement a feature importance analysis of the LSTM model. Moreover, to enhance sustainability, it is recommended to utilize a large-scale clean data set and incorporate an active learning framework with confidence scores to reduce data noise. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of the LSTM model in determining public sentiment on Weibo and provides recommendations for further improving the algorithm's performance. Although the algorithm is currently capable of analyzing Weibo data, it is proposed that it could also be applied to other social media platforms, such as Twitter, with suitable modifications. To facilitate replication and further research, the study's data and code are available for download at the specified URL.

The model includes an explicit component for monitoring air quality, as well as the physiological effects of volatile organic compounds emitted by strawberries on disease development. Key factors like weather, air quality, and the plant's biochemical responses influence disease development, making it a complex multi-scale process. The model was utilized to analyze the impacts of management decisions, weather conditions, and air quality on disease development, and a decision rule was implemented to minimize future disease incidence. Decision rules were developed through a method that calculates optimal control actions based on current and predicted states of the system, taking into account future consequences of present actions. These rules were designed to account for the effects of current decisions on future disease development, despite the complex and unpredictable nature of the disease development process. The resulting system learns from experiences and adapts to changing conditions, incorporating new state and prediction information to optimize decisions in a continuously evolving disease environment. The developed decision rule significantly reduced future disease incidence in the model, and the learning algorithm proved efficient in the model, but further research is needed to assess its effectiveness in actual fields. The model can be a valuable tool for commercial strawberry growers in Southern California, helping them make informed decisions to manage disease pressures and improve production and profitability. The approach used to develop this model can also be applied to other high disease pressure crops, such as tomatoes and strawberries in other regions with similar climate conditions. The approach has the potential to be extended to a system that learns from multiple locations across different regions, but this would require consideration of additional factors, such as the effects of weather and disease on production across different locations. Immersive videos offer an engaging, first-person perspective but require significant processing power for efficient playback. A crucial step in optimization is predicting which parts of the video will be visible to the user within a certain time frame. Various studies have explored this challenge, and recent research has shown that using additional information, such as video subtitles, can enhance prediction performance. However, the common approach of the field relies heavily on large, distributed models, which raises concerns about computational efficiency, data privacy, and model deployability. To address these issues, this paper introduces a subtitle-enhanced, self-supervised viewport prediction framework that utilizes video subtitles to improve prediction accuracy and operates within a single model. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of incorporating subtitles and the framework's efficiency on various video datasets. Furthermore, the study highlights the advantages of self-supervised training in real-world applications. The proposed framework provides a viable solution for optimizing the playback of immersive videos on head-mounted displays. Additionally, the research provides the IMV-Base dataset, a new dataset consisting of subtitles and viewport labels for 50 videos, along with the proposed framework's source code on publicly accessible repositories.

The infrared renormalons in the momentum structure of the parton distribution can be studied through the use of conformal mapping, specifically in the context of the operator product expansion. By applying this technique to the twist-2 correlator of a quark field in QCD, we find the contribution of infrared renormalons to the quark's spectral function, and as a result, we derive the minimum virtuality required for the approximation of the quark's spectral function in terms of the perturbative spectral density. We demonstrate that a similar approach can also be used to investigate the infrared renormalons in the gluon distribution within a parton model, and in doing so, we determine the uncertainty associated with the gluon distribution at an arbitrary energy scale in terms of the renormalization scale. Furthermore, we discuss how this uncertainty can be mitigated through the use of matching coefficients in global PDF fits. We also examine the renormalon contribution to the evolution of the singlet quark distribution, and in doing so, we propose a new evolution kernel which is free from renormalon uncertainty up to the order of the perturbative expansion used. We conclude that a similar approach can be applied to a broader range of global PDFs, and in doing so, we introduce a new class of PDFs: momentum-dependent PDFs, which are defined through the use of the quark's spectral function in terms of the momentum of the electron in deep-inelastic scattering. We provide a preliminary analysis of the $u$ and $d$ flavor PDFs in this new class of PDFs, and in doing so, we determine the minimum virtuality required for the approximation of these PDFs in terms of the perturbative expression. For a regular tree of degree greater than 1, certain self-avoiding walks and frog models on it exhibit similar patterns of transition from transience to recurrence at a critical edge degree. However, when the tree is highly connected with degrees close to 1, both the walks and the frog models behave asymptotically like Brownian motion, regardless of edge degree. This study investigates the critical degree of a tree that distinguishes these two scenarios from a probabilistic perspective. It is shown that, regardless of tree size, the fraction of edges that causes a sudden shift from transience to recurrence is less than 1 and greater than 0. This result is achieved through analysis of the norm of a random walk on the tree's edge adjacency matrix, which incorporates techniques related to Weyl's eigenvalue distribution theorem and more specific properties of trees. This finding provides a probabilistic explanation for earlier discovered spectral patterns. This work also formulates a conjecture about the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues for forest graphs that, if true, would result in a more precise expression for the critical edge degree. This conjecture is supported by both numerical simulations and theoretical arguments based on existing knowledge of random matrix properties. It is suggested that these findings may contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between graph structure and the behavior of associated stochastic processes. This understanding, in turn, may provide insights into the long-term performance of algorithms employed on these graphs. This work is distinguished from standard research studies by its focus on the qualitative properties of algorithms and their performance on specific types of graphs, described through parametric equations that represent the structure of these graphs. It is also set apart by its use of analytical techniques to address probabilistic questions, with the solution to one problem informing the formulation of related conjectures. It is hoped that this work will spark further exploration of the interplay between graph structure, associated stochastic processes, and the performance of algorithms on those graphs. In this study, a novel type of magnetophotonic crystal is investigated, which exhibits an unusual combination of surface plasmon interference, Rayleigh anomaly superimposition, and helical symmetry. Theoretical and experimental analysis reveal rich spectral features arising from the interaction between these anomalies in the transmission spectrum. A detailed examination of a specific wavelength reveals the presence of multiple resonances contributing to the formation of magnetic field distribution peculiarities. The outer regions exhibit an alternating magnetic field due to the Rayleigh anomaly and surface plasmon interaction, resulting in resonant energy concentration and subsequent magneto-optical properties. The inner regions, however, exhibit a distinct helical spin distribution resulting from the plasmon's helical nature, leading to notable spectral features and potential for magneto-optical function enhancement. This research demonstrates the capability to design the electronic and magnetic properties of a photon by engineering a magnetophotonic crystal at the nanoscale. This involves the systematic study of interference between surface plasmons and Rayleigh anomalies, as well as the plasmon's helical nature, to understand this complex phenomenon. This knowledge is crucial for the development of applications involving magnetophotonic crystals, including magnetophotonic optoelectronics, where manipulating atomic spins is essential. This work is a significant step towards developing this technology, needed to tackle challenges associated with conventional photon-surface interactions. This research also provides a foundation for investigating other exotic phenomena in magnetophotonic crystals, such as the Harper-Aizenman effect, and may lead to the discovery of new physical phenomena. Furthermore, this work offers a framework for designing magnetophotonic crystals with unique properties using plasmon's helical nature, and may result in the development of new magneto-optical properties through this approach. This study may thus pave the way for the development of novel magnetophotonic devices that leverage the unique interactions within these crystals. This includes the potential for magnetophotonic anti-sensors, magnetophotonic phase switches, and other devices that could exploit the intricate interactions between surface plasmons, Rayleigh anomalies, and the helical spin distribution in these crystals. This research may therefore lead to a new generation of magnetophotonic devices that can effectively manage atomic spins to enhance their functionality. In recent years, knowledge distillation has proven to be a powerful approach for compressing large neural networks into more compact models while maintaining similar performance. While traditional distillation methods rely on accessing the pre-trained network's parameters or intermediate features, a new alternative, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3), has been explored for scenarios where the base network's internal information is inaccessible. In this research, we first identify the limitation of current DB3 methods due to their focus on single-task training scenarios. To address this constraint, we propose a novel framework called Multi-Task Decision-based Black-box Knowledge Distillation (MT-DB3), enabling the compression of multi-task networks via DB3. Within this framework, we develop two central contributions: (1) a new decision-based student network architecture, facilitating accurate decision-based training; and (2) a mechanism for assigning relative importance weights to expert models for MT-DB3. Experimental results on various datasets and scenarios demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of our proposed framework. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NJ-UDD.

reconstruct its submodule lattice using its composition factors, combined with
the structure of its submodules under the action of the centralizing algebra.
This method encompasses both the basic and derived functors associated with
the composition factors. To illustrate this process, we apply it to a specific
multiplicity-free module, obtained from the regular module of the general linear
group via a combinatorial construction. The resulting submodule lattice is then
analyzed in relation to Schur-Weyl functors and its dual, revealing its
composition factor structure and the underlying algebra responsible. Alongside,
we establish connections to both the fundamental and exterior functors. Lastly,
we explore additional examples of multiplicity-free modules and their submodule
lattices in the context of Schur-Weyl representations. These examples emerge
from applying endomorphism algebras to submodules of the regular module of the
general linear group, and include modules with composition factor structures
characterized by both simple and induced modules. These findings contribute to a
better understanding of the structure of multiplicity-free modules and their
submodule lattices, also offering insights into the representation theory of the
symmetric group and its relation to the general linear group. To facilitate
extensive exploration, a dedicated software has been devised to visually present
the submodule lattices discussed in this paper. This software enables the display
of many different submodule lattices, encompassing both known and newly
discovered examples, allowing for an intuitive exploration of their structures. 
The associated algebra structures can also be graphically exhibited for each example
considered. This software is the result of combining several programming languages,
including Python, its related notebooks, and a cutting-edge graphical visualization
tool. The code developed for this project is freely available on GitHub, along with
the submodule lattices presented in this paper. Furthermore, this code can be used
to generate various other submodule lattices, also visually representable, given
its highly flexible architecture. The principles of module construction employed
here also facilitate open-ended exploration of new modules and their submodule lattices. 
This code is an innovative expression of the ideas presented in this paper, serving
as a dynamic companion to the theoretical module theory discussed. It enables the
visual representation of numerous submodule lattices, also offering a versatile tool
