Policy optimization using imitation learning is often facilitated by a set of labeled samples, but obtaining these samples can be difficult and expensive. We propose the TRAIL algorithm, an efficient method for imitation learning that relies on a smaller set of positively labeled samples and an unlabeled dataset. The algorithm leverages a part of the positive labels to create a compact policy feature space, and then utilizes the remaining labels and the unlabeled data for tractable policy optimization. The TRAIL algorithm achieves optimal sample efficiency improvements over baseline methods and demonstrates superior performance in a flight simulator environment using the MuJoCo physics engine. The algorithm's efficacy is further highlighted by its ability to effectively learn from a single positive label in a simple gridworld environment. The code for the TRAIL algorithm is now available online.

CoImLearn: Our proposal introduces a groundbreaking Co-imitation learning framework, 
which allows joint learning with both self-expressed actions and expert demonstrations. 
This framework significantly expands the capabilities of imitation learning by showing 
that expert knowledge is not always necessary for all actions. 
This is particularly useful when obtaining expert demonstrations is costly or time-consuming. 
Our method divides actions into two categories: those that can be learned through self-exprimentation 
and those that require expert guidance. 
This is achieved by establishing a relevance score for each action based on the differences 
between self-expressed actions and the expert demonstrations provided. 
Our method incorporates a multi-task learning approach involving two processes: 
one learns the category-specific skills and the other learns the general skills shared 
among all actions, with both processes running concurrently. 
This is accomplished by implementing a novel joint loss function that combines both 
self-expressed actions and expert demonstrations. 
Our method surpasses baseline methods across various complex benchmark tasks in both 
robotic manipulation and multi-finger manipulation scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness. 
The significant expansion of imitation learning enabled by our proposal is largely 
unexplored, and we hope our work lays the groundwork for further research in this area. 
The code for our method is available online at the specified website.

Each subchannel is given a specific "polarized cutoff rate" that ranges from the minimum rate of zero to the maximum rate of the channel's capacity, effectively dividing the channel into multiple sectors. We are interested in understanding how a sequential decoder's performance is impacted by the polarized cutoff rate, particularly when the decoder is programmed with a certain bias value that reflects the average of the polarized cutoff rates. However, due to the diverse nature of the channel, there is significant variation in the performance of the decoder, with some areas resulting in high error rates. Our goal is to identify the probability distribution of error rates across the different subchannels, as well as how the decoder's performance is affected by the extreme values of the polarized cutoff rate. We have developed a theoretical model that enables us to analyze the decoder's performance and determine the probability distribution of error rates in each subchannel, which can be characterized as a mixture of logistic distributions. As a result, we are also able to study the performance of the decoder when the polarized cutoff rate follows a specific probability distribution, such as the normal distribution, by applying the method of order statistics. Our findings have significant implications for the design of efficient decoding algorithms and provide a theoretical framework for understanding the complex digital channel. Recent studies combining reinforcement learning with traditional machine translation models have demonstrated significant potential. To further accelerate progress, we propose incorporating two innovations into the framework: assembling action spaces and testing time policy gradient methods. Our experiments conduct comprehensive comparisons between the proposed methods and established techniques while exploring different configuration combinations. We find that leveraging multiple action samples and testing time policy gradients significantly enhances performance. Introducing an action space assembly technique, where actions are aggregated from multiple candidates, yields an particularly notable increase in performance. This action space assembly technique particularly amplifies performance when data is limited. Our findings also highlight the particular benefits of testing time policy gradients in situations with constrained action spaces. We have made our code and data publicly available for further research and development. The ultimate goal is to contribute a foundation for future investigations into reinforcement learning for machine translation. The underlying code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/rrmt, and the datasets used in experiments are hosted on Google Drive at https://drive.google.

The LAMOST time-domain survey, a two-year project, started observing in 2014 and aimed to monitor 4500 targets across five bands using the LAMOST spectrograph. The catalog comprises 1078 candidates in the Galactic bulge, 1269 in the disk, and 1670 in the halo, along with 11 candidates linked to the GApS II. Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have significantly excelled in various image segmentation tasks while their complexity remains manageable on processing units with modular architectures. However, incorporating external data into the training process has been shown to significantly boost their performance. In this study, we explore an alternative approach where the input image is divided into multiple regions and different CNNs are applied to each section. We argue that by dividing the input image into equal parts, a specialized CNN can be designed to handle each section and provide accurate segmentation results. We then develop Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs) that utilize edge-maps to divide the input image into regions and gate the CNNs. The use of EG-CNNs leads to improved performance on several datasets on semantic and multi-organ liver segmentation tasks. Our approach offers a scalable and efficient way to enhance the performance of DCNNs on image segmentation tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/Edge-Gated-CNN. This study examines the concurrency control mechanisms used in MongoDB's distributed storage system by analyzing the source code of three MongoDB deployments: WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER. Our analysis reveals that WIREDTIGER employs a variant of snapshot isolation with conflict-free transactions, while REPLICASET implements a form of two-planner transaction isolation using lock-timeout strategies. SHARDEDCLUSTER, on the other hand, leverages a lock-based approach for two-planner transaction isolation with timeout strategies. Our research demonstrates that none of these deployments can guarantee serializability or strict two-planner isolation in the presence of transactions conflicting with past database states. Instead, they maintain consistency through various recovery mechanisms and transaction management strategies. As such, we propose classifying the concurrency control methods used by these deployments as Weakly Isolated and provide a theoretical framework for classifying other similar systems. Furthermore, we propose a strong isolated system that integrates atomic conflict-free transactions and two-planner transactions, and demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through a sharded MongoDB deployment on top of a MongoDB node. Our evaluation of this system reveals that it can achieve high performance, with transaction throughput rates exceeding 5000/second and supporting a wide range of use cases, including atomic operations across distributed documents, semi-fuzzy queries, and applications requiring strict consistency. We explore the notion of $e$-positivity for the chromatic symmetric function, focusing on the subset of Dyck paths that have a particular structure. These structured Dyck paths correspond to posets, specifically navigating from the bottom element to the top element. We establish an ordering based on the concept of inclusion among these structured Dyck paths. We then utilize this ordering to express the corresponding chromatic symmetric functions as a sum of elementary symmetric polynomials, and we show that the coefficient of a specific monomial is nonnegative. This result can be viewed as an application of the Kauffman-Lusztig formula for the character of a poset. By examining the structure of the structured Dyck paths more intimately, we are also able to derive the nonnegativity of coefficients in a different context, related to the product of two Schur functions. This analysis involves constructing a detailed, combinatorial proof of the formula involving the structure of structured Dyck paths. Along the way, we establish a connection between the enumeration of structured Dyck paths and the evaluation of internal edges in certain graph configurations. This evaluation can be viewed as a instance of a more general problem that is known to be nontrivial. We conclude by suggesting that the concept of $e$-positivity could be explored for additional functions, such as the sum or the product of two Schur functions, with specific restrictions. This conclusion is motivated by the remarkable stability of the coefficients in question. Moreover, this stability suggests that the underlying combinatorial reasoning behind the expression of these functions as a sum of elementary symmetric polynomials may also be stable and amenable to analysis in contexts where $e$-positivity is not known to hold generally.

We introduce the novel task of hindsight summarization, where we aim to create a earlier version of text that best captures recent information. This is driven by a theoretical insight that previously generated content often contains unnecessary information causing later generations to produce errors. In order to reduce these errors, a learning process can benefit from a condensed earlier version of the text. Building on this idea, we propose a new task and demonstrate both theoretically and practically that our proposed objective helps minimize prediction error. Despite being an unsupervised task, we achieve notable gains on both the C4 dataset using BART as our base model, and the ALBERT dataset using ALBERT as our base model. Notably, our approach demonstrates robust performance across various sampling strategies. In addition to outstanding summarization performance, our model also exhibits excellent ability to handle sequential data, producing accurate summaries of earlier generations in a reverse ordering of the original text. Human evaluations confirm our results, revealing preferred scores for both automatic metrics and human assessments. The code for our method is openly available at https://github.com/ghrua/Hindsight-Summarization.

The success of all-digital medical image analysis largely relies on deep neural network models, which can suffer from generalizability issues due to implicit biases present in clinical image datasets. This problem is compounded by the inclusion of demographic information in radiology reports, which can lead to further biases in modeling. We've developed a framework that combines explanatory modeling and strategic sampling to eliminate biases from datasets. This framework includes an implicit bias detector, which uses mutual information to measure the difference in demographic information due to input images. A subsequent optimization process identifies the most influential biases and selects a representative subset of data. This subset can be used for model training, ensuring generalizability across demographic groups. Experimental results on the National Cancer Institute's Breast Cancer Detection Dataset demonstrate that our framework reduces biases by increasing the accuracy of density detection from 73.99% to 80.95% (a 9.96% improvement) and the accuracy of malignancy classification from 65.82% to 77.83% (a 12.01% improvement). This technique has significant potential to enhance the performance and generalizability of medical image analysis models. Additionally, code and data are available at https://github.com/hưng-đinh/DemBias.

We're investigating the behavior of Ising spins within a network of interconnected triangle shapes, specifically how they're influenced by various types of interactions between the spins. Our research focuses on the effects of these interactions as we apply an external magnetic field and then reduce the field to negative values. Our studies reveal distinct patterns of behavior in the spins' behavior, both in the presence of positive and negative interactions, and how these patterns change over time. These patterns take the form of shapes within graphs that describe the spins' behavior, and we're examining how the shapes change in response to different types of interactions. Our results show that the structure of the network of triangle shapes plays a significant role in determining the spins' behavior, and we're using a method that allows us to study the behavior of the system indefinitely, which enables us to fully characterize the spins' response to changing magnetic fields. Accurate measurements of beam-beam interactions at particle accelerators can provide valuable insights into long-baseline experiments. Specifically, measuring the shift in closed orbit positions at interaction points with precision is directly observable and crucial for validating theoretical models of beam-beam effects. To achieve this goal, we introduce an extended 3D geometric model that accounts for the influences of beam-beam forces on the motion of particle beams within the scope of General Relativity. Through this model, we successfully describe the effects of beam-beam forces on closed orbit positions at interaction points, especially focusing on the parallel component. To apply this model to real-world measurements, we discuss the challenges associated with detecting beam-beam induced orbit shifts in the Large Hadron Collider. To overcome these limitations, we propose possible solutions involving the use of existing beam-beam limit data and suggest that integrating this model with machine learning algorithms could lead to meaningful interpretations of machine data. Finally, we outline the potential for comparing predicted results with actual measurements when suitable data becomes available.

A key challenge in distributed optimization, where data is shared among agents, is addressing uncooperative agents that deliberately provide inaccurate information. As the number of uncooperative agents typically cannot be controlled and their identification is difficult, our study focuses on developing an efficient adaptation method for a robust distributed optimization approach. We divide the system into two interconnected networks: a communication network among agents and a signal network representing the distributed variables. Each agent adapts its communication strategy based on a state that reflects the previous communication experiences, leading to a dynamic optimization process. We establish an equilibrium model and analyze the asymptotic behavior of the system. Our findings show that if the communication network has a certain structure, the system converges to an equilibrium state. We also explore the implications of our results on robust distributed optimization. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical simulations. Moreover, we derive the adaptive optimization algorithm from a general perspective that is applicable to various network architectures. The proposed method can be applied to various distributed optimization algorithms, including extrinsic constraint optimization and multi-agent extreme learning machines. The code used in the simulations is publicly available. The paper's contributions extend the scope of adaptive communication networks to account for uncooperative agents. By leveraging this improvement, we achieve more precise measurements of fundamental physical constants in deep underground neutrino detectors, and even develop the capability to convey the uncertainty of these measurements without being tied to specific experiment parameters. Furthermore, our approach allows us to tackle other complications, such as managing background levels and interpreting detection signals, and we outline possible strategies for addressing these challenges in upcoming experiments, including the search for dark matter and neutrino physics. We also outline possible applications of this methodology to other experiments and potential extensions to its use cases. As a complementary benefit, our approach facilitates collaboration among experimental and theoretical physicists working on this project. We plan to publicly release the source code associated with this methodology in the near future. BART, a popular transfer-learning method for sentence generation, has primarily been focused on feeding a full sentence into the model. This study adapts BART to a word-ordering task, where only partial sentence information is provided. Our results show that BART can achieve impressive performance on word ordering, surpassing a specially designed linearization model. Interestingly, we discovered that when given complete input, BART's performance on word ordering is similar to its performance on full-sentence generation. Additionally, we found that BART's word-ordering performance is less accurate than its full-sentence generation performance, especially for longer sentences. To further investigate these findings, we created a partial tree linearization task. Our results indicate that BART can be highly effective on this task, often outperforming a model designed for the related task of word ordering. This study offers valuable insights into the capabilities of BART and provides data for research on sentence-generation models. The simple yet effective approach used here can likely be applied to other transfer-learning tasks. We hope this study sparks interest in adapting BART to other parsing tasks and encourages the creation of more datasets for partial tree linearization. The data and models developed during this research are available for public access.

Researchers study the degree sequence of random graph ensembles using average degree and degree-degree correlation as key metrics. A recent study established that a negative degree-degree correlation is essential for LDPC codes to maintain decent error-correcting performance. Moreover, work has shown that, for certain degree sequences, the erasure graph ensemble exhibits asymmetric degree distribution, leading to new insights into the decoding performance. To investigate the impact of degree-degree correlation on decoding performance, this research focuses on a specific ensemble: random sparse half-weight ternary linear codes. By analyzing the degree sequence of the ensembles and using branching process theory, this research reveals that a negative degree-degree correlation is sufficient for good degree-correcting performance and proposes a new metric to evaluate the code performance. Additionally, this research explores the trade-off between the average degree and degree-degree correlation and provides concrete examples. Notably, it is shown that some high-density code ensembles with negative degree-degree correlation can tolerate a higher erasure probability than their low-density LDPC code counterparts. A recently created model for a vacuum and weak decoy state QKD system has been found to contain an undetectable threat from an all-knowing eavesdropper. By inspecting the system's source code, it was determined that both the weak decoy state and vacuum measures share the same characteristic of having a measureable photon count of less than half of the expected value. As a result, the difference between these two measures is insufficient to determine if an eavesdropper is interfering with the weak decoy state. However, it was discovered that the system's security relies heavily on the high photon measure, specifically that the gap between its actual and expected photon counts should remain significantly larger than half. Although it might seem counterintuitive, even a significant reduction in the weak decoy state's photon count is insufficient to prevent an undetectable attack on the system. As a result, it is recommended to greatly increase the photon count of the weak decoy state in order to effectively protect the system from this threat. Furthermore, it was found that the system's security under certain conditions is compatible with the weak decoy state having a very low photon count when the baseline measure is changed to a single photon source. When this change is applied, it was found that the system's security can be achieved with a significantly reduced decoy state photon count, one that is significantly lower than the photon gap required in the original model. As a result, it is proposed that this new approach serve as a standard for the weak decoy state QKD system. They demonstrate that inequalities of the form $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \lambda_i^{f_i}$ are equivalent to statements about the densities of Galois extensions of number fields, and specifically, result from combining multiple density conditions in separate finite Galois extensions. Initially, they derive this product formula by linking local fields with valuation fields, and then establish the general case through a process involving Kummer theory and class field theory. The current investigation focuses on characterizing the interactions between a nitrogen jet and a surface near a critical point of instability, where turbulent patterns emerge due to the shear flow's stability and an adverse pressure gradient formed by the surface. Unlike previous studies, which characterized interactions at higher pressures, this research uses a low-pressure environment to examine how decreased pressure affects the gradient's resolution and the distribution of characteristics within the mixing layer. The investigation takes place in a pressurized water tank, where a nitrogen jet with the same initial velocity is studied at two pressure conditions: 1 atmosphere and 4.5 atmospheres. The results show that increasing pressure from 1 to 4.5 atmospheres significantly enhances the shear layer's stability, shortening the turbulent distance and reducing the amplitude of fluctuations in both directions until a new equilibrium is reached. The distribution of characteristics within the mixing layer also changes in response to increased pressure, becoming more similar to the initial conditions, but still retains a bimodal structure. The effects of pressure on the interaction also include a more pronounced impact of the adverse pressure gradient, with the intensity of the double peak at a new equilibrium that forms at a longer turbulent distance. The findings suggest that increasing pressure can delay or reduce the onset of turbulent patterns in similar jet interactions with surfaces experiencing high pressures. The implications of these results are considered in the context of commercial jet engines operating at high pressures and temperatures, where turbulent patterns of similar etiology may contribute to turbulent flow and noise at the engine's exit. The study demonstrates the value of small-scale experiments in understanding large-scale engine turbulence, and suggests areas for further research. The results also highlight the challenges of predicting noise from engines with a similar architecture despite significant scale differences, as well as the need for a deeper comprehension of the physics and mechanisms underpinning turbulent patterns in such flows. The study presents a new approach to analyzing turbulent patterns, incorporating both time-averaged data and instantaneous snapshots, in order to better capture the complex characteristics of turbulent flows. The findings from the water tank experiments are compared to previous studies of the same flow interactions in air, and reveal notable differences despite similar initial conditions, attributed to the dissimilar density ratios between air and water. The density ratio in air is approximately 1, whereas it is highly non-uniform in water due to the presence of two distinct fluids with significantly different densities, producing two separate character distributions within the mixing layer, as well as two peak coefficients of turbulence at a double peak structure. The study also introduces a new parameter for determining the turbulent distance

A protoplanetary disk's behavior in the early stages of its development influences how planetary systems form and shape themselves. Despite being experimentally unobservable, researchers can use hydrodynamic simulations to study the effects of gravity on the disk's behavior. These simulations show that a stable, self-sustaining pattern of about a meter in diameter forms in the disk's middle section and helps create small planets through a process of cumulative growth, but only works if the star is intermediate in size. If the star is too small, dust accumulates in a ring; if it's too large, dust is swept up in a disk. This finding suggests that planetary systems consist of two possible architectures based on the size of the star. If the star is intermediate in size, it produces a planetary system similar to our own. If the star is too small or too large, it produces a different system. This theory needs to be verified through the observation of exoplanets. It also predicts that planetary systems will be found in a broad range of stellar categories. In the decentralized learning setting, the decayed delay DR-DSGD algorithm was previously analyzed for a static network, but its convergence rate was not clear. Additionally, the average convergence rate of DR-DSGD on dynamic networks was unknown. We investigated the convergence rate of DR-DSGD on both static and dynamic networks, finding that it converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{KT} + \mathcal{O}(K/T) + \mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})).$ Further, we found that the number of devices $K$ affects the convergence rate by adding an extra $\mathcal{O}(K/T)$ term. Forsage introduced a cutting-edge, decentralized system for creating a pyramid scheme without potential victims - itself. By utilizing smart contracts on the Binance Smart Chain, Forsage allowed participants to earn money through referrals, with a success rate of around 99%. However, our analysis revealed that nearly all users (around 90%) lost money in the scheme, with the remaining 10% who profited taking in around $180 million from 200,000 losers between July 2020 and June 2022. Using the Random Phase Approximation, we studied the electric dipole poles of the $^{16}$O nucleus, specifically the high-energetic side of the giant resonance resonance. Our calculations were based on relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov interactions, derived from the effective interaction of the A18 relativistic meson-exchange interaction and the density-dependent $\sigma \tau$ interaction. Our findings reveal that at energies above the giant resonance, RPA poles originate from the excitation of positive-energy particle and hole states. Our results further indicate that the density-dependent $\sigma \tau$ interaction has a significant influence on the relative weights of RPA poles, and that by comparing the components of the one-body transition density, it's possible to distinguish between isoscalar and isovector dipole states. In conclusion, our work establishes a robust framework for investigating the microscopical basis of nuclear resonance phenomena within the RPA framework. In complex networks, identifying how the spatial distribution of an epidemic changes during its spread is crucial, especially when understanding how to concentrate interventions. To address this, we introduce an observable called the delocalized component, which measures the average distance between closely connected individuals in the network. It is essential to note that this measure is distinct from measuring spatial dispersion, as it is influenced by the network's structure more significantly. We study a continuous process where an infectious agent diffuses through a network, driven by a birth-death process, and analyze how the delocalized component changes across different epidemic prevalence levels. Specifically, we investigate the critical point at which a sharp transition occurs near this network's percolation phase and demonstrate that the delocalized component displays a distinct increase before converging to a value that aligns with the network's structure. Furthermore, we provide an expression that estimates the variance of the delocalized component and demonstrate that expressing variance as a function of the delocalized component results in a power law relationship. The parameters that characterize this relationship are determined by the dimension of the network and its connectivity, providing a general framework that applies to any ergodic network. Additionally, we apply our methodology to a specific example, namely a regular lattice with multiple interconnected rings, and compare our theoretical findings to simulation results. Lastly, we believe that our approach will prove useful in analyzing other diffusion processes across complex networks.

By introducing a fixed correlation structure, HiP-RSSMs increase efficiency and enable learning and inference on complex systems by reducing the risk of overfitting. Through a fixed-point iteration method, HiP-RSSMs perform both state and parameter updates, avoiding issues with convergence. The algorithm learns a state distribution, a parameter distribution, and weights in an unsupervised manner, and we show that it can be trained in an unsupervised way using techniques like contrastive learning for state inference and patch reinforcement learning for parameter inference. HiP-RSSMs can handle systems with multiple states and variables, and we show its effectiveness by applying it to continuous control tasks in multi-asset economy environments and robotic control tasks with multiple state variables and actors in a scene. The significance of polarization measurements in social networks lies in their utility for identifying and addressing conflicts within those networks. However, the methods employed to determine polarization often prioritize computational efficiency over effectiveness, relying on dubious assumptions that can yield misleading results. Furthermore, these methods usually involve intricate algorithms that are impossible to verify visually, thereby obscuring the degree of polarization they claim to measure. In this research paper, we examine the methods used to measure polarization in social networks and criticize their methods, algorithms, and visualizations. In doing so, we highlight the importance of discriminating between intrinsic and extrinsic factors that contribute to polarization through a simple, easy-to-visualize method. In addition, we introduce the concept of measuring polarization as a non-hierarchical task that can be accomplished using a simple ensemble method. This approach produces more accurate results and offers several advantages over the conventional method, including lower errors and better scalability. In our analysis, we compare our method to the widely accepted method of measuring polarization and include recommendations for future research in this area. We examine the stability of states in multilayer networks with interlayer dynamics by introducing a simplified model that leverages the powers of the network's component matrices. This approach allows us to explore the stability of complex systems and identify the conditions under which explosive fluctuations emerge. To further investigate these phenomena, we apply our model to analyze the stability of a stock market multi-layer network and an epidemic spread within a multilayer population. Our study reveals that our approach effectively grasps the fundamental aspects of the systems' dynamics, especially when compared to traditional approaches that struggle to handle large-scale networks. Our model highlights the critical role that connections between different network layers play in the spread of epidemics and the possible explosive fluctuations that can occur. Moreover, our analysis of the stock market network reveals that our approach identifies stability losses associated with the trading of specific stocks and highlights the possible explosive fluctuations that can occur when these stocks experience significant price changes. For the stock market, our model also shows that stability can be achieved through appropriate trading policies and monitoring of critical events. Our study paves the way for the use of our approach in answering more comprehensive questions about the stability of multilayer networks and the impact of system changes on complex systems. This study is part of a series of investigations that aim to advance our understanding of the dynamics of multilayer networks through the use of simplified models. HyperPrompt is an innovative approach that allows for multiple prompt designs to be efficiently combined to achieve improved performance on natural language processing tasks. This is accomplished by employing HyperNetworks to map prompt designs to model weights, and our specific implementation builds upon this concept by establishing a method to achieve efficient HyperPrompt methods. We evaluate our approach through comprehensive experiments on both the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks, and our results show that even though the system is parallelizable, even with a small number of workers, it is highly effective in reducing the cost of developing high-performing prompt-based models. Our findings indicate that our method can result in significant decreases in tuning time and sample complexity, and our evaluation of the scalability of the method reveals that it can produce models with top-level performance with just a few thousand tuning samples. Moreover, we discover that our method has the capability to effectively handle a variety of prompt formats, including physics-based prompts, and we release the code and data used in our experiments for the community to build upon. 

In addition, our research introduces a new technique for learning the HyperNetworks that incorporates an additional network that identifies the functional relationships between prompt tokens, and this method proves particularly effective at handling physics-based prompts. The novel approach involves multi-task learning on two tasks: using the primary HyperNetwork to map prompt designs to model weights and using an additional network to determine the relationships between prompt tokens. And interestingly, we find that the additional network can also enhance performance on prompts that do not necessitate a deep understanding of prompt structure. 

Our experiments reveal that our method is not merely an efficient means of combining prompts but also a powerful tool that can also contribute to the development of high-performance prompt-based models, and we believe that our findings will serve as a foundation for the development of additional HyperPrompt methods and learning strategies for HyperNetworks. Furthermore, we hope that our research will also spark interest in the study of the structural properties of prompts and how they relate to model weights. 

In conclusion, our work on HyperPrompt represents a significant breakthrough in the use of prompts to develop high-performance NLP models, and we are excited to make the code and data used in our experiments publicly available for the NLP community to build upon. The odd photon is typically not observable due to conservation of parity, but it can be converted into an observable optical field through the use of a phase modulator. We have developed a straightforward distributed algorithm that enables a network with connected components to estimate the size of its total node count. The protocol works by activating a random node, which then activates another at random, with this process repeated until a steady state is reached, at which point the average degree of activated nodes gives an approximate measure of the total node count. We analyzed the efficacy of this algorithm under the model of edge activations, where each edge has a dedicated ID and activates the node with the lowest ID among its endpoints. We demonstrated that the estimated network size achieves the square root of the actual size at a rate of $\sqrt{\log k}$, where $k$ represents the degree of each node. Furthermore, we show that this algorithm performs notably better than a well-known conventional approach called the "counting experiment," which triggers a significant number of $O(\log n)$ node activations. Our proposed algorithm has the added benefit of being easy to implement across various types of networks, including distributed hash tables, peer-to-peer networks, and random networks with connected components. Our theory explains an unusual Nernst effect observed in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, where a heat current generates a voltage that varies inversely with temperature. This phenomenon is associated with microscopic interactions between thermal gradients, magnetic fields, and temperature fluctuations resulting from an antiferromagnetic structure. We calculated the anomalous Nernst effect in relation to these interactions and found it to be proportional to the square of the magnetic field, which is a rare observation in most materials. This phenomenon is particularly common in transition metal oxides with honeycomb structures, like Mn$_3$Ga and Mn$_3$Ir, where interactions between thermal gradients, magnetic fields, and temperature fluctuations result in anomalous Nernst effects that can be manipulated by external magnetic fields. This could lead to the development of more efficient thermoelectric materials. We also found that lattice connectivity affects the anomalous Nernn effect, with materials with connected tunnels displaying larger effects than those with isolated ones. This could potentially enable the design of improved thermoelectric materials by modifying the lattice connectivity. We validated our theoretical predictions with experimental data from Mn$_3$Ga and Mn$_3$Ir. Finally, we propose that other materials with honeycomb structures could also exhibit significant anomalous Nernst effects.

It is common for beam to be diverted or lost due to mechanical malfunctions, design flaws, or inherent limitations of circular systems. Often, beam loss is initiated by a single particle drifting from its intended path, which then attracts nearby particles. Once started, the beam loss phenomenon accelerates in intensity until slowed by the circular setup's design features, often resulting in persistent beam loss at a steady state. To mitigate this behavior in the Large Hadron Collider, we are developing a fast beam loss monitoring system capable of detecting and responding to beam loss incidents within a 300 μs time frame. This system will ultimately improve the safety barriers protecting the beam from recurring small-scale losses. In this report, we outline the basis for this system and present initial results from pilot tests. In addition, we discuss potential applications and future directions for further development. Quantum annealing is an influential algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems in a wide range of applications, including those in quantum dynamics and statistical physics. Its performance, however, heavily relies on the characteristics of the system's Hamiltonian and is prone to limitations from environmental influences. The structure of the Hamiltonian plays a crucial role in quantum annealing, with specific gradual transformations needed to prevent the creation of unwanted states and ensure the target ground state is reached. This work investigates how environmental decay affects the success of quantum annealing, focusing on systems where the Hamiltonian has distinct stages and the interactions with environmental modes vary. We examine the impact of decay on annealing and consider both static and dynamic quantum annealing. The comparison between decay-induced state changes and the annealing schedules reveals how the algorithm can be designed to counter environmental influences. The findings demonstrate that, despite decay's negative effects, quantum annealing can remain superior to classical simulated annealing. The superior performance of quantum annealing is attributable to the anomalous behavior of decay-induced transitions in systems with periodic Hamiltonians. The influence of environmental modes with varying lifetimes on the success of quantum annealing is also analyzed. The study's results provide guidance on the development of robust quantum annealing protocols capable of overcoming environmental decay. Due to Groningen's location, the government provided the institution with limited funding, reflecting the city's lesser population. This led to the appointment of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who secured additional funding and played a crucial role in determining the laboratory's research focus from 1939 to 1957. During his tenure, van Rhijn established a team of distinguished astronomers, including Hendrik Christoffel van de Hulst, Paul Wild, and Jan Hinrich Oort, who made significant contributions in various fields of astrophysics. This report celebrates the laboratory's 100th year by highlighting its major achievements during van Rhijn's leadership. It outlines the institution's main research projects and major discoveries in three areas: the Milky Way, quasars, and cosmic radio source systems. It also includes brief biographies of the key scientists involved. It further discusses the laboratory's participation in international collaborations, its influence on the development of the Netherlands' astronomical community, and its traditional and current activities in education and outreach. Lastly, it looks back on the laboratory's legacy and its continued contributions to the advancement of astronomical knowledge. It concludes with an overview of the institution's current status and future plans. Recent studies utilizing local critic training for convolutional and recurrent neural networks have shown significant improvements. However, the underlying reasoning behind these enhancements remains somewhat unclear. We delved deeper into the subject by systematically examining the influence of local critic training on network component efficiency, progressing from a basic analysis of individual neuron learning dynamics to a comprehensive study of full-network dynamics. Our results reveal that local critic training optimizes network efficiency by allocating learning resources to handle error propagation imbalances. Moreover, we found that using local critics enables networks to leverage the efficiency benefits of sub-network training. We anticipate our findings to serve as a foundational understanding for future research and applications of local critic training. Additionally, we incorporate an analysis of the efficiency gains of using recurrent activation mechanisms. We also introduce an efficient model, the $LCT$ encoder and trainer module, which achieves superior performance on compact models while reducing training time. Our results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on both compact and full-size models across multiple datasets. We have made our code and model weights available on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdwq/LCT. We have also published the paper on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.03404. We have included the project page link https://hjdwq.github.io/project/lct/ for more details.

We've developed a sophisticated version of the Lotka-Volterra model, which incorporates elements of predator-prey interactions from the Ross-Grenfell-Altman model and applies them to a population dynamics context. This advanced model includes three distinct variants of intelligent behavior: predators with perfect perception, prey with perfect perception, and predators with partial perception. We've analyzed these models using a stability test and found that in some cases, they exhibit chaotic behavior. Our results show that two of the intelligent behavior variants can lead to the coexistence of species, while the third may result in the extinction of the prey due to the prey's intelligent behavior. This is illustrated in our models by numerical simulations. Furthermore, we've derived a comprehensive mathematical expression that describes the boundaries within which the prey exists in a spatial domain. This expression highlights the significant impact that the prey's intelligence has on its survival in different environmental scenarios. Additionally, we've simulated our models in a spatial domain using the XPPAUT program and obtained corresponding graphs. These simulations demonstrate the dynamic, dynamic-driven patterns of species coexistence or extinction in both temporal and spatial domains. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the effects of intelligent behavior on the coexistence or extinction of species in a complex ecosystem. It also paves the way for exploring other aspects of population dynamics influenced by intelligent behavior. Lastly, we've established that our model has implications for analyzing systems where a driver is influenced by a controller that is, in turn, affected by the consequences of its actions. Unlike static graphs, dynamic graphs' changes can be predicted by monitoring network modifications, offering valuable side information. Despite advances in deep learning and graph neural networks, several issues persist, such as determining appropriate substructures and developing flexible representation models. These problems arise because current GNNs rely heavily on node features and learn fixed representations for static graphs. To address this, we propose DECENNT, a deep learning model that utilizes dynamic side information to derive evolving representations for dynamic graphs. DECENNT uses an integral method to process side information and combines it with a dynamic representation updating scheme, enabled by a flexible attention mechanism. By incorporating side information into the graph structure, we can extract evolving substructures and develop a prism-like representation model for dynamic graphs. Experimental results show that DECENNT achieves superior performance in classification tasks on various dynamic graph datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art competitors by achieving a 10% boost in macro F1 score. Moreover, DECENNT is capable of predicting modifications to complex dynamic graphs with high accuracy (95%). By examining the complex parameters of the top-quark sector, we find that the squark contribution varies significantly, depending on the phase angle, ranging from a minimal effect when the phase is zero to a substantial influence when the phase is $\pi/2$. To further analyze this phenomenon, we develop a simplified effective theoretical description and utilize on-shell matching to recruit the relevant effective field theory into the full set of possibilities afforded by the effective Lagrangian. By exploring the phase-dependent properties of the resonance in the energy spectrum, we identify the resonance in the energy spectrum, and demonstrate that the resonance's total width can be distinguished from a heavy Higgs boson of a certain energy by means of squark-induced decay processes. Additionally, we demonstrate that the production rate of the resonance can be modified by the phase-dependent properties of the top-quark sector, and that certain production channels are sensitive to the phase angle, providing a potential means of measuring the phase angle through the production of heavy Higgs bosons. As a further analysis, we investigate the impact of the resonance on the top-quark effective field theory, and find that the resonance's influence on the $t\bar{t}$ scattering cross-section is modest, but that its total cross-section can be modified by as much as a factor of two at high energy scales. As a byproduct, we also compute the resonance's contribution to the $t\bar{t}$ spin-correlation observable and the $t\bar{t}$ asymmetry observable, and find that the resonance's influence on these observables is also non-negligible. The backward pass, a critical component in calculating gradients for optimization, can be costly due to its extensive iterative circulation throughout optimization trajectories. Despite this, the backward pass is often constructed without consideration for the original problem structure, which inevitably leads to suboptimal performance. In this research, we demonstrate that problem structure can be harnessed to accelerate the backward pass. Specifically, by taking advantage of sparsity, proximity, or differentiable patterns, we can significantly speed up computation. We also introduce an intuitive and flexible algorithm for structurally informed derivative computation, which can be applied to various models and datasets. This approach, which we refer to as Structural Backward Propagation (SBP, pronounced "tribe"), enables explicit integration of problem structure into the computation of gradients, leading to a faster and more efficient backward pass. In our experiments, we show that incorporating SBP results in faster training, better generalization, and increased model capacity, without increasing parameters. Notably, we observe SBP to be particularly effective when combined with batch normalization, where a notable acceleration in training is achieved. We also explore the benefits of SBP in other contexts, including multi-task learning and deep reinforcement learning. In these scenarios, we find that incorporating SBP leads to better policy learning. We offer SBP as an innovative approach to enhancing the efficiency of the backward pass, and we look forward to it spurring further research and development in this area. To understand how cells change shape in response to forces within structures like stress fibers, it's essential to study the mechanical properties of these fibers. We've developed a new way to measure the mechanical behavior of individual stress fibers by using microscopes to track the movement of cells cultured on specialized substrates and calculating the properties of these fibers based on that data. With this approach, we found that contractility primarily affects the fibers' ability to generate force and resist stretching, while other factors have a greater impact on their ability to bend. Furthermore, our method showed that stress fibers have a non-uniform mechanical behavior along their length, with properties varying significantly over short distances. It also became apparent that stress fibers aren't necessarily the longest possible paths through the cell, but rather tend to connect specific points of high contractility. Finally, by using our approach to measure stress fiber properties over time, we observed that these structures can change their mechanical properties in response to changes in the cell's contractility, with changes occurring quickly and being consistent with fluctuations in molecular binding, rather than changes in the actin filament itself. Ultimately, our findings reveal the complex mechanisms governing stress fiber mechanics and suggest they may play a key role in cells changing their shape in response to changes in contractility, potentially driving changes in cell shape and organization.

We explore a challenging variant of the contextual linear bandit problem, where the context $X$ and action $A$ variables follow no discernible structure, the action outcomes' expectations $f(A,X)$ are difficult to estimate without a significant risk penalty, and a limited amount of data is available to establish a connection between the context and action. Notably, this research investigates a communication constraint where the context $X$ is completely observable but must be aggregated into a one-dimensional summary $s=s(X)$ to simplify the learning process, leading to a reduced amount of data available for the summary. Our goal is to minimize the long-term expected regret while managing the average bit requirement for communicating the summary. Although the context is unstructured and no prior knowledge exists, we have an extensive set of aggregation functions $s=\eta(x)$ at our disposal and can collect an unlimited amount of data theoretically. To tackle this complex problem, we employ a two-stage approach. First, an offline algorithm is used to select an optimal reduction function $\eta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}$ based on the available data, ensuring the Regret Bound of $\tilde{O}(K^2|A|)\cdot\|\Theta\|^2/\beta_X^2$ and a bit requirement of $\tilde{O}(K^2|S|)\cdot\log K$. Next, a linear bandit algorithm is designed to generalize the selected reduction function $\eta$ in an online setting with changing context distributions, resulting in a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(K^2|A|)\cdot\|\Theta\|^2/\beta_\eta^2$ and a bit requirement of $\tilde{O}(K^2|S|)\cdot\log K$. Notably, the chosen context summary $\eta$ has a significant impact on the algorithm's performance, influencing the regret bound by a factor of $\|\Theta\|^2/\beta_\eta^2$ and the bit requirement by a factor of $|\mathcal{S}|/\beta_\eta^2$. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we present a simple aggregation function that reduces the context dimension from $\mathbb{R}^d$ to $1$, resulting in a big reduction in the bit requirement for communicating the summary. Finally, we outline a potential application of our research, proposing the use of a contextual linear bandit algorithm in a system where the context is observed but difficult to interpret without aggregation. This paper examines the performance of binary and adaptive power control methods in a large wireless network with many users. We consider two scenarios: one where the number of users is fixed and has no significant impact on the performance, and another where the number of users has a significant impact on the performance. For the first scenario, we found that in a large network with many users, the binary power control method performs nearly as well as the optimal power control method. However, in the second scenario, the binary power control method's performance is not as good, but it still performs better than adaptive power control and much better than fixed power control. Additionally, we found that increasing the number of users significantly reduces the performance of both the binary and adaptive power control methods. However, this decline can be mitigated by increasing the number of base station antennas, which leads to a more significant performance improvement from binary power control relative to adaptive power control. This leads to the potential for further research into the efficacy of binary power control in networks with a large number of users and multiple antennas. Our model builds upon the successful Applied Stemming Technique used in Corpus Topic Models (ACTM) and naturally incorporates the inherent hierarchial structure present in networks. In contrast to conventional methods, HDTM effectively handles word variations without relying on pre-built dictionaries of word patterns, thereby providing more accurate results. We demonstrate the capabilities of HDTM by applying it to a Russian corpus within the Yandex encyclopedia network and compare its output to that of a straightforward Document Topic Model. The findings show that HDTM offers superior performance in terms of topical coherence and clarity. Additionally, our analysis indicates that incorporating network hierarchy enhances the model's ability to identify prominent topics across the network. In relation to computational efficiency, HDTM exhibits moderate sensitivity to the level of network hierarchy, while document hierarchy has a more significant impact on model performance. Furthermore, our study discovers that the mixture component of HDTM is key to its effectiveness, with successful topic identification occurring when the document hierarchy corresponds to a level within the network that is closely tied to the supertopics. We conclude that HDTM represents a valuable approach to analyzing large corpora within information networks, offering a powerful tool for extracting meaningful topics from complex data structures. Moreover, we believe this model can serve as a relevant benchmark for evaluating other information-based network analysis methods. As a supplementary asset, we offer the Yandex encyclopedia dataset in a pre-processed format to facilitate further research and comparison with our results. We investigate how the presence of a deconfinement phase transition affects quark stars of one solar mass mass at different temperature values, assuming the MIT bag model and a transition temperature of 145 MeV. Our findings indicate that if the bag constant is greater than (4.8×10^-11) MeV^2, a phase transition leads to the presence of a neutron star with two distinct layers. However, such a large bag constant would result in a quark star with a mass greater than one solar mass. We also discovered that increasing the transition temperature above 145 MeV significantly reduces the quark star's radius, with the effect becoming more pronounced at higher temperature values. Additionally, we found that when the bag constant is set to 6.76×10^-11 MeV^2 and the temperature is 50 MeV, a quark star can consist of two distinct layers with a density ratio of approximately 6:1. Our research confirms that quark stars can undergo phase transitions with matter located in two different states within the star, further supporting the possibility of using phase transitions to explain the existence of intermediate density stars. Nevertheless, such an interpretation faces complications unless the bag constant is sufficiently small. Our study also raises the potential that a phase transition with a high-density hadron phase could help explain the behavior of high magnetic field neutron stars. The increased sensitivity of these telescopes will also enable the detection of persistent X-ray spectra from quark stars or white dwarfs, potentially providing valuable information about the microphysics of these objects. Determining whether a tree corresponds to a subtree of another tree is known as the Tai mapping problem. For trees without distinct node labels, the problem of constructing the heaviest Tai mapping requires comparing all possible Tai mappings and has a computational complexity of O(n^3), where n represents the number of nodes. However, if the trees are labeled uniquely, the problem simplifies to finding an anti Tai mapping, a task that can be solved in O(n) time. We propose a new algorithm to find the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two trees, even if the trees are not labeled differently, and we demonstrate that this algorithm has a computational complexity of O(n^2). The algorithm involves first constructing a matrix that represents the comparisons between all possible Tai mappings and then applying a variant of the Smith-Waterman algorithm to find the maximum-weight Tai mapping. We also present an alternative algorithm that has the same characteristics but uses a different method to construct the matrix. The maximum-weight Tai mapping is a crucial problem in phylogenetic tree reconstruction, and existing algorithms assume a linear time complexity, making them impractical for large datasets. In contrast, our algorithm can handle such datasets due to its quadratic time complexity. As an added benefit, the score assigned to each Tai mapping can be utilized to confer a level of confidence to the reconstruction process. Moreover, the maximum-weight Tai mapping provides a way to measure the similarity between trees by focusing on the subsets of nodes. The algorithm that we propose can be applied to a broader range of applications that involve comparing substructures within complex objects, a topic that deserves further research. Our investigation focuses on a key aspect of the compass state - a quantum system that uses spatial coordinates to represent system parameters - known as the number variance. We initially examine the relationships between the number variance, entanglement, and correlation as the compass state evolves under the influence of diffusion and damping. Subsequently, we considered the performance of the compass state in determining the rate of damping without initial knowledge of the number distribution, employing tools from quantum estimation theory. Ultimately, our findings indicate that both the maximum efficiency of damping estimation and the optimal variance achieve the highest value when the average number of photons follows a specific, optimally estimating condition, which we derive mathematically. Notably, we observed that both diffusion and damping cause a decrease in variance and improve estimation efficiency, despite increasing entanglement and correlation in certain scenarios. Finally, we propose the compass state as a viable means to study quantum systems using spatial coordinates, offering a new perspective on metrological applications. Additionally, our results provide guidelines for optimizing the performance of damping estimation by adjusting the average number of photons, offering a valuable quantum phenomenon that could be utilized in other systems. Lastly, we hope this investigation sparks further interest in exploring the compass state and its associated variables in quantum information processing and metrology. Our analysis revealed that this cooling effect is likely exacerbated by the presence of extreme stellar radiation in the disk around UV Cet. Notably, UV Cet exhibits an unusual spectral line pattern in the far-ultraviolet range, suggesting an extraordinary intensity of $10^{32}$ erg/s in extreme stellar radiation. This extraordinary intensity may be attributed to the destruction of small dust particles by extreme stellar radiation, thereby impeding cooling in the outer disk regions. Alternatively, it could be caused by an extremely intense stellar radiation field resulting from a low level of dust extinction, which allows cooling to be impeded in the outer disk regions. However, if this latter hypothesis is correct, it would raise concerns about the suitability of UV Cet as a benchmark for observational comparisons with the T Tauri star AD Leo. Despite the uncertainties surrounding this phenomenon, it is clear that UV Cet exhibits an unusual disk environment that requires further observation and theoretical analysis. Recent research into machine learning security has focused extensively on the development of hidden threats, with studies on data poisoning being particularly expansive. While early work on poisoning focused on manipulating models through persistent attacks, the field has recently shifted towards shorter-duration attacks. These rapid attacks pose an implementation challenge due to their brief duration, requiring significant adjustments to either the trigger label or the model. In response to this obstacle, our work introduces the concept of a dynamic backdoor, characterized by a trigger that can be activated through either the label or the input feature, allowing for flexibility in attack implementation. To further complicate matters, we are incorporating the challenge in our experiment by limiting the trigger's label persistence to a single data point. To overcome this difficulty, our study proposes a new approach to the problem, one which leverages a feature-based trigger that can be activated through either the label or the input feature. To test this method, we conducted experiments on various classification tasks, including the sensitive attribution of gender from the CelebA dataset and the sensitive attribution of vehicle types from the VehicleX dataset. Our results showed that even in cases where the trigger persists for only a single data point, our method can still achieve high accuracy in activating the backdoor, with an accuracy of over 90% on all experiments. Additionally, our study indicated that both the trigger-based and model-based approaches can achieve high accuracy in activating the backdoor, with the method chosen depending on the specific application and dataset. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/chenzh1996/Dynamic-Backdoor-Attack. The Shape of the Wildling distribution As the precision of astrometric measurements
enhances, smaller changes in apparent motion's direction and pace become
detectable, including a change in parallax. This study assesses the impact of
solving binary stellar systems on the detection of exoplanets, particularly in
systems with a large orbital period. By simulating a vast sample of binary
systems, we map the frequency distribution of the ratio of the innermost point
of an orbit to the radius of sensitivity, or breakdown point, in response to
astrometric data quality. This distribution, which we call the Wildling
distribution, depends on the type of binary system and is dominated by
short-period S-type systems. For these systems, the breakdown point is
proportional to the semi-major axis of the orbit, often falling within the
reach of future high-precision astrometry, such as that offered by the
Plato telescope. Systems with longer orbital periods, however, result in breakdown
points that exceed the limits of current or near-future observational capacity,
while systems with close approaches below 3 times the radius of sensitivity
break down into two distinct components, further dependent on the location of
the host star within the binary system. Ultimately, we find that binary systems
account for around 15% of around 2000 solved binary systems, and around 55% of
these have orbital periods under 10 days, with around 1% having orbital periods
above 100 days. Additionally, around 7% of these binary systems exhibit
eccentric orbits. Through various scenarios, we demonstrate that even the most
sensitive space-based astrometry can miss around 90% of binary systems with
apparent parallax, resulting in around 100,000 potential contaminants in a given
year of data, or around 3% of false positive planetary detections, unless
account is taken of the location of systems within the Galactic plane, particularly around regions with high ecliptic latitude. This study provides the basis for a tool that enables users to model the impact of solving binary systems on the detection of exoplanets in specific cases, as well as the broader Wildling distribution, in response to varying astrometric data quality, binary system parameters, and other factors. When these two solitons are placed in a potential well and interact through a similar but opposite force, it's observed that the soliton with negatively effective mass is pushed away from the well by a similar but opposite force, ultimately leading to its destruction. In contrast, the soliton with a positively effective mass is retained in the well. The success of question answering systems relies on accurate knowledge representation and efficient knowledge retrieval. Most current methods, including deep learning-based approaches, often fall short of achieving both factors simultaneously. To address this limitation, we propose a semantic-driven knowledge retrieval approach that prioritizes semantic similarity between questions and knowledge entries. This method enables the incorporation of new knowledge without retraining the model, thus enhancing scalability and flexibility. We evaluate our approach on the LAMBERT dataset, comparing it to a traditional knowledge retrieval method that relies on sequence similarity. Results show that the semantic-driven approach yields better performance and outperforms the sequence similarity-based method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach succeeds in incorporating new knowledge without retraining, showcasing its scalability and flexibility. Additionally, we explore the effects of semantic similarity thresholds and knowledge graphs on performance. Our method achieves the best results in our dataset and outperforms the baseline transfo-xgrl model when using all types of knowledge. We observe that high semantic similarity thresholds can lead to better performance but may result in the failure to utilize very knowledgeable knowledge entries. Moreover, we find that incorporating all types of knowledge leads to better overall performance but may cause performance variability across individual knowledge entries. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-e-mustafa/semantic-knowledge-retrieval. Our approach can be viewed as an alternative to ranking-based methods, such as transfo-xgrl, and our results suggest that it succeeds in incorporating new knowledge without retraining, thus making it suitable for large-scale knowledge-based question answering systems. While our approach achieves the best results in our dataset, it is possible that ranking-based methods will perform better in datasets with different characteristics. To facilitate further research, we include the embedded semantic similarities for all question-knowledge pairs, along with the predicted labels, in the LAMBERT dataset, which is available at https://github.com/huseyndiyalev/lambert_dataset. We hope that providing the embedded semantic similarities will enable researchers to investigate new methods that incorporate both knowledge and semantic similarities, thus moving closer to building effective knowledge-based question answering systems. We also offer the source code for the baseline transfo-xgrl model that used the traditional knowledge retrieval method, along with the sequence similarity-based method, at https://github.com/ghulam-e-mustafa/lambert_baseline. We plan to explore other approaches to knowledge retrieval and consider the complex interconnections between knowledge entries in future work. These connections could provide valuable additional semantic similarities that would further enhance our method

Due to their simple structure and low number, combining all relevant data on your own becomes impractical for full spectral modeling of smaller molecular cations that contain oxygen, such as H2O+, CO+, and CN+. To tackle this challenge, this model is designed to use limited experimental data and extensive theoretical calculations of energy levels for each particular cation, significantly reducing the necessary computational data by approximately two orders of magnitude. In order to test the model's performance, a synthetic dataset was generated through quantum mechanical simulations of all feasible isomers of these cations across their stable vibration states, resulting in 114 different cations and over 1,500 unique energy levels. By assessing the model's predictions against the actual values, it was found that it could accurately determine 72% of the levels within 0.1 eV of error or better, surpassing the current state-of-the-art methods like multi-configuration wavefunction and configuration interaction approaches. To further validate the model, a theoretical spectrum of the CO+ cation in its ground state was compared with experimental data, showing good agreement and outperforming existing theoretical methods. This novel approach not only addresses the challenge of creating full spectral models for smaller molecular cations containing oxygen but also showcases the potential of machine learning to tackle complex many-body problems through the exploration of low-energy states. As a result, this model can become a valuable tool to aid in the experimental discovery of new optical transitions within these cations. In order to facilitate further development and improvements, the data used to train the model is also available for review and modification. To build upon this work, suggestions for possible enhancements to the model are also included. Individuals suffering from mental health disorders are more likely to engage in criminal activity, even when accounting for the consequences of their mental illness on personal relationships and employment. As a result, mental health issues remain a primary concern for the justice system. By analyzing North Carolina prison releases from 1999 to 2014, this study discovers that individuals with mental health conditions who are reincarnated into the prison system within three years have recidivism rates 35 percent higher than those who don't have mental health conditions once their initial prison term is factored out. Furthermore, individuals with mental health conditions who are reincarnated into the prison system within three years have a 12 percent higher chance of being charged with violent crimes, such as assault or robbery, and a 24 percent higher chance of being charged with non-violent crimes, such as counterfeit or fraud, compared to those who don't have mental health conditions and are reincarnated into the prison system within three years. The most significant reductions in recidivism due to mental health treatment can be found in individuals charged with counterfeit or fraud, with a 43 percent decrease, and those charged with violent crimes, with a 41 percent decrease. The vast majority of those who receive mental health treatment and experience a decrease in recidivism have conditions such as depression, anxiety, or substance abuse. We suggest using interpolation-based mixing as a semi-supervised learning technique for medical image segmentation. Typically, semi-supervised learning techniques rely on labeling data to reduce the risk of overfitting, but our approach uses unlabeled data for regularization. We demonstrate that simply interpolating between labeled and unlabeled image predictions promotes a regularizing effect that, for certain models and applications, can yield comparable results to more complex techniques. We evaluate our method against current semi-supervised learning approaches for cardiac MR segmentation, in both cross-validation and open datasets, achieving superior or competitive performance. To facilitate further research, we provide the code and models used here: https://github.com/katsura-kenji/semisup-interp. Our findings indicate that interpolation-based mixing can be an effective and accessible semi-supervised learning technique.

The Future Extended Range Engineering (FEX) project aims to enhance the ATLAS Level 1 trigger with a 1.8 GSps jet trigger module featuring 168 input fibers. This project involves designing a 10-fold scalable readout system for ATLAS's LHC Run 3 on a similar prototype. The proposed jet FEX system is expected to process 12.6 Tbps of data at 1.8 GSps, achieving a 10^(-10) bit error rate through 10 meters of optical links. This project also introduces a new approach to clock recovery and data demultiplexing utilizing a dual-stage phase detector and low-parasitic charge particle digital counter. Furthermore, this project includes an innovative proposal for the Level 1 Central Trigger Editor to utilize a multi-wavelength optical signal for improved performance and reduced power consumption. This could result in a potential 10-fold reduction in power consumption compared to the current electronic implementation. The project has successfully demonstrated its functionality with an ATCA board, achieving a 10^(-12) bit error rate. The proposed design has been validated through simulation of the LHC conditions and is anticipated to operate effectively with the LHC's upgraded detectors for the High-Luminosity era. The development of this jet FEX system has been ongoing and the production timeline is expected to align with the ATLAS's LHC Run 4. The knowledge gained from this project is also expected to contribute to the development of future particle physics experiments. The proposed system has been submitted for review by the ATLAS experiment and production approvals have been granted. However, the full production approval is still pending in favor of a hybrid approach involving a combination of the proposed system and the current electronic implementation for the LHC Run 4. Articulated Neural Rendering (ARNR) addresses the challenge of using neural networks for creating realistic images of complex, dynamically changing objects, such as human faces with moving lips. This approach builds upon the success of Implicit Neural Rendering (INR) by extending its capabilities to represent multiple aspects of an object and their movements using a single neural network. ARNR improves upon previous rendering frameworks in several ways. Firstly, it uses a single function representing various object aspects and their movements. Secondly, it includes a learning-based method for determining rendering targets. Thirdly, it uses both implicit functions and rendering targets to generate accurate images. ARNR's ability to handle multiple object aspects makes it particularly useful for creating realistic animations and generating synthetic video content. This approach also offers a framework for exploring new rendering techniques and contributing to the advancement of implicit rendering beyond the face category. By incorporating spatial information, graph neural networks effectively capture these configurations by transforming atomic positions into graphical representations and processing them to predict material properties. However, the traditional approach requires training separate models for each prediction task, dimensionality of input data, and type of material. This limits their application and makes it difficult to maintain a large number of pre-trained models. To accommodate different types of materials, a simple yet effective node feature transformer is incorporated into the builder module. The experimental results show that this approach achieves high accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art models in multiple predictions, demonstrating its versatility and ability to handle various materials.
