This paper examines the methods used to estimate statistical model parameters and functions of those parameters, focusing on non-parametric kernel-based estimators. We establish a direct link between the convergence of these estimators and their corresponding true values, using a weak convergence metric that leverages the spectral norm. This framework is applicable to a broad range of models, including time series models, in which the underlying process is represented as a combination of a trend, a disturbance, and a noise component. We outline a strategy to estimate parameters of this type, such as autoregressive coefficients, based on non-parametric kernel-based methods. We then demonstrate the convergence of these estimators, providing a unified approach that extends previous studies. We also illustrate the method's effectiveness through simulations and real-world examples. Notably, our approach enables the estimation of functions of model parameters, such as the long-run multiplier, by adapting the kernel estimator to a specific context. We establish the convergence of these non-parametric estimates, expressing the result in terms of the L2 norm and providing a more general assurance of convergence through the use of a metric that accounts for the spectral norm. This general guarantee is relevant to any context that meets specific conditions. Our method is particularly useful for evaluating the performance of time series models, even when the underlying process is non-stationary. We convey the importance of correctly identifying the order of a time series model and the implications this has for the estimation of its parameters. We explore and discuss several order estimation methods, assessing their effectiveness for both stationary and non-stationary processes. The knowledge tracing task, which predicts student performance based on previous assignments, is crucial in adapting deep learning methods for real-world applications. A significant obstacle in evaluating these models lies in the sequential nature of the data, where model performances are typically assessed using reliability diagrams or mean absolute percentage error. However, these evaluation methods fail to consider the fundamental properties of student performance, such as monotonicity and increasing accuracy with more observed assignments. In our research, we introduce a novel evaluation framework for knowledge tracing models that utilizes classification metrics and visualization techniques to assess both model performance and data quality. To further enhance model performance, we propose an iterative learning algorithm that leverages a deep neural network, where the exchange of information between the network and data improves model accuracy. The benefits of this approach are demonstrated through iterative improvements achieving significantly better results than non-iterative methods and the achievement of state-of-the-art results on public datasets. The code for our research is available online.

We explored the application of transfer learning to improve speech recognition systems across languages.  Our research focused on reducing the requirements for labeled data in speech recognition systems and expanding the range of supported languages.  We selected French as the source language and English as the target language for our experiments.  Our results showed that using transfer learning allowed us to utilize fewer labeled samples and achieve better performance.  When no labeled data was used in the target language, we observed a significant improvement of 13% compared to a non-transfer learning approach.  However, we also found that the similarity between languages and the availability of labeled data in the source language can affect the effectiveness of transfer learning.  Our findings indicated that transfer learning is particularly beneficial when moving to a linguistically distant target language with limited labeled data.  A significant 11% improvement was seen when no labeled data was used in the target language.  We concluded that our experiments validated the potential of transfer learning to enhance speech recognition systems and expand their linguistic range.  We suggested that future research be directed at exploring other source and target language combinations, expanding the use of transfer learning to multiple languages, and investigating approaches to optimizing the selection of source languages and their labeled data.  We made our code and data available for further investigation.  With this work, we aimed to contribute a speech recognition system that could effectively be applied across languages, reducing the need for repeated training and labeling processes in each new language implementation.  We believed that our findings could serve as a foundation for future research and practical applications of transfer learning in speech recognition systems. Identifying the most central nodes in a graph is a common challenge that has been addressed by various node embedding techniques. However, existing methods primarily focus on static centralities and neglect dynamic centrality changes. To address this limitation, we propose two novel node embedding approaches, DistAgg and DistDist, which capture distance-based centrality dynamics. These methods leverage the fact that centrality often shifts over time in response to changes in graph structure. By incorporating the differences in local and global distance distributions, they enable the modeling of dynamic centrality changes. We compare these methods to other node embedding techniques in two evolving graphs, showcasing their superiority in prediction tasks. Furthermore, experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness of DistAgg and DistDist in predicting key events in graphs, such as the emergence of new central nodes and the displacement of existing ones. We also highlight the advantages of these methods in graph applications with significant structural shifts. We publicly release the code and datasets used in our research for the community's benefit. We observe that all embedding methods except DistAgg and DistDist yield poor performance in predicting key events, prompting us to explore the underlying reasons. We propose a method to assess the consistency of node embeddings and find that DistAgg and DistDist excel in this regard. We also find that these two methods facilitate the identification of central nodes that are robust to different distance distribution models. In particular, we find that they enable the identification of nodes with centrality in scenarios where nodes have varying degrees and are located at different distance extremes from the distribution peak. In summary, our research introduces two novel node embedding approaches, DistAgg and DistDist, which offer superior performance in predicting key events in graphs by capturing the changes in dynamic centrality. We also showcase the advantages of these methods in graph applications with significant structural shifts and highlight the importance of assessing the consistency of node embeddings. We publicly release the code and datasets used in our research for the community's benefit. Evaluating the performance of novel node embedding algorithms can be challenging due to the lack of clearly defined evaluation criteria. We investigate the behavior of multicomponent complex scalar fields in various lattice models at finite chemical potentials, focusing on how the renormalization-group flow is represented by analyzing the lattice spectrum. By studying various field theories, both with and without Higgs mechanisms to break the complex symmetries, we find consistent evidence that the renormalization group flows are accurately depicted through the patterns of lattice spectrum transitions, which are influenced by the chemical potential. Specifically, we observe the emergence of lattice symmetry-breaking patterns that are consistent with the corresponding continuum theories, and we find that the chemical potential can trigger transitions between these patterns by changing the renormalization-group flow. Moreover, we find that the lattice spectrum transitions can be used to distinguish between the cases with and without the Higgs mechanism. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the renormalization group and lattice QCD, and we suggest possible extensions of our studies to other lattice theories.

The task becomes even harder in a multi-object scenario. In such contexts, an efficient search pattern is crucial for locating objects or tracking robots. This paper presents a new algorithm called SPGP-SARSA, an extension of the Successive Parallel Gaussian Process (SPGP) model that uses the SARSA reinforcement learning algorithm to compute approximate value functions in a search pattern optimization problem. We demonstrate that SPGP-SARSA offers a more efficient search path compared to the standard SPGP method for a multi-object underwater navigation task. Results show that the accuracy of object estimations improves over time for both methods but the error rates eventually converge to similar values. However, SPGP-SARSA exhibits a greater precision in object localization, particularly when there are multiple objects to track. Furthermore, we find that SPGP-SARSA produces a search pattern with a higher coverage rate than the standard SPGP method. We also validate the effectiveness of the SPGP-SARSA algorithm through a trial where it is applied to a real-world data set of ocean currents in the Maldives. The outcome indicates that SPGP-SARSA can be an useful method for tracking ocean robots equipped with GPS in a realistic scenario. We have investigated the optical and magnetic properties of the 5d transition metal oxide GdInO$_3$, which exists in the form of a bilayer perovskite structure, and has been successfully synthesized through the Flux method. Our initial assessment of the crystal includes X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy, which have confirmed the distorted bilayer perovskite structure and provided vibrational modes at 487 K. Optical studies have revealed a band gap of 2.22 eV, while the analysis of dielectric functions has shown a direct band gap. The magnetic properties of the material have been found to follow the characteristics of localized spin dynamics, with the internal magnetic field being influenced by the strength of spin-orbit coupling and graded by the Bertoni factor. A comparison with theoretical models has enabled us to interpret the spectral features, and our results have enabled us to differentiate GdInO$_3$ from other 4f and 5d transition metal oxides. Additionally, the Flux method has allowed us to adjust the crystal size and study the effects of size on optical and magnetic properties. We conducted a thorough analysis of the HII region population within the galaxy UGC 8839 by utilizing wide-band photometry. This study revealed a significant correlation between the surface brightness of HII regions and their distance from the galaxy's center, a trend also observed in spiral galaxies like NGC 628 and M101, although the extent of this correlation varies. While the inner areas of UGC 8839 host small, bright HII regions, the outer regions are characterized by larger, less luminous HII regions. Additionally, the distribution of these objects within UGC 8839 follows a linear relationship when plotted against a spiral arm template, further supporting the theory that these HII regions are generated by the star formation processes associated with spiral arms. By calculating the radii of these HII regions relative to their birth places, we found several objects that have moved farther from their birth locations, indicating an outside-in star formation pattern in UGC 8839. A comparison with M101 showed that the HII region distribution in UGC 8839 has a larger radial extent. However, both galaxies share similar specific ranges of radial distribution for their HII regions. The star formation rates in UGC 8839 and M101 are comparable, but the galaxy with lower total mass, UGC 8839, exhibits a greater extent of its spiral arms. As a result, we propose that spiral arm instability plays a significant role in the galaxy's star formation process, particularly in low mass spiral galaxies. The presence of several small HII regions within the galaxy's central areas suggests the existence of a bulge with low mass-to-light ratio, which may be the result of a bulge dissolution triggered by massive star formation. The overall structure and star formation pattern of UGC 8839 support its classification as a low mass, typical spiral galaxy. The unique perspective on UGC 8839's structure offers a better understanding of this galaxy, which is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the study of spiral galaxies. Understanding how constraints in optimization problems for machine learning affects model performance is crucial, especially when the problems are non-convex and inherently complex, as is the case with supervised learning. By examining the minimal unsatisfiable cores in the problems' logical formulation, we can identify the key factors influencing a model's behavior. In this study, we enhance the Generalized Linear Discriminant Analysis (GLDA) framework by incorporating learning algorithms' complexities and developing a new formulation that leverages minimal unsatisfiable cores for hyperparameter optimization. By testing the proposed method on various datasets for supervised learning and one dataset for unsupervised learning, our results demonstrate that it outperforms traditional methods for hyperparameter optimization and facilitates a deeper understanding of the underlying data structures affecting model performance. Additionally, our findings indicate that the algorithm's complexity plays a significant role in the minimal unsatisfiable cores, enabling future exploration of its applications in other optimization problems. The precise detection and segmentation of surgical instruments are crucial components in developing effective automation systems for surgical assistance. To enhance the processing speed and accommodate variable input images, we propose the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet), a convolutional neural network that performs concurrent multi-task learning on instrument classification, segmentation, and boundary detection. In DDANet, two concurrent decoder modules with shared parameters process input images at different spatial resolutions. Each decoder module is equipped with an attention module that ensures focused feature extraction and combines output features to produce the final segmentation map. In experimental evaluations, DDANet demonstrated superior segmentation accuracy and processing speed compared to other deep learning networks, including U-Net, LinkNet, and FCN. Notably, DDANet achieved a notable increase in processing speed (33.33 FPS) without compromising segmentation accuracy (0.932), making it exceptionally well-suited for real-time surgical assistance applications. Furthermore, DDANet performed effectively across different datasets and demonstrated robustness in handling missing boundary annotations. Despite the growing demand for Re-identification (ReID) systems, the limited number of annotated images poses a challenge for universal ReID models. Unsupervised ReID has therefore gained significant attention recently. Contrasting methods, in particular, have shown notable success in this area by learning distinct codes for probe and gallery codes. However, these methods require manual label adjustment and time-consuming pair selection processes. In response, this paper introduces a novel contrastive ReID approach that automatically identifies contrasting samples from unsourced images. Based on the principle that images from the same identity have similar visual features, this method learns a projection function to reduce the dimensionality and promote visual feature similarity for images sharing the same label. Unlike traditional contrastive learning, this method incorporates a unique contrastive loss function that automatically identifies contrasting samples from unsourced probe images, thereby expanding the usable data for training. What's more, this method leverages the projection function to predict codes for unsourced probe images, thereby enhancing its effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to current unsupervised ReID methods and systems, including baseline methods such as Deep Allison and Coarse to Fine. What's more, this method successfully applies supervised and semi-supervised learning scenarios, showcasing potential for further research in this area. This study presents a new methodology for Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecasting, overcoming the limitations of the traditional GARCH model. By leveraging the advantages of long-short portfolios in enhancing VaR performance, we've developed an alternative framework. We observe a significant improvement in VaR prediction accuracy using our method over a common GARCH model in our specific data set, consisting of daily returns for eight major stock market indices from 2007 to 2018. Our approach also demonstrates a strong performance in relation to the Cuoco-Ludovico (CL) model, particularly when utilizing a minimal model, and exhibits superiority in VaR performance when utilizing a minimal model, particularly in tail risk estimation, as measured by the Extended Cuoco-Ludovico (ECL) model. We've further validated our framework's effectiveness through economic interpretation of results. Our proposed method has the benefit of incorporating economic insights without compromising VaR forecasting efficacy. Consequently, we believe this approach offers a viable alternative to the widespread GARCH models for VaR forecasting. Additionally, the features extracted from our model have the potential to be utilized in other applications involving financial time series. We analyzed the effectiveness of various sampling algorithms used for exploring pulsar timing array data, specifically focusing on the random walk algorithm. Iterative strategic sampling of parameter combinations was evaluated based on its ability to cover the underlying data space, and significant findings were for a specific dataset when the sampling interval was set to 0.35 days, or four times the expected value. However, it was also found that this optimal sampling setting is highly dependent on other factors such as data quality, pulsar characteristics, and the presence of gravitational wave signals. Consequently, further research is necessary to better comprehend the behavior of sampling algorithms in this context. Additionally, our study found that implementing a random walk algorithm results in a highly correlated sampling schedule, and that incorporating a pulsar's residual behavior can lead to more efficient coverage of the data space, ultimately suggesting that a random walk algorithm may be an effective tool for determining optimal sampling schedules. Nevertheless, it is also suggested that the choice of algorithm should be based on a thorough examination of data from multiple observations, rather than individual datasets. Finally, our study proposes utilizing the Thomas algorithm, known for its simplicity and efficiency in sampling parameter combinations, and provides a framework for implementing it in the context of pulsar timing array data. This research is part of efforts to enhance the sensitivity of pulsar timing array experiments in detecting gravitational waves, specifically by increasing the signal-to-noise ratio in timeseries data, and is currently available online as part of the Pakala Package on GitHub. These findings demonstrate the continued accuracy of lattice QCD predictions for the relationship between quark mass and the pion's properties, and further confirm previous studies on this topic. People confront uncertainty about the causes of poverty, which affects how they view the need for wealth redistribution. This research explores the varying expressions of this uncertainty in a simplified economic model consisting of three segments: those fortunate enough to have opportunities that may be influenced by luck, those whose opportunities are entirely determined by luck and are therefore unchangeable, and those whose fortunes are entirely determined by luck and can be altered by changing opportunities. The goal is to examine how the expression of uncertainty about the nature of poverty influences attitudes towards redistribution. The findings indicate that people are more sympathetic to giving money to those whose misfortune is seen as unlucky, whereas they are more supportive of altering opportunities to benefit those whose misfortune is viewed as a result of bad luck. These findings have real-world implications, as people's views on the role of luck in determining income may shape their reactions to various policies that aim to shift opportunities and ultimately affect the distribution of wealth. Furthermore, our study reveals that the tendency to overestimate the probability of events that benefit others in probability experiments, such as the lottery or charity giving, is linked to the expression of uncertainty about luck's impact on opportunities, rather than its impact on income. This research also discovers that people tend to assume that luck has a greater impact on opportunities than it actually does, according to our model, and that this misconception drives the expressed willingness to give to those whose misfortune is seen as unlucky. The duration of preference expression for giving to those affected by lucky opportunities is measured to be around five months, with a significant decline in expressed willingness after this period. The findings also highlight individual differences, as some people are less swayed by the uncertainty about luck's impact on opportunities and do not exhibit a clear preference for giving to those affected by lucky opportunities. Ultimately, our study suggests that people's reactions to poverty are influenced by the uncertainty about the cause of poverty, especially when it comes to the distinction between luck's impact on opportunities and its impact on income. The study also reveals that people's views on the expression of this uncertainty can shape their attitudes towards redistribution, and that this expression holds significant value in understanding various social phenomena, including charity giving, poverty, and the distribution of wealth. Additionally, DataScope enables more effective data fixing, with better model performance and reduced data retrieval costs. This paper explores the task of inferring high-dimensional structures, specifically hypergraphs, from lower-dimensional structures, namely graphs and their embeddings. We investigate two scenarios: first, reconstructing a hypergraph from a single graph; second, hypergraph reconstruction based on multiple graphs that represent different projections of the same high-dimensional structure. We discuss theoretical limitations as well as possible approaches and examine the feasibility of hypergraph reconstruction through a practical example involving the analysis of a musical composition. We propose a hypergraph reconstruction method that leverages network flow algorithms and demonstrate its effectiveness in a simulated environment. Our findings suggest that this method is robust in correcting errors that arise during the reconstruction process. However, we also identify challenges associated with the noise-to-signal ratio that influences the accuracy of hypergraph reconstruction. The Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework has been proven effective in learning from scratch for offline multi-agent systems. However, the current assumption that all agents start from the same initial state limits its application to natural environments. To overcome this hurdle, we propose an iterative method to compute the shared trajectories, allowing agents with different initial conditions to converge to the same final state distribution. This approach enables the efficient use of offline data, collected through human agent interactions, for training agent policies. By leveraging an efficient algorithm to compute the shared trajectories in reverse time, we can utilize existing trajectory methods to learn the state distribution. Furthermore, we introduce a method to compute the shared trajectories at the goal state, enabling the efficient incorporation of reward functions defined across the entire state space. Through experiments on practical scenarios and complex scenarios with human-provided data, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods. We investigate how single-particle entanglement among distinct subgroups affects nonlocality, steering, and correlation patterns in two-mode Gaussian states. Our analysis reveals that these phenomena are not solely governed by the entanglement between individual pairs of modes, but also exhibit significant non-classical behavior resulting from entanglement within the mult-mode context. Specifically, this intra-group entanglement is responsible for contributing to nonlocal effects and steering in quantum systems. Moreover, our findings indicate that the distinction between continuous-variable mult-mode entanglement and its single-particle entanglement counterparts is not fundamental, given the latter can be transformed into the former through linear unitary evolution. Notably, this insight applies even in the presence of non-Gaussian states, as demonstrated by an appropriate example. Consequently, we propose that mult-mode entanglement should be viewed as a form of single-particle entanglement residing within specific subgroups of the system, thereby refining our understanding of this concept. Furthermore, this perspective offers a new perspective on the discussion of entanglement within continuous-variable systems. Lastly, we provide an explicit example of a two-mode Gaussian state that exhibits mult-mode entanglement without single-particle entanglement, along with a general condition for the absence of intra-group entanglement among distinct subgroups. This condition is applicable to any wide-sense monogamous entanglement and holds even in the presence of non-Gaussian states. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the entanglement within specific subgroups is equivalent to correlation patterns arising from unitary evolution of single modes within those subgroups, thereby refining our understanding of entanglement within continuous-variable systems. Our approach utilizes a combination of entanglement simulation and error metrology, enabling us to assess the average physical error rate and logical error frequency even when physical errors become large and categorize gates into acceptability classes based on physical error rates. We create a new metric called gate usability, which measures the number of physically acceptable gates within each acceptability class and demonstrate its utility in understanding gate reliability. We utilize simulation results to outline strategies for improving gate reliability through iterative development and testing, which can be applied to various quantum storage systems. Furthermore, we propose a physical benchmarking protocol that distinguishes between two types of physical error processes assumptions and provide an analysis of its applicability and efficiency in distinguishing between these assumptions and the associated error rates. Additionally, we outline the potential for this protocol to be extended to fault-tolerant logical gate operations. We illustrate our framework's utility in evaluating the performance of quantum gate arrays constructed from parity-check qubit measurements and discuss its implications for quantum computing scalability. Our research provides a comprehensive benchmarking foundation that enables effective evaluation of quantum gate reliability and efficiency in multi-qubit system operation. In urban settings, automated vehicles can benefit from connected technology to optimize their journey through intersections. This study explores how connected automated vehicles can utilize real-time traffic signal data, particularly the yellow and red phases, to minimize delays and potential collisions. To achieve this, we develop a trajectory planning model that takes into account the signal phases and estimates the behavior of human drivers on the approach lanes, ultimately enabling the connected vehicle to anticipate their actions and navigate the intersection safely. By simulating this approach in a real-world environment, we demonstrate a significant reduction in travel time and lane changes compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, our simulation indicates that connected vehicles can reduce collisions with human-driven vehicles at the approach lanes by at least 45%. This showcases the potential of connected vehicles to mitigate human errors at urban intersections and sets the stage for future research in this area. Moreover, our method prioritizes cooperative behavior, enabling connected vehicles to conserve energy through decreased acceleration and braking. Ultimately, this trajectory planning model serves as a foundation for more advanced strategies in connected automated vehicles and can be integrated with other safety-critical systems. To facilitate replication and advancement of this work, the associated data and source code are available for public use. This approach can be further improved through additional optimization techniques and a larger, more diverse dataset of human driving patterns. Despite its limitations, our simulation shows a substantial improvement over current methods and sets the stage for connected vehicles to safely navigate urban intersections in the future. The extensive, persistent polar vortices in a planet's stratosphere are areas where the atmosphere rotates at a different speed, creating stable and slow-moving air. Studies of these vortices, known as storm systems, have focused primarily on Jupiter and Saturn. This study moves beyond storm systems, examining less explored vortices in the polar regions of Jupiter and Saturn. Using data from the Cassini and Hubble Space Telescopes, we previously identified an unusual vortex forming in Saturn's north polar region and characterized its 1996 appearance. This vortex had a central temperature drop, surrounding winds that moved in a circular pattern, and a steady flow of air bringing mid-latitudes to the south pole. As expected, it disappeared with the arrival of summer in the northern hemisphere. This study extends our previous research, using infrared observations from 1996 to 2020 to monitor Saturn's north polar vortex and comparing it to the south polar region during the same period. Notably, the south polar region showed similar conditions to the north polar region, but only during the winter months in both hemispheres. As spring and summer arrived in the south, the vortex dissolved, while it persisted in the north until the arrival of the solar wind in the summer of 2020, when it broke apart. This finding highlights the unique atmospheric conditions at the south pole during the southern hemisphere's summer, which include a broken vortex and enhanced auroral activity, and suggests that the south polar vortex is influenced by the weak rotation and unique geometry of the south polar region, allowing polar mid-latitude air to reach the south pole, causing the vortex to disappear. In contrast, the north polar vortex may remain intact due to the stronger rotation and different temperature distribution in this region. This study provides the first extended monitoring of a polar vortex in our solar system and offers a broader perspective on the complex atmospheric systems in our solar system. It also highlights the need for further research into the interactions between the solar wind, magnetic field, and atmospheric rotation in Saturn's upper atmosphere and the potential effects of changing solar radiation on these systems. Additionally, it suggests that the unique conditions at the south pole during the southern hemisphere's summer may be analogous to the conditions observed at the north pole during the northern hemisphere's summer, and that the south polar vortex could provide a model for understanding the summer months in the north polar region. Additionally, we establish an optimal lower bound for the duration of blow-up in the presence of a boundary, and this boundary contributes to the formation of soliton-like behavior within the remaining unbounded region. Our findings are achieved through an accurate analysis of the symmetries and a new method of estimating the concentration of energy using a weighted energy approach. This method is applicable not only to the given equation but also to a broader class of nonlinear Schrödinger equations under specific symmetry conditions. In the case where the boundary does not interact with the support of the initial data, we can derive a stronger result, demonstrating that the blow-up rate remains consistent with that observed in the unbounded case. To further analyze the dynamics within the bounded domain, we introduce a new variable that represents the time-reversal of the solution, and by estimating the concentration of the new variable using a weighted energy approach, we are able to derive an optimal lower bound for the blow-up time in the presence of a boundary that does not interact with the support of the initial data. This method of estimation also provides insight into the formation of soliton-like behavior within the remaining unbounded region. Our findings are achieved without relying on the method of stationary solutions, making this approach generally applicable to a broader class of nonlinear Schrödinger equations. In the context of the given equation, we are able to establish the existence of soliton-like solutions, both with and without the presence of a boundary. When the boundary does not interact with the support of the initial data, we can demonstrate the existence of soliton-like solutions within the remaining unbounded region. In the presence of a boundary that does not overlap with the support of the initial data, we can establish the existence of soliton-like solutions within the entire domain, including the boundary. In matrix optimization, where the objective and constraint are factorized as $f(U,V)=\psi(U)+\sum_{i=1}^n\rho_i(V_Ux_i), V_Ux_i \leq b_i, x_i \leq e_i$, we demonstrate that under restricted strong convexity and smoothness of $\psi$ and $\rho$, the geodesic convexity and smoothness are inherited by the factorized objective $f$. This property is further utilized to establish a non-ergodic $O(1/\kappa^2)$ iteration complexity for an inexact proximal recursive algorithm. Moreover, we derive an inexact version of the algorithm, which can handle large-scale matrices by employing a combination of block Bregman projections and the Pythagorean theorem. This innovation enables the generation of a new inexact scheme for an iterative method. We also establish the convergence of the inexact scheme and the resulting iteration complexity remains $O(1/\kappa^2)$. To accommodate general Bregman distances, we introduce an inexact proximal recursive algorithm with an alternating update structure, which can be viewed as a special case of the proposed inexact algorithm. We also provide a theoretical guarantee for the convergence of the alternating update method. To illustrate the performance of the proposed inexact algorithm, we conduct numerical experiments on various applications, including matrix decompositional techniques and robust matrix estimation. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed inexact algorithm, particularly when dealing with large-scale matrices and datasets. The implementation of the proposed inexact algorithm is also open to further customization and extension. The source code for the numerical experiments is available online at https://github.com/zhangyudong/InexactProximalRecursiveAlgorithm. The code has been successfully run on MATLAB R2018a and TensorFlow 1.14.0 on a computer with Ubuntu 18.04 operating system and CPU specifications of 2.60GHz and 7.79 with 64GB RAM. The total running time for the experiments is approximately 1.53 hours. The proposed inexact algorithm has significant implications for matrix optimization and related applications, and the results provided can serve as a starting point for further research and extension of the algorithm. In 1990, J.A. Gomez-Pando proposed a conjecture about bipartite graphs with maximum degree 3, stating that a strong edge-coloring with 3 colors is possible. This conjecture remains unconfirmed. We've established a related result for double-cubic bipartite graphs of finite order, where a strong edge-coloring with 3 colors is applicable. Additionally, an infinite class of bipartite graphs has been identified, called double-cubic trees of infinite order, characterized by using a specific construction method. We've proven that these graphs do have a strong edge-coloring with 3 colors. This leads to our new conjecture about double-cubic graphs: if they have a strong edge-coloring with 3 colors, then it should be possible to create an analogous coloring on its double-graph counterpart. To support this, we present evidence through our established results and a few additional examples. This work also introduces a novel approach using (1,1)-edge-mappings to examine strong edge-coloring in bipartite graphs. This technique allows us to derive a few general properties related to (1,1)-edge-mappings and its connections to strong edge-coloring. We've already mentioned the construction of our infinite class of graphs named double-cubic trees, but what distinguishes this construction from regular construction is that it uses edge-mappings between its component parts. We've further expanded on this construction and demonstrated its flexibility by generating multiple variants. Among these variants, we've confirmed that a strong edge-coloring with 3 colors is always present. This has given us a new upper limit for the number of strong edge-colorings in double-cubic graphs of finite order. We've also explored the relationship between our construction of double-cubic trees and other types of cubic graphs, such as Paulus construction and snarks. Finally, we've established a few more general results related to the number of strong edge-colorings in graph parameters. These results relate to the work of J.A. Gomez-Pando and provide new upper limits for the number of strong edge-colorings in certain types of double-cubic graphs of finite order. These new limits are more restrictive than previously confirmed values. Moreover, we've confirmed that our construction of double-cubic trees also applies to some of the smallest possible world records in cubic graphs. The background of gravitational waves produced by the big bang's primordial turbulence may be distorted if heavy particles existed in the early universe, potentially influencing cosmological observations. The impact of such distortions on the effectiveness of future gravitational wave detectors is assessed, with the involvement of various particle properties and interaction strengths. The analysis indicates that if the primordial gravitational wave signal is sufficiently loud, even a small distortion can significantly diminish the practical usefulness of these detectors, with some scenarios requiring a signal ten times more intense to achieve the same detection capabilities. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the properties of the primordial gravitational wave spectrum can be inferred through the analysis of the gravitational wave spectrum produced by the universe's thermal fluctuations, without needing additional information about the universe's early stages. This analysis also enables the determination of the appropriate parameters for future gravitational wave experiments, such as the sensitivity requirements for detectors, and provides a framework for reevaluating the feasibility of gravitational wave experiments in various scenarios. With future experiments capable of detecting a very loud primordial gravitational wave signal, it becomes imperative to incorporate the properties of the primordial gravitational wave spectrum into the design of these experiments. Additionally, it is essential to account for the influence of the primordial gravitational wave signal on the cosmic gravitational wave background in order to accurately determine the parameters of the early universe. The development of more sophisticated theories of gravity, such as the Palatini approach, may also be tested through the analysis of the primordial gravitational wave signal, with a possible indication of new physics beyond the standard model of particle interactions awaiting discovery in the primordial gravitational wave spectrum. With the scheduled upgrade to the Einstein Telescope, which will significantly enhance the sensitivity to gravitational waves, it is now more crucial than ever to understand the primordial gravitational wave signal and its implications for the effectiveness of these experiments. With multiple gravitational wave detectors set to operate in the future, it is possible that the presence of a primordial gravitational wave background with distinct characteristics can be confirmed through a multidetector analysis, even if the signal itself is relatively faint. The ability to distinguish between the primordial gravitational wave background and the cosmic gravitational wave background, which consists of fluctuations generated during the universe's transition from the quark-gluon plasma phase to the hadronic phase, will be crucial in this confirmation process. The parameters of the standard model of particle interactions, such as the number of light quarks and leptons, can be inferred from the properties of the primordial gravitational wave background, with any deviation indicating the presence of new physics beyond the standard model.

Our research investigates how a helical swimmer's navigation is impacted by interacting particles on a surface that has a "snowman-like effect," where the force of attraction becomes repulsive due to an angle-dependent transition, influenced by the swimmer's size and position. By modeling a helical swimmer with varying diameters and heights, we find that its motion can be significantly affected when the transition zone is located near the swimmer's midpoint. Specifically, we found that large helices experience a significant locomotion decrease due to this interaction, while smaller helices can continue moving despite it. Moreover, we found that the snowman-like effect can cause helical swimmers to move in the opposite direction, and that this phenomenon is more prevalent for larger swimmers. Additionally, we found that increasing the diameter of a helical swimmer results in it being pulled back by the surface, while reducing the diameter allows it to navigate past the transition zone. Finally, we found that our model applies not only to helical swimmers but also to other surface swimmers, such as rods and circles, and that the snowman-like effect is relevant to lozenge-shaped swimmers only when their long diameter is comparable to the swomer's height. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how surface swimmers are impacted by forces that change direction at specific angles, and have implications for the design of swimming machines that can effectively navigate through environments with complex forces at play. Additionally, our research reveals that even small changes in the behavior of forces can have a major impact on the performance of surface swimmers. Lastly, our study suggests that there are still many aspects of the locomotion of complex swimmers that are yet to be understood, and that there is significant room for further research in this field. This study explores how the Hamming distance from optimal solutions evolves during
optimization processes driven by co-evolutionary genetic algorithms, comparing social
learning to individual learning strategies. Our analysis focuses on the Hamming distance
associated with the expected nearest neighbor of each individual within their population,
as this represents the minimum improvement required for the individual to become the
fittest within two distinct learning scenarios. Our research reveals a significant differ-
ence in expected Hamming distances between social and individual learning scenarios,
notably in early optimization stages. Nevertheless, our findings suggest that both
learning approaches converge to similar Hamming distances as optimization progresses. 
To investigate the effects of population size and selection pressure on optimization
processes, we conducted multiple experiments using both social and individual learning
strategies in co-evolutionary genetic algorithms. Our results demonstrate that both
learning approaches converge to similar Hamming distances, notably independent of
population size, yet vary significantly during early optimization stages. Consequently,
this study provides initial evidence supporting the notion that "group thinking" can
exceed "individual thinking" in co-evolutionary genetic algorithms. In addition, our
results highlight notable distinctions in Hamming distance evolution between early,
mid-and late optimization stages. Furthermore, our analysis of TSP instances reveals
that both learning approaches converge to precise Hamming distances, both prior to and
following optimization, although they distinguish itself in mid-optimization stages. 
In contrast, our experiments on LP instances show no notable differences in Hamming
distance evolution between social and individual learning strategies, despite both
learning approaches converging to similar Hamming distances at various optimization
stages. Ultimately, our research paves the way for theoretical analysis of co-evolutionary
genetic algorithms through empirical data, while also highlighting the complex
evolution of Hamming distances in dependency on problem type, population size and
selection pressure. Consequently, this study advocates for a multi-faceted, problem-
type aware approach to analyzing CEGAs. As a by-product of this research, we introduce
a novel method for calculating expected Hamming distances from Nash Equilibrium, both
for co and individual learning scenarios. This study builds upon our preceding research
presenting results for the Hamming distance from optimal solutions in optimization
processes driven by co and individual learning strategies in CEGAs. As such, this study
contributes to a broader theoretical analysis of CEGAs through empirical data, while
also exploring the complex evolution of Hamming distances in dependency on problem
type

Unfortunately, the sheer amount of data available poses a significant challenge. Existing approaches struggle to tackle this issue due to limitations in deep learning techniques and the absence of large, secured datasets. We propose a novel method utilizing bidirectional LSTMs in a multi-task framework to enhance the accuracy of security concept extraction. In this model, an encoder handles both the input text and the security concept label, facilitating the exchange of contextual information between them. We also introduce a large dataset called DREBIN, comprised of 5000 Android application descriptions, along with their vulnerability labels, available for securing two well-known concept extraction datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the enhanced performance of this model on multiple datasets, achieving a notable improvement of around 10% in F1-score over basic LSTM and the base model. We introduce a one-dimensional mixed opinion formation model, where individuals can hold either "Ising" opinions, represented by magnetic dipole moments, or "continuum" opinions, described by a normalized temperature. The model integrates the standard opinion formation dynamics with heat exchange between spies, resulting in a system where spins interact through both pairwise magnetic forces and thermal influences. The equation that describes the time evolution of the magnetization in this model is analogous to the magnetization equation for a pure Ising model, yet with an additional term representing the effect of the continuum opinion component. By applying a suitable change of variables, we rewrite the magnetization equation to resemble the equation derived for a pure Ising model, allowing us to identify specific stationary solutions. Through a similar transformation of the variable that captures the time dependence of the continuum opinion, we obtain an equation whose solutions are identical to those of the corresponding equation for the pure Ising model. The corresponding solution for the continuum opinion is a nonlinear diffusion equation with a non-constant diffusion coefficient, influenced by the average magnetization. This coefficient can be either positive, resulting in the destruction of correlations, or negative, leading to the enhancement of correlations. The non-stationary solutions of the continuum opinion variable exhibit power law behavior in both time and its square root. The model's spatial correlation function displays a similar structure to that of the Ising model, yet with the additional effect of correlations in the continuum opinion component, influencing the magnetic correlations. The model exhibits a phase transition from a disordered to a ordered state at a non-zero temperature, indicative of the appearance of a spontaneous magnetization. The specific heat capacity displays a divergent peak at the same temperature as the magnetization, indicating an intense peak. The model's lattice size has a substantial impact on the behavior of the magnetization and correlation functions, resulting in differences that fade into the infinite lattice limit. The model can also accommodate multiple spontaneous magnetizations, giving rise to the coexistence of multiple opinions in the asymptotic state. The particular case of a binary Ising model can be viewed as the model with continuum opinions fixed at specific, extreme values. The model's symmetry results in the spontaneous formation of chiral charges and resulting external magnetic field, which can be used to explain certain observational data. The model's chirality-driven external magnetic field is comparable to the large-scale magnetic fields observed in the interstellar medium. Research into COVID-19 transmission through droplets has focused primarily on three factors: droplet size, the surrounding environment, and time spent around infected individuals. To investigate the impact of these factors, we developed a mathematical model that incorporates them. However, our model distinguishes between large droplets that carry maximal viral loads and smaller droplets that may still infect individuals. We analyzed how infections behave under these conditions both theoretically and through numerical simulations. Our results indicate that infections can vary greatly depending on the values of alpha, beta, gamma, sigma, and tau. Specifically, we found that certain combinations of sizes and environments can prevent the spread of the virus entirely. Moreover, we identified the role that air current speeds play in empty spaces and how they can cause the virus to survive in settings with minimal circulation. To further understand our model's predictions, we compared them with existing studies that modeled the transmission process continuously. Through this comparison, we gained insight into the behavior of the model for large droplets and how it relates to the law of large numbers. To make our model more applicable to real-world scenarios, we proposed modifying it to account for multiple infected sources and discussed potential future directions for the model, including the addition of protective measures such as masks. Through this modification, we were able to derive a model that reflects the benefits of wearing masks and provides a possible explanation for the disparity in infection rates between men and women. To validate our model, we planned to compare its predictions with existing data from different countries, but this comparison remains a topic for future exploration. Ultimately, our study presents a novel approach to understanding the transmission of the virus through droplets and highlights the significance of factors that influence its spread. However, further analysis with empirical data is necessary to thoroughly validate the proposed model. Additionally, there are numerous directions for extending this model to better comprehend the complex mechanisms underlying the spread of the virus, especially when multiple sources are present. As a supplementary file, we include numerical solutions to the closed-form expressions discussed in the article. Furthermore, we have initiated a computational tool using MATLAB that enables users to adjust parameters, obtain numerical solutions, and visualize the results. This tool is available upon request. We have already initiated conversations with researchers affiliated with the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to compare our model's predictions with existing data from various countries. We plan to present the outcomes of these comparisons in future updates. Despite the several hypotheses our model proposes, the exact mechanism by which the virus is released from droplets remains an unsolved mystery

Inverse and ill-posed problems pose a significant obstacle in various applications and have substantial practical implications, and their challenging nature demands a careful approach. Recently, Deep Learning models have shown considerable promise in solving such problems by constructing a solution set that includes the desired answer. This paper provides an overview of our research on incorporating prior knowledge and regularization techniques within Neural Networks to solve inverse problems. We explored multiple strategies including Tikhonov, early stopping, and support vector machine methods, and found that they can be successfully integrated with Deep Learning by incorporating the prior information into the regularization term and minimizing the distance between the measured data and the model's output. We also analyzed the effectiveness of these techniques in combination with Neural Networks for both synthetic and real-world image reconstruction scenarios, and found that they can effectively enhance the quality of the reconstructed image, and successfully demonstrated the incorporation of prior information within the network, and found that it successfully guided the reconstruction process towards the actual solution. This research paves the way for the use of Deep Learning models in inverse problems, particularly those involving large data sets, and could also be applied to other optimization problems by constructing a suitable loss function. Using a holographic method, we calculate the thermal partition functions for SU(N) and U(N) groups in $d$-dimensional space. These calculations apply to finite values of N. We find that the partition functions can also be represented as the thermal free energy of a fundamental M2-brane in a specific PP wave geometry. This geometry is based on the SU(N) or U(N) algebra and does not depend on any linear combination of the rank N's charges. Notably, the partition functions of SU(N) and U(N) exhibit distinct differences for finite N, whereas they converge to the same value for large N. This distinction arises because the partition functions can also be given by the M5-brane's thermal free energy in a geometry correlated with the fundamental M2-brane, although this correlation only holds for finite N. Additionally, we derive the partition functions' leading N charge by determining the M2-brane's dimensionless charge in various geometries, including the PP wave and the D$(d-2)$-brane's background. This understanding enables us to extract the M2-brane's thermal pressure, which is found to be equal to its thermal energy multiplied by $(d-1)/d$. We also establish that the M5-brane's thermal pressure can be obtained by dimensionally increasing the M2-brane, and that both the M2-brane and the M5-brane have the same thermal pressure in ratios that are independent of N for finite values of N. However, these results for the M2-brane are only valid for finite N. For large N, they converge to a different expression. We find that certain ratios of the M2-brane's thermal free energy or pressure to those of the M2-brane in the PP wave geometry are all equal to $N^2$ or $N$, respectively. These ratios again rely on the fundamental M2-brane and hold only for finite N. Furthermore, we derive the M2-brane's thermal pressure by considering the M5-brane's thermal free energy and find that it equals the M2-brane's thermal free energy multiplied by $N^2$. In deep learning systems, silent data corruption can cause significant issues by introducing errors in training data, which can then be propagated to influence critical decisions. SDH, a recent approach, addresses this challenge by introducing non-uniform degree restrictions on input data, ensuring that only substantially altered inputs can influence the model during training. We contribute to this line of research by exploring the concept of non-uniform range restrictions and investigate their potential to prevent silent data corruptions in neural networks. Our study demonstrates that a simple layer-wise bit flipping technique can effectively implement these restrictions and showcase its efficacy on various models, including multilayer perceptrons, CNNs, and LSTMs. Moreover, we validate the efficacy of this technique by conducting experiments on multiple datasets, revealing a notable suppression of silent data corruptions along with concrete examples illustrating how this technique can safeguard model accuracy in high-noise environments. We also examine the fundamental properties of this technique and explore potential avenues for further research. We are confident that our study will serve as a crucial starting point for exploring other innovative approaches to address the challenge of silent data corruptions in deep learning systems. In an economy, graph algorithms can help find the best solutions for graph-related issues.
For example, consider a situation where multiple companies are trying to make deals with each other, and the deals involve sending goods.

Building upon previous work, we examine the generalization of the Jordanian twist and its relationship to the simple Jordanian twist under Lie algebra deformation. We demonstrate that the generalized Jordanian twist can be explicitly represented in terms of Borel bicrossproduct algebra structure, and that this involves the simple Jordanian twist as a particular case. Additionally, we derive the star product corresponding to the simple Jordanian twist, and show that this product is commutative. Furthermore, we establish that both the generalized and simple Jordanian twists yield the same quantum deformation of the Lie algebra structure. Lastly, we explore the concept of'simple' within the context of Jordanian twist and propose that it may be equivalent to the algebra being solvable. This proposal is supported by examples, and also holds true for the su(2) algebra, which can be considered as having'simple' twisted forms. However, we also find that both the generalized and simple Jordanian twists fail to provide meaningful quantum deformations for complex Lie algebras such as su(3). Instead, these twists result in structures that are non-algebraic or depend on non-commutable elements, thereby rendering them impractical in this context. Consequently, our findings suggest that the term'simple' within the context of Jordanian twist is synonymous with the solvability of the underlying algebra. Moreover, our results indicate that both the generalized and simple Jordanian twists yield meaningful deformations solely within the domain of solvable algebras. Lastly, we propose that such twists fail to serve a fundamental purpose beyond this domain, and that the term'simple' in this context is merely a descriptive label. As such, our work does not encompass an scientific advancement over existing knowledge, but rather a thorough examination and interpretation of established results. Our research examines various particle ratios in different collision systems and energies as part of the ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC. By analyzing the data, we identify trends in particle production that emerge across small and large collision systems, and across low and high energies. At high energies, particle ratios remain consistent across different collision systems, exhibiting little dependence on the number of participating nucleons. Conversely, at lower energies, differences in particle ratios become more pronounced as the number of participating nucleons increases, likely due to enhanced secondary particle production. Furthermore, our analysis reveals an 'energy-bounce' phenomenon in mid-scale collision systems, characterized by particle ratios that resemble those seen in smaller or larger collision systems, depending on the energy level. The 'energy-bounce' is observed in mid-scale Pb-Pb collisions at an energy comparable to that of p-Pb collisions, and in mid-scale Cu-Cu collisions at an energy comparable to that of $A$-A collisions. The origin of the 'energy-bounce' is attributed to the interplay between primary and secondary particle production. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of the interplay between short-range and long-range physics in high-energy collisions. In addition, we observe an 'energy-bounce' in antiparticle-to-particle ratios, which indicates that the creation of antiparticles relative to particles maintains a similar trend to that of particle production itself. Consequently, we propose that the 'energy-bounce' phenomenon could serve as a reference point for investigating the properties of quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions, given its sensitivity to secondary particle production and potential connections to other mid-scale collision systems, such as nuclear multifragmentation. Alternatively, leveraging clean labels as a regularization constraint can effectively contain the error propagation to some extent. Experimental results demonstrate this approach to be an effective strategy for reducing noise's adverse impact on model performance. The proposed method is evaluated on the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge data, and the findings suggest that it facilitates more robust model training capable of overcoming noisy labels. The technique is particularly prudent as real datasets hardly contain marked errors, thus making it a viable approach for employing large clean datasets in training models with labeled data with extremely low noise rates. However, when confronted with substantial noise levels (above 20%), the method loses efficacy. Deep learning-based visual-inertial optimization models have achieved high accuracy
results in recent times. These models utilize computation power to process vast
amounts of data, in contrast to traditional VIO methods which rely on careful
evaluation to achieve optimal results. This paper delves into the unknown regions
of VIO by proposing a new approach, based on a deep learning model, specifically
a PoseNet system. This model is part of a larger framework called DirectVLLO,
which aims to optimize a multi-camera VIO system using a PoseNet system. The
framework is capable of processing continuous video input, with the PoseNet system
being replaced or updated between each optimization iteration. The paper includes
theoretical analysis and practical applications of this method, also showcasing its
implementation using a Tesla V100 GPU. Experimental results show that the proposed
approach runs in real-time, capable of processing up to 30 frames per second, and
achieves accurate optimization results when utilized with the ONTOS camera system. 
The proposed method's code will be made publicly available on the author's website.

Intelligent Robots and Systems, in Berlin, Germany.

Three-dimensional Weyl semimetals possess unique "square-root" topology, related to higher-order Weyl points. These higher-order points can be classified into two categories based on their response to certain symmetries, resulting in the folding of Weyl loops at high-energy levels. Despite the complex nature of these systems, particularly those with multiple Weyl points, existing theories fall short in explaining their band structures from first principles. To address this limitation, we develop a full microscopic theory to describe multiple Weyl points in three dimensions, including the interaction between distinct Weyl points. Our general framework identifies two primary mechanisms influencing the folding of Weyl loops: the direct combination of nearby Weyl points and the more complex folding resulting from the combination of more distant Weyl points, mediated by topological surface states. Through explicit calculations and analytical treatments, we demonstrate the essential features of several representative systems, including TaAs, TaP, and EuIn. Our findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the electronic structures of these systems and will facilitate the theoretical description of other systems with multiple Weyl points. Furthermore, we anticipate our general theories to stimulate ongoing and future research on higher-order Weyl semimetals. We introduce a novel perspective on the knowledge amalgamation problem, which involves a student model learning from multiple instructor models. A saliency-based method is proposed to identify the most effective combinations of instructor models, by highlighting the knowledge areas where the student will gain the most accuracy. To achieve this, we utilize an intermediate model to gauge the impact of each instructor model on the student's performance, as measured by the change in log likelihood. A statistical analysis is conducted to establish a relationship between the proposed saliency-based method and traditional approaches, which reveals that the proposed method can be viewed as a special case of the minimum distance method. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully identifies the most effective combinations of instructor models, as verified by high accuracy rates. Furthermore, the proposed saliency-based method is comparable to the existing method in terms of amplitude, but outperforms it in terms of amplitude under certain conditions. Additionally, an analysis of the proposed method is conducted from a computational learning perspective. The code for the proposed method is publicly available on GitHub.

Although the brain's spatial coding system relies heavily on grid cells with precisely spaced activation patterns, research suggests that grid cells can also accommodate varying activation patterns in response to external cues. This study investigates how cues affecting perceived environment size influence grid cell activation and its relationship to place fields in rats. Results indicate that grid cells with sensitive place fields, regardless of their order, exhibit distinct characteristics, including shorter periodic distances, broader angle preferences, and preferential focus on place fields located near the origin. Moreover, rats' ability to navigate based on visual size cues was found to trigger a higher level of grid cell oscillatory activity immediately following placement, with this activity eventually returning to a steady-state after a short period. Interestingly, rats with impaired navigation abilities due to visual size cue manipulation showed distinct variations in grid cell periodic distances and angle preferences when placed in large or small environments, with these variations disappearing when the underlying place fields were re-mapped through repeated exploration. These findings provide evidence that grid cells respond to external cues affecting perceived environment size by adjusting their activation patterns, as well as shed light on the underlying mechanisms governing grid cell adaptation in response to changes in place field mapability. Furthermore, they reveal that grid cells integrate sensory cues with their internal navigation experiences, involving a process that varies significantly when place fields are temporarily re-mapped. Additionally, the research suggests that grid cells are capable of distinguishing between temporary changes in place field mapability and permanent changes, as well as adapting to different modes of navigation, such as navigating based on visual size cues, which finds parallel evidence in computational models simulating similar behaviors in response to external cues. This research expands our understanding of the complex, dynamic nature of grid cells within the brain's spatial coding system, as well as the broader implications for the brain's ability to encode and navigate through diverse environments. at various rotation rates, particularly in slowly rotating stars with magnetic cycle 
activity. To achieve this, we integrate the memoryless mass flux constraint into the 
standard two-wave phase average dynamo theory, applying it to both the alpha-quenching

alpha-quenching dynamos cannot maintain magnetic cycles. This leads us to conclude

By calculating the time-dependent change in entropy at all stages, we find that it can be understood through a simple average of the initial state's correlations among the Harper states. Furthermore, we develop a temperature-like variable for the quench process, which remains relatively stable and is linked to the average of the harmonic oscillator energies corresponding to the initial states. Our analysis indicates that the irreversible entropy production during the quench is directly related to the difference between the average energies at the starting point and the new energy average. Additionally, we propose that the quench can be seen as a process involving successive small jumps that result in exponential decay of the harmonic oscillator energies at distinct points in time. We examine the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex within a unit cube $Q_n$ with interpolation nodes. Specifically, we investigate the condition $\binom{n+1}{2}$ for the number of interpolation nodes, and our findings regarding the nondegeneracy of the regular simplex are confirmed by numerical examples in dimensions three and four. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the number of interpolation nodes required to ensure the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex in $Q_n$. This lower bound is achieved without relying on probabilistic methods, and it offers a more precise understanding of the relationship between the number of interpolation nodes and the dimension of the unit cube. Finally, our work paves the way for an exploration of the geometric properties of interpolation nodes and their corresponding univariate functions. These investigations may lead to further insights into the convergence rates of the Kolmogorov width in $L_\infty(Q_n)$.

The formation of silicon surface structures through high-density anisotropic etching presents an interesting opportunity for creating optical components with unique properties. Combining etched silicon with layers of thermal oxide and buffer oxide allows for the formation of insulating surfaces within these structures. Research has demonstrated the ability to modify the internal and external surfaces of these structures through anisotropic etching, yet there remains a limitation to achieving accurate optical performance due to inherent differences between etched silicon and etched oxide. This discrepancy stems from distinct carrier concentrations within each material type. This paper compares carrier concentrations in etched silicon and etched oxide, identifying that etched silicon exhibits a negative carrier concentration, whereas etched oxide has a significantly more pronounced positive carrier concentration. Furthermore, this difference in carrier concentration is shown to affect the refractive index of each material, resulting in a visible difference in intensity between light passing through etched silicon and etched oxide. Additionally, this discrepancy is demonstrated to contribute to beam steering when light passes through these structures. Techniques are presented for adjusting etched silicon and etched oxide to match their carrier concentrations with one another, resulting in a negligible difference in refractive index. Finally, this research is applied to a sensor that utilizes a microinterferometer to detect thin film thickness variations, showcasing the effectiveness of these findings. The sensor's performance is enhanced through the modification of etched silicon and etched oxide, allowing for accurate measurement of film thickness despite environmental temperature fluctuations. The sensitivity and measurement range of this sensor can be adjusted through the modification of etched silicon and etched oxide. Successful operation of this sensor is demonstrated through a working prototype. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of modifying surface structures, allowing for the optimization of their optical performance. If these elements, cyclically returned to the surface through interior processes, were released into the atmosphere, they would greatly exceed current estimates of volcanic gas emissions, drastically changing the planetary climate. This concept, known as the "interior-exterior coupling hypothesis," suggests a feedback loop between the mantle and atmosphere, where elements cycle between the two, influencing climate and geology. Despite its implications for the Earth's history, this hypothesis remains untested. To evaluate its validity, we need to consider if the elements essential for life on Earth could have become trapped in the mantle during the planet's formation, and if there are enough volatile compounds in the mantle to modify the atmosphere through volcanic activity. Analyzing these conditions in our model, we find that the Earth's atmosphere would have been significantly different if the elements necessary for life had become isolated in the mantle. However, even then, we find that the interior-exterior coupling hypothesis has a strong presence in our simulations. The reason for this is that even if all the elements that became trapped in the mantle were released into the atmosphere, there would still be enough volatile compounds in the mantle to drastically alter the atmosphere through volcanic activity. Our team has theoretical insights that support the higher methyl ion yield hypothesis proposed by Sato et al. We used a combination of density functional theory and statistical mechanics to analyze the structures of 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PDO) and 1,3-propanediol (1,3-PDO) at different temperatures, as well as their oligomerized forms. Our data reveal that both PDO forms exhibit similar structures at room temperature, but 1,2-PDO produces more methyl cations than 1,3-PDO due to differences in oligomerization. Additionally, our results indicate that the most abundant structures of both PDO forms undergo an ordered-to-disordered phase transition at higher temperatures, aligning with the experimental M+/M+ ratio increase observed by Sato et al. This is anticipated to enhance methyl ion production in the higher temperature environment of an ion source. However, further investigation is needed to validate the link between this phase transition and the increased methyl ion yield. Our study provides a theoretical basis for the higher methyl ion yield hypothesis and offers a possible explanation for the difference in methyl ion yields between 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO. It is suggested that this difference originates from the distinct oligomerization tendencies of these two isomers, resulting in varying methyl cation production. The most abundant structures of both PDO forms, which exhibit similar structures at room temperature but differ in oligomerization, serve as the starting point for this investigation. Oligomerization is critically examined in the gas phase through a combined approach involving theoretical optimization and statistical mechanics, with the focus on identifying the most probable structures of PDO monomers, dimers, trimers, and larger oligomers up to 5 units at 298 K. The relative stability of these oligomers is determined by calculating their free energies, which provide valuable insights into the structure of PDO in the gas phase. It is observed that 1,2-PDO forms more stable dimer and trimer than 1,3-PDO, whereas 1,3-PDO exhibits higher stability for oligomers consisting of 4 or more units. In cancer research, understanding the disease's progression and development is crucial for developing effective treatments. To achieve this, graph neural networks have shown significant promise in analyzing complex tissue structures and their cellular components. A major limitation of existing approaches lies in their reliance on manually curated annotations and training data. In our study, we build upon a previous framework by Vinni et al., which utilizes a graph neural network to classify tissue representations in cancer research. We enhance their findings by introducing a method that extracts cellular features without relying on label information. Our approach includes a graphical model with cellular characteristics, which can be learned through a process called self-supervision. We apply this model to analyze tissue structures within lymph nodes affected by breast cancer, using data from the MLscope challenge. Our results show that our method delivers a precision rate of 78%, outperforming conventional methods and demonstrating the potential for unsupervised learning in this domain. Moreover, we observe that our approach provides cellular feature extraction in line with established norms in the field. We also explore the influence of different neural network components on our model's performance and provide code availability for further research. Our study presents a foundational framework for graph-based analysis of complex tissue structures and encourages the exploration of additional challenges and research questions.
