To accelerate the computation of gravitational forces in large astrophysical simulations, we integrated the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) into the Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) framework of the AREPO code. To maintain consistency with the existing implementation of stellar winds, we modified FMM to account for wind velocity effects, thus enabling its integration into the code. Through FMM integration, we achieved a significant improvement in computational performance, with a speedup of approximately 10 times when solving for gravitational forces. However, we also encountered a limit to FMM's efficiency, specifically when resolving highly complex interactions within dense regions of star clusters. In response, we developed a hybrid approach that leverages FMM in combination with the direct summation method to adaptively tackle these challenging scenarios. As a result, we were able to further enhance computational performance by an additional order of magnitude in certain situations. Through this work, we successfully developed a high-performance method for computing gravitational forces in star clusters and other astrophysical applications, with our new approach set to become a key component of the AREPO code in future simulations. Furthermore, our research provides an invaluable contribution to the development of similar simulation codes. Additionally, our study includes detailed analysis and relevant parameters for applying this method to various simulations. This paper introduces a novel contrastive learning algorithm for cross-anatomy domain adaptation, which enables the segmentation of complex anatomical structures. By incorporating semi-supervised learning, our method enhances the adaptation capability by introducing similar and distinct sample pairs across domains. We develop a contrastive loss function based on both label-driven and feature-driven similarities, which leverages both domain-labeled data and paired unlabeled data to enhance the adaptation performance. Furthermore, we introduce a coarse-to-fine adaptation process to adapt a source domain expert network to the target domain, leveraging the contrastive distances from the contrastive learning stage. Empirical evaluations on two critical medical applications, organ segmentation in chest and abdominal CT scans, and brain tumor segmentation in MRI images, confirm the superiority of our method over existing domain adaptation techniques. We examine the properties of a plasma waveplate used in magnetized plasma to change the polarization of microwaves, and determine the minimum thickness required. This thickness is found to be influenced by plasma electron density and magnetic field strength, and further, we find it should be greater than a specific multiple of the electron cyclotron wavelength. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the plasma waveplate and a plasma layer that can be used to convert left-handed microwaves into right-handed microwaves, and discuss its connection to a layer that can convert left-handed microwaves into left-handed microwaves, but with a lower density and half the thickness. If this layer with a density lower than half of the critical density is launched by a weak electromagnetic wave, it can modify the dielectric properties of the main plasma layer with significant density, resulting in a thick waveplate with specific characteristics. This could potentially allow for the conversion of microwaves of various frequencies, including those in the millimeter range, and even X-ray microwaves. This could also enable the study of the cyclotron maser in magnetic fields with cyclotron wavelengths of a few centimeters or less. This could be achieved with current-day gyrotrons, and also offers the possibility of using plasma waveplates to convert the beam from a backward wave oscillator and produce a useful output. This could be particularly useful for the development of more efficient and cost-effective next-generation particle accelerators. This concept of a plasma waveplate can also be applied to the study of high-density plasma, such as in the case of Xe targets irradiated with X-rays in x-ray free electron lasers. Finally, we propose the design of an experiment to test the properties of a plasma waveplate at the 80T TRISTAN magnet in Moscow. This experiment has the potential to demonstrate the conversion of Xe X-rays into the opposite polarization, and further, could investigate the emission of X-ray harmonic frequencies generated in highly dense iridium plasma by X-rays. Selective labeling techniques address this challenge by allocating high-quality sample labeling to specific locations, where the model's uncertainty is greatest. The spread of fake news through social media has become a pressing concern in the fight against disinformation. Machine learning models that learn from the context in which information is presented have shown potential in combating this issue effectively. As these models typically operate on a single-article basis, they may not fully capture the underlying dynamics present in sets of related articles. In contrast, deep learning methods that incorporate contextual information from these sets have been shown to yield superior results in various tasks. However, very few studies have examined the suitability of these methods for tackling the dissemination of fake news. In this work, we investigated the possibility of employing a deep neural network that incorporates context within sets of related articles to classify individual articles as true or false. Our findings indicated that while standard machine learning models perform poorly on this task, introducing contextual information significantly enhances the accuracy of fake news detection. Furthermore, we observed that using context has a greater impact on harder-to-detect false information. Local metric maps in robotics, such as Seemaps, rely on distant sensor readings to build a detailed understanding of environment and navigate within it. Our approach, HiTMap, diverges from this strategy by maintaining a simplified, coherent map of your surroundings through continuous, near-by observations. By limiting its scope to the present view and past navigational history, HiTMap significantly reduces navigation computations in comparison to grid-based methods, capitalizing on the fact that future navigation routes are likely to mimic present navigation patterns. Quantum electronics incorporates the principles of quantum mechanics into the study of electronic devices, offering a precise approach for calculating the average properties of these devices. However, studying the entanglement within these devices is a more complex task. To tackle this challenge, we apply two different methods to measure entanglement: the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix method. By examining a wide range of devices, including diodes, transistors, and photon devices, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in assessing entanglement and providing insights into the quantum mechanics underlying the devices, even when individual measurements yield unclear results. Our research provides a powerful tool for analyzing the quantum properties of microelectronic devices. Furthermore, we propose the concept of entanglement inheritance, where a change in the quantum properties of a component is passed down to the entire system, even when the component itself undergoes a significant change. This concept is applicable to both linear and nonlinear devices. Our research offers a new perspective on quantum mechanics, where the properties of a system can vary depending on the inheritance of entanglement within that system. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for exploring entanglement in quantum electronics.

Our research aims to advance the study of sDP and its applications in machine learning and data analysis.

We refer to this core as "veiled" because its underlying shape remains unknown and undetected. To tackle this challenge, we divide cloud structures into two parts - a thick, outer layer and a possible core - and use two separate mathematical formulas to model them. The outer layer is represented by a formula that accounts for optical thickness, air density, and particle size, while the core is modeled using a more general formula that can produce various shapes, including plates, tubes, and spheres. By combining these models and solving inverse problems, we can map cloud structures and their cores, even when the core remains hidden from view. We applied our approach to analyze real clouds observed from satellite and compared our results with model simulations, revealing that our method can both map cloud structures and core, even when the core remains hidden, and that our approach detects the same categories of clouds as the kinetic theory of gases. A notable arrangement of planets has been identified around the K-dwarf star AD Leo, comprising two mini-Neptunes that transit their star. The properties of these two planets were determined through a combination of photometric, radial-velocity, and spectroscopic astronomical observations. The results show that both planets have masses under 35 Earth masses and periods of around 6.5 to 19.2 days. The habitable zone of AD Leo is home to two worlds that could potentially host life, and due to their transits, will be prime targets for studying the atmospheres of potential life-bearing planets through spectroscopy of their transits. Additionally, the large angle between their orbits presents an opportunity to study the interactions between these two planets through their gravitational connection, and potentially even observe effects of tidal heating. Existing data, supplemented by new observations from ELODIE, it is determined that the two planets have a mass ratio close to equal, which may indicate a tidal interaction between them. As a result, the system AD Leo deserves closer examination to explore its unique characteristics in the context of exoplanetary physics. Finally, it is also worth mentioning that the detection of the third planet, AD Leo d, which has a long orbital period of around 49.7 days and is also located in the habitable zone, further highlights the exceptional planetary array surrounding the star AD Leo. Further research is needed to completely understand the setup of the system and its evolution, as well as to uncover more about the planets themselves, but without a doubt, the discovery of the transiting planets around the star AD Leo has brought attention to a high-priority target for upcoming missions aimed at studying exoplanets. Through new observations from the Kepler spacecraft and the TESS mission, more is being learned about the system and its unique characteristics, which hold many clues about the physics of planets and their development. Ultimately, the exceptional array of planets around the star AD Leo makes it an ideal subject for study in the context of exoplanetary physics. We have conducted an in-depth examination of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2, investigating their behavior both in interstitial and substitutional states. Our analysis, which combines density functional theory and classical force field methods, reveals significant differences in the properties of interstitial and substitutional impurities. In interstitial sites, carbon and nitrogen atoms exhibit similar behavior, with their lone pairs pointing towards neighboring oxygen atoms and resulting in a net negative charge on oxygen and a positive charge on the titanium atoms nearby. In contrast, when these atoms substitute for titanium, the extra electrons are transferred to oxygen atoms, leading to a shorter Ti-O bond and a higher energy state. Our results also show that interstitial nitrogen impurities can form pairs or clusters, which are not observed with substitutional nitrogen. Furthermore, we found that both interstitial and substitutional impurities have high mobility, with the latter being influenced by the motion of oxygen atoms nearby. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2. The long-term stability of liquid foams typically depends on two key factors: the surface tension and the viscosity of the liquid films, and a third factor known as the roughness factor, which represents the relative thickness of a liquid foam's films. Until now, the roughness factor has only been measured indirectly through the analysis of films' rheological properties in isolation. This study demonstrates that the roughness factor can be directly quantified by examining the collective behavior of a liquid foam as a whole, specifically through the interpretation of pressure-area isotherms, which reflect how air pressure affects the surface tension between film layers. By linking the bulk properties of a liquid foam to pressure-area isotherms, we are able to directly measure the roughness factor, providing a new perspective on the physics underlying the stability of liquid foams. This approach also allows us to differentiate between two previous hypotheses proposed to explain the relationship between the roughness factor and rheological properties of liquid films. Furthermore, by altering the composition of the liquid films, we are able to modify their roughness and viscosity, thus demonstrating the independent control of these properties. Finally, our research reveals that the stability of liquid foams is optimized when the roughness factor is in the range of 0.1 to 0.3, and that this factor has a significant impact on how liquid foams respond to external stresses, particularly in situations involving long-term forces. Additionally, we observe that the behavior of proteins on the surface of liquid films can be understood in a way that is independent of the proteins' specific functions, and that their stability is optimized when the surface pressure reaches a critical value related to the roughness factor. This study provides new insights into the physics governing the stability and behavior of liquid foams and has significant implications for a better understanding of biological systems that involve liquid films, including pulmonary surfactant, skin lubrication, and food foams. It also paves the way for the development of more realistic models that describe how liquid films respond to stress and pressure. These models are essential for predicting how biological systems that involve liquid films will behave in different scenarios and for designing strategies to improve their stability and function. In our research, we seek to enhance convolutional neural network (CNN) performance on image classification tasks. We investigate the benefits of ensemble learning, where multiple CNNs are trained to provide overlapping probability distributions, and subsequently select the most confident prediction from each estimator. Our studies indicate that in comparison to training a single, accurate CNN, ensemble learning yields superior results, outperforming CNNs with lower mean accuracy by up to 6%. Notably, we observe that the choice of selection strategy has a limited impact on overall results. Moreover, we find that using the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) method for prediction results in the best outcomes. We further explore applying ensemble learning to a well-performed pre-trained CNN, specifically BatchNorm-based CNN, and achieve remarkable success, obtaining an overall accuracy rate of 73.8% on the large-scale ImageNet dataset. Our work offers empirical evidence for the efficacy of ensemble learning in CNN-based image classification, and makes our code and data available for replication and further research. We have released our code and data according to the guidelines stated in the paper, and it is accessible on our project website.

We argue that the average change in microscopically defined internal energy reflects average changes in phase space, which are dictated by nonequilibrium drift forces. These forces drive the system toward equilibrium by reducing a nonequilibrium entropy rate. We demonstrate that the nonequilibrium entropy rate and microwork done per unit time are equivalent and vary among different nonequilibrium microstates. We further establish that the average nonequilibrium entropy rate and the average microwork done per unit time both equal the difference between the heat and heat flux. We then propose that the work done by the system on the surrounding environment be defined as the sum of the heat added and the change in average microwork done by the system. This definition aligns with the total entropy increase of the system and its surroundings. We apply this perspective to nonequilibrium chemical reactions, where the work done by reaction products is balanced by the work done on reactants. We also examine the case of a harmonic oscillator undergoing residual oscillations in the presence of damping. We introduce GraphMatérnGP, an efficient model that enables learning from multiple data sub-settings, without requiring posterior inference. By leveraging graph-based spatial structures and drawing from the wide range of Matérn Gaussian process models, GraphMatérnGP allows for multiple useful extensions, including multi-task and semi-supervised learning applications. We discuss how GraphMatérnGP can be applied in a non-conjugate setting, making it suitable for large-scale implementations, and further explore its capabilities in multi-task and semi-supervised learning scenarios through comprehensive experiments. We demonstrate the flexibility of GraphMatérnGP by employing it for the interpretation of complex deep neural networks. Our work provides a starting point for the exploration of graph-based Gaussian processes in deep learning, offering multiple practical applications and facilitating the development of new methodologies. Unlike conventional Gaussian process implementations, GraphMatérnGP enables efficient computation and easy integration with other models, and as such, it has already given rise to several novel multi-task Gaussian process models. Despite its efficiency, GraphMatérnGP's performance is on par with that of its conventional Gaussian process counterparts. We have publicly released the code and data associated with this project on the GraphMatérnGP GitHub site.

This coexistence state can be understood through a phase-plane analysis of a simplified system. The model and its results provide insights into the complex interactions between the host insects and the killing agents, offering a framework for exploring other similar host-killing agent interactions. To address this challenge, a novel method is proposed to estimate lateral displacements from ultrasound images using a deep generative adversarial network, specifically a GridGAN model. This model generates complete lateral velocity profiles from ultrasound data at specific axials, and includes an adversarial component to produce realistic outcomes based on medical expertise. A GridGAN model was developed and tested on simulated and real-world data, with the former demonstrating the benefit of adversarial components in output precision, and the latter yielding comparable results to axially estimated values from clinical trials. This method provides a new way to enhance elastography, and the code is available for other researchers to utilize. We challenge the long-held assumption that camera calibration requires specific image features and models. Instead, we suggest using a simple direct regression approach to bypass image processing. Our results show that this method competes with traditional methods and outperforms them in some cases. We successfully demonstrated this approach's effectiveness on multiple datasets, including the EPN, CMU, and CMU2 datasets. We achieved similar performance to traditional methods with direct regression on the EPN dataset and surpassed them on the CMU and CMU2 datasets. Our direct regression strategy consists of two parts: the initial estimation and refinement stages. We employed multiple models, including linear regression, LSTM, and CNN, and achieved the best results with a simple linear regression model in the initial estimation stage and CNN in the refinement stage. We introduced an innovative prediction approach, called the 'one step ahead' method, to enhance performance by incorporating previous predictions. Our results indicate that direct regression can compete with traditional methods and offers a more compact model with minimal components. This approach also facilitates better model generalizability and interpretability, ultimately providing a more straightforward camera calibration method. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexfeydi/Direct-Regression Camera Calibration.

This paper delves into the use of a specific generative adversarial network variant, the conditional Wasserstein GAN, for approximating Bayesian posterior distributions in image-related applications, like X-ray computed tomography image reconstruction. We introduce a regularized version of the CGAN, trained in a supervised manner, which enhances the network's performance by minimizing a weighted conditional Wasserstein distance, subject to an additional constraint ensuring a maximum variance when generating posterior samples. We evaluate our proposed method on synthetic CT images and show it outperforms state-of-the-art GAN-based algorithms, including the recent Bayesian GAN, both visually and numerically. Additionally, we explore the impact of the regularization parameter on the algorithm's effectiveness. Source code is available online.

This paper examines the concept of invariance in fractional order systems and establishes the requirements for linear subspaces to remain unaffected under the systems' dynamics. We demonstrate that the condition of invariance depends on the systems' dynamics and that this condition can be satisfied with different subspaces that include the original subspace. Furthermore, the paper discusses the role of the Mittag-Leffler function in analyzing system invariance and presents an alternative analysis method using Laplace transforms. We apply this analysis to a specific example, namely a mass-spring-dampener system, and explore the impact of system parameters on its invariance properties. The study also introduces the concept of discrete-time fractional systems and investigates the relationship between their continuous and discrete-time counterparts. We provide a condition for a discrete-time fractional system to have an invariant subspace that is also invariant in its continuous-time counterpart. This condition facilitates the implementation of discrete-time systems that maintain specific invariance properties. The study concludes by discussing potential applications and future research directions in the field of fractional order systems, including their interaction with nonlinear systems and the development of adaptive control methods. Annotating large sets of text documents for machine learning remains a challenging task due to its labor-intensive and time-consuming nature. Even with the most efficient annotation strategies, the process proves costly when dealing with extensive, publicly available datasets. In response, researchers have been exploring methods to automate or partially automate annotation by utilizing natural language processing techniques. In our work, we've developed an innovative approach called CoAnno, a concurrent annotation framework that enables a user to accurately annotate multiple text documents simultaneously. CoAnno leverages natural language understanding by incorporating a simple model that reflects the user's underlying knowledge and allows them to make informed annotations from the start. Furthermore, the framework includes a complex model that utilizes transfer learning and multi-task training to analyze annotated documents and derive generalizations for enhanced model performance. In our experiments, we observed a notable increase of up to 4.5 times in annotation speed without compromising model accuracy. Our results demonstrate the potential of CoAnno to streamline the annotation process while producing high-quality models for natural language processing tasks. The code for the CoAnno framework is now available on GitHub at https://github.co/username/CoAnno, and we've released the dataset used in our experiments at https://github.co/username/CoAnno-Dataset. The family of CoAnno models has been deployed on an inference server and is accessible through the CoAnno website at https://coanno.io. In addition, we've introduced the CoAnno Taskboard, a cloud-based platform for managing annotation tasks and model builds, along with the CoAnno Model Repository, where users can browse and build custom models from pre-trained benchmarks. Ultimately, we believe the CoAnno framework, along with the resources we've developed around it, will empower researchers and practitioners to achieve better annotation efficiency while producing top-notch models for natural language understanding. This study examines how the composition of gases like carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and ammonia varies in temperate planets' upper atmospheres, based on multiple scenarios of planetary systems. We test two cases: systems similar to our own, and systems with high metal content. Additionally, we consider different stellar energies and planetary masses. The findings indicate significant alterations to these gases' abundance levels, influenced by the system's characteristics. For example, increased metal content in the system leads to greater abundance of CO, CO2, and NH3, whereas greater planetary mass results in reduced abundance of these gases. The study also reveals that a planet with a highly conductive core, like Jupiter's, may offer a more suitable explanation for the observed amounts of these gases. The research further shows that atmospheric circulation patterns play a crucial role in shaping the upper atmosphere's gas composition, and that a stable planetary system may lead to visible spectral signatures of these gases. However, the study indicates that detection of these gases through space-based missions may be challenging, whereas a mission capable of observing during dawn and dusk hours may increase the chances of detection. The research suggests that exoplanets similar to Jupiter or Saturn could be identifiable through their atmospheric composition, whereas those like Uranus and Neptune may be more difficult to detect through this method. The study's results provide a foundation for investigating how these gases' abundance levels are maintained in temperate planets' upper atmospheres. Our study investigates the impact of finite temperature on zero-energy peaks resulting from non-Majorana behavior at the end of a semiconductor nanowire by incorporating outcomes from finite difference numerical simulations. At zero temperature, these peaks remain unchanged, but with increasing temperature, they become broadened and ultimately disappear due to the influence of spin polarization. The temperature at which the peak vanishes varies depending on the nanowire's stability at low energy and can be either before charge spillage occurs or after the peak has already faded. Furthermore, the temperature at which the peak disappears is found to be inversely proportional to the Fermi energy at the peak location. The origin of this behavior is attributed to the combination of the Fermi golden rule and the availability of energy states within the nanowire's Bessel function-based confinement model. Additionally, our findings are compared to experimental data and demonstrate that accounting for temperature effects provides a more accurate explanation for observed results than the conventional tunneling formula does. Nevertheless, this explanation may be further validated through additional simulation and experimental analysis. The presence of a wide range of states within the nanowire's energy spectrum also enables the peak's magnitude to be manipulated by adjusting the height of the Fermi sea, thereby allowing for the possibility of isolating signatures specific to non-Majorana behavior. Mobile data collection platforms are transforming the way roads are inspected by allowing field agents to share information directly with central authorities. However, these agencies still face the challenge of managing large amounts of data collected in real-time. To address this issue, we have developed RoadAtlas, a mobile data collection application that utilizes a spatial query engine to optimize location-based data collection for efficient road inspections. By organizing data collection into a hierarchical structure, based on geographical proximity, the system reduces data collection trips, minimizes mobile data traffic, and prioritizes data collection for quality control. Additionally, RoadAtlas generates interactive maps and reports to provide real-time feedback to field agents and central authorities. We tested the system's effectiveness by conducting a real-world trial with WakaGPS, New Zealand's road data collection platform. The results showed that RoadAtlas could collect same-day data for quality control, achieve a 30% reduction in data collection trips, and decrease mobile data traffic by 60%. Furthermore, the system enabled central authorities to identify and prioritize areas for quality control within 24 hours. Our findings demonstrate that RoadAtlas can significantly enhance the efficiency of road inspections and we believe the system's concepts can be applied to various location-based data collection scenarios. The system is available online at https://roadatlas.nz. The source code can be accessed through GitHub at https://github.com/WakaGPS/RoadAtlas. The system's development has resulted in significant contributions to the development of open-source spatial query engines and mobile data collection frameworks, which can be utilized for other location-based data collection domains. We have also incorporated several prominent mobile data collection platforms into the system, contributing the data models and methodologies to the relevant research communities. Ultimately, we are initiating the RoadAtlas initiative to foster collaboration and contribute the system's development as an open-source platform for the development of efficient location-based data collection systems. We invite participants to join the initiative and collaborate with us in enhancing the system and exploring its applications in various location-based data collection scenarios. Participants can engage with the initiative through the Google Group at https://groups.google.com/g/roadatlas. We look forward to collaborating with data collection agencies, mobile data collection platform developers, and the broader research community in shaping the future of the RoadAtlas initiative. We have already contributed the system to the New Zealand government's data collection agency, WakaGPS, and have initiated a national trial to further develop the system in conjunction with the agency. We have also contributed the system to the Eastern Regional Road Management (ERRM) system used in Eastern Australia.

This study extends topological Hochschild homology from its traditional base of structured rings to the more flexible framework of bicategorical constructions known as shadows. The key innovation involves proving that the refined HH functor, initially defined for structured rings by the first author, corresponds to a specific incarnation of topological Hochschild homology for shadows from the E_n singularity category. The refinement is crucial in establishing a direct relationship between HH and the functor computing the shadow. In addition, this research establishes a similar connection between the flat refined HH functor and the flat shadow from the E_2 singularity category, with the underlying ring replaced by the structure ring of a differential graded algebra. This relationship is then utilized to derive various consequences, including the determination of the shadow on the category of complexes over Z, and the computation of the derived functors of the flat refined Hochschild homology. The study also explores the interplay between topological Hochschild homology and the E_n singularity category, with specific results on the computation of shadows and derived functors for the E_2 singularity category. The paper concludes by establishing a refinement of the HH functor for shadows, and investigating its connection to the E_n singularity category. We introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 8057 sound source videos with diverse labels, used to evaluate the ability of models to identify sound sources from raw video frames. This benchmark, based on the MS-COCO framework, incorporates detailed object annotations that can be utilized for sound source separation and target localization. We create a new dataset called VGG-SS, which comprises 8057 video clips, incorporating 80 distinct sound source categories, by modifying the existing VGG-Sound dataset. Our dataset encompasses various challenging situations, such as overlapping targets, background noises, and camera movements. To evaluate the performance of models, we create multiple evaluation metrics including source segmentation, target localization, and sound source classification. To facilitate automated sound source classification from video clips, we also introduce a dataset of clip labels. The complete VGG-SS benchmark, including code, dataset, and evaluation metrics, is openly accessible at https://www.vggsound.org/ss.html. The dataset demonstrates significant differences from existing sound source classification datasets, which are characterized by simple annotations and limited overlap. Instead, VGG-SS is distinguished by complex annotations and a wide range of challenging scenarios. In conjunction with the release of the benchmark, we also introduce a novel multi-task model called Duo-Concurrent Sound Source Network, which incorporates concurrent model structures and produces source segmentation, target localization, and sound source classification outputs concurrently. The proposed model surpasses existing sound source classification methods with minimal training data and achieves superior performance on VGG-SS with extensive training data. The advancements made by the model on VGG-SS outperform previous achievements on VGG-Sound by a significant margin. The research on VGG-SS paves the way for further studies on automated sound source classification from raw video frames. Recently, hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (HGCNs) have gained popularity due to their ability to represent large-scale graphs efficiently. However, most existing HGCNs focus solely on node classification, neglecting the importance of node representation. This leads to a critical limitation, as model performance suffers from a lack of diverse node features. To address this limitation, we develop the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a novel hyperbolic graph neural network that enhances node features through a layer-wise representation learning approach. Notably, LGCN includes an attention mechanism in each layer, enabling it to learn a weight vector that identifies discriminative node attributes. By incorporating this attention mechanism, LGCN demonstrates superior performance over existing HGCNs on multiple benchmark datasets, as evidenced by our experimental results. Moreover, we provide a theoretical analysis of the rotation invariant property of LGCN and demonstrate the model's efficiency in node representation learning through a synthetic dataset. To facilitate reproducibility, the code for LGCN is available online. Generative adversarial models (GANs) have seen significant usage in medical imaging applications due to their ability to generate realistic, high-quality images. A key attribute of GANs, once learned, can be easily manipulated to change the characteristics of the images, such as shifting age or modifying a trait. This capability, known as latent code manipulation, enables new situations and goals to be achieved with only limited labeled data. However, the underlying representation of the code remains poorly understood, consistently presenting authors with unclear choices on how to structure it. In this work, we investigate the latent code structure in GANs for medical imaging applications by conducting an in-depth analysis of several popular GAN architectures, incorporating both theoretical and practical aspects. Our research involves conducting numerical experiments using both synthetic and real MRI data, which provided us with valuable insights into the structure of the code. Furthermore, our findings suggested that the representation becomes more linear with increasing depth, and this understanding can be utilized to enhance the performance of medical imaging GANs. In particular, we proposed a straightforward approach to modify the code structure, combining this with a method known as linear order preservation, that led to improved performance in several scenarios, including cases where the code needs to be extended to represent new conditions from a different distribution. Our results, achieved without any additional training, revealed a notable improvement of at least 5% in IS score on the MRI dataset. The code structure analysis facilitated another significant contribution of this work, enabling the introduction of a new challenge for medical code-conditioned image generation challenges. Advanced data visualization is crucial in exploring, checking, and communicating complex data dimensions.  Many organizations rely on Microsoft Excel, a popular and user-friendly data visualization tool, for this purpose.  However, Excel often uses incorrect measures of distance or contains misleading visuals due to its limitations in effectively representing high-dimensional data.  These shortcomings can result in inaccurate data interpretations and ultimately, poor decision-making.  To address these challenges, we present ViDaExpert, an interactive Excel add-in that utilizes visual comparisons to provide precise reductions in data dimensions, thereby ensuring reliable data interpretations.  ViDaExpert's user-friendly interface incorporates intuitive graphical displays, allowing users to easily understand the efficacy of its data reduction methods.  Furthermore, ViDaExpert incorporates a comparative technique, allowing users to visually assess the effectiveness of different data reduction approaches.  We demonstrate the advantages of ViDaExpert through a real-world application involving the analysis of credit risk data.  In this example, ViDaExpert's dimensionality reduction techniques are compared to the popular PCA method.  The findings, obtained through interactive visualization and a subsequent survey of experienced data analysts, reveal that ViDaExpert's recommended approaches result in the most accurate classification models.  Therefore, ViDaExpert can serve as an useful tool to guide Excel users in effectively visualizing and analyzing high-dimensional data sets. This research focuses on developing a high-order two-dimensional monomial approximation, similar to the approach created by IJsselmuiden and van der Valk, but with an adaptation for a third-order polynomial. The new method can be used to determine the coefficients that best fit a linear combination of a single mesh element's boundary and interior sample points. This technique is particularly suited for polynomial functions that contain terms up to the second order. However, researchers have discovered a novel method to approximate third-order polynomial functions by combining the previous approach with an alternative strategy. Although this method cannot be expressed through the standard finite element method, it offers a useful alternative for certain applications. Through various examples and assessments, it has been demonstrated that the proposed method successfully reproduces high-order polynomial functions over a single mesh element with a high degree of accuracy. In specific cases, a very precise approximation was achieved – essentially exact up to machine precision. This research also explores the impact of increasing the degree of polynomial functions on the accuracy of the approximation and investigates how the method performs under different orientation and rotation scenarios. Finally, this study showcases the ability to accurately approximate linear and quadratic finite element functions through inter-element extrapolation. This involves using function values from a single mesh element to accurately reconstruct the global representation across an entire element. The success of this research has significant implications for the development of more efficient algorithms in the field of computational physics and will play a crucial role in enhancing the performance of direct numerical simulation of fluid dynamics. This could result in a significant reduction in computational time and ultimately a substantial increase in the simulation of observable events within the next decade. This progress will be achieved without the need for a massive increase in processing power, but rather through the improvement of existing algorithms and the introduction of new and innovative techniques. This study is a crucial step towards this goal and lays the groundwork for further research into the expansion of this method to a broader range of applications. This could include exploring alternatives to the least-squares approach when determining the best-fitting coefficients, developing a more efficient implementation, and investigating the potential for the method to be incorporated into popular computational fluid dynamics frameworks. Additionally, future work could see the introduction of new monomial approximation approaches, the development of a higher-order version capable of handling fifth-order polynomials, and the introduction of a symbolically-defined interface for custom-made polynomial functions. This would allow for the derivation of analytical expressions for extrapolated inter-element functions, enabling significant improvements to the accuracy of approximation.
